objectives: 136. The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to ensure the full implementation of sanctions regimes concerning Da’esh, Al-Qaida and the Taliban, which include targeted arms embargoes, asset freezes and travel bans.
strategy:
137. To contribute to the objective, the Monitoring Team will provide updated information to the Security Council, the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions Committee and the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1988 (2011).

139. performance.title: National police authorities improved police performance and enhanced security in Haiti
performance.narrative:
In 2025, BINUH provided daily strategic and operational advice to Haitian National Police (HNP) and the Penitentiary Administrative Directorate (DAP) on critical policing matters, including anti-gang and anti-kidnapping operations, intelligence, election security, judicial police, criminal investigations, weapons and ammunition management, gender equality, legal framework, and police integrity and oversight. Additional support was provided to the Command, Control, Communication and Intelligence Centre, the Directorate of the Strategic Planning and Development for the preparation of the next HNP Strategic Development Plan, a fundamental planning and operational guide which directs the development targets for the HNP on a 5 year horizon, accompanied by diagnostic forums and meetings with participation of HNP and international partners, as the first step toward formulating the new strategic plan.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 60).

planned.narrative:
In 2025, the mission supported and undertook advocacy, outreach, dialogue facilitation, technical advice, and good offices actions to advance the political and electoral processes, sustaining and supporting the complex political process in Haiti. The fragmentation of the political and social landscape, with more than 300 political parties officially registered, required BINUH to facilitate consultations in Port-au-Prince and Cap Haïtien, which brought together civil society organizations, political parties, and private sector representatives, including the participation of women and youth.
BINUH provided advice and guidance to the Haitian Provisional Electoral Council, specifically on the electoral legal framework and inclusion of women in the electoral process. BINUH coordinated the effort of the UN and international partners to ensure a coherent and well-coordinated approach recommended by the 2024 needs assessment mission.

31.III.10 In the context of sustained financial constraints across the United Nations system, coordinated action was undertaken to safeguard mandate delivery and operational integrity. To harness the collective strength of the United Nations system for transformative change, the High-level Committee on Management launched far-reaching efficiency initiatives designed to simplify, integrate and modernize core business operations. In 2025, the Committee rapidly converged on priority areas in relation to procurement and supply chains, finance, human resources, digital foundations and shared services, which demonstrated the potential to reduce fragmentation and cost and to unlock efficiencies at scale. As a dynamic set of solutions, the far-reaching efficiency initiatives help find efficiencies, avoid duplication and ensure that United Nations system organizations stay focused on delivering on their mandates in the most efficient and effective way possible.

overview.name: United Nations support for the Cameroon-Nigeria Mixed Commission
objectives: The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to achieve an orderly and peaceful implementation of the judgment of 10 October 2002 of the International Court of Justice delineating the course of the land and maritime boundary between Cameroon and Nigeria.

performance.title: Political commitment to continued dialogue to resolve remaining disagreement areas
performance.narrative:
In 2025, the mission continued its collaboration with the parties to resolve the three long-standing areas of disagreement. As a result, various meetings were held, including the Sub-Commission on Demarcation meetings in Dakar and Geneva, as well as the Project Steering Committee meeting in Geneva. These sessions resolved the three remaining areas of disagreement, resulting in an agreement on the full land boundary and laying the groundwork for completing the demarcation process. Key outcomes also included the adoption of the provisional boundary line and coordinates, and the terms of reference for a field assessment mission collectively known as the “Geneva Agreement, 2025.” The field assessment mission was conducted at the end of the reporting period, with its report scheduled for adoption by the Sub-Commission in January 2026.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 19).

planned.title: land and boundaries demarcated and accepted by both States in a peaceful and orderly fashion
planned.narrative:
In 2025, preparations for the final phase of the boundary pillar construction were completed, with the revised plan increasing the total number of pillars from 230 to 410 to reflect higher population density along the boundary. As a result, overall project completion is now estimated at 86 per cent, compared with 91 per cent in 2024. Construction activities planned for 2025 were deferred due to delays in resolving outstanding disagreements and have been rescheduled for 2026 in accordance with the Geneva Agreement.
Further efforts were carried out in partnership with the United Nations country teams in Cameroon and Nigeria to jointly develop and consolidate needs assessment reports to support confidence-building initiatives for communities affected by the demarcation process.
The mission learned that the Chair’s bilateral engagement with delegation leaders accelerated consensus and fostered cooperation. Building on this, it will increase high-level meetings with State leaders and technical experts, supported by community sensitization, coordinated political, technical, and security efforts, and strong UN country team partnerships to finalize Cameroon–Nigeria demarcation. The Mixed Commission will continue implementing security measures and raising awareness among local authorities and communities to ensure safe access and reduce risks at pillar sites.

overview.name: Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate
objectives: 268. The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to enhance Member States’ counter-terrorism legislation and policies, institutions and operations by ensuring the full and effective implementation by Member States of Security Council resolution 1373 (2001) and other relevant Council resolutions, to inform the efforts of United Nations entities and other implementing agencies to provide related capacity-building and technical assistance and to analyse new and emerging terrorism threats, trends and challenges.

performance.title: Road maps to improve the capacity of Member States to counter terrorism and violent extremism conducive to terrorism
performance.narrative:
276. In 2025, the Committee adopted reports on visits to ten States (Canada, Ecuador, Kazakhstan, Malta, Mauritania, Montenegro, Malawi, Tanzania, Thailand and Turkmenistan). The Executive Directorate completed five overview of implementation assessments and electronic detailed implementation surveys. It also facilitated technical assistance and developed eight road maps for select beneficiaries as part of several capacity-building programmes spearheaded by the Office of Counter-Terrorism to enhance Member States’ compliance with relevant Security Council resolutions and international standards. For instance, CTED led capacity consultations under the UN Countering Terrorist Travel Programme to help increase implementation of advance passenger information (API) and passenger name records (PNR) pursuant to Security Council resolution 2396 (2017) and ICAO standards. In 2025, CTED led seven national consultations on API/PNR, bringing the total number of Member States assessed to 49. The positive impact can be illustrated with the latest reporting of Member States using goTravel (the software provided under the Programme) who reported a significant number of hits in their passenger information units. These hits are generated through the systematic screening of API and PNR data against targeting rules as well as watchlists and law-enforcement databases. All these hits would have gone unnoticed without the capabilities that CT Travel has built in beneficiary Member States. Another Member State developed a roadmap under the Global Programme on Countering Terrorist Threats against Vulnerable Targets.
277. Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see figure V).

The target was not met owing to a combination of factors, including inadequate staffing. The Executive Directorate nevertheless provided advice on several thematic areas such as border control and law enforcement, human rights and countering the financing of terrorism, including the adoption of two non-binding guiding principles: “Algeria Guiding Principles” on preventing, detecting and disrupting the use of new and emerging financial technologies for terrorist purposes, and “Valletta Principles on National and Regional Counter-Terrorism Strategies”. The Executive Directorate continued to advance its mandates on countering the financing of terrorism, as outlined in Security Council resolution 2462 (2019) and other relevant resolutions. CFT priorities were integrated across CTED’s assessment activities and informed the design of targeted technical assistance by implementing partners.

It will further enhance the use of its overview of implementation assessment and electronic detailed implementation surveys data to identify emerging trends and issue technical guidance.

entities.name: Department of Economic and Social Affairs
priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
9.3 The world continues to suffer setbacks in development progress, characterized by heightened global challenges, including climate change, debt distress and high and rising inequalities. These are now further compounded by policy uncertainty, financial volatility, growing fragmentation and weakening international development cooperation. Countries in special situations, including the least developed countries, landlocked developing countries and small island developing States, remain particularly challenged. Middle-income countries still face challenges in achieving sustainable development.
9.4 Amid these challenges, a coherent and integrated approach in support of Member States is critical to accelerate progress in achieving the Goals.
9.5 The Department continues to champion synergistic, future-focused approaches to sustainable development, addressing multiple, interlinked challenges to improve the lives and livelihoods of all people. This includes its work on climate action, sustainable infrastructure investment and risk-informed development cooperation. The Department continues to adapt its work to address the rapidly changing global policy landscape.
9.6 The Department deploys foresight to anticipate economic, social and population trends. It generates, analyses and compiles a wide range of data and statistics to inform Member States and other stakeholders as they take stock of policy options to address global trends.
9.7 The Department identifies emerging trends and policy options for eradicating poverty, addressing climate change and inequalities and promoting opportunities for global progress.
9.8 In 2027, the Department will intensify its intergovernmental, analytical and capacity-development efforts to support Member States for the 2027 Sustainable Development Goals Summit, focusing on accelerating progress towards the Goals in a rapidly changing global policy environment shaped by rising uncertainty and fragmentation. Core areas of delivery include the implementation of the Sevilla Commitment, with an emphasis on mobilizing development financing, reforming the international financial architecture and improving international tax cooperation; the follow-up to the Doha Political Declaration of the “World Social Summit” and the Pact for the Future; support for the General Assembly review of the Economic and Social Council and the high-level political forum on sustainable development processes; and the strengthening of data systems and evidence for monitoring the Goals through capacity development. The Department will continue to provide strategic substantive support to the resident coordinator system and United Nations country teams, enhancing national implementation of internationally agreed objectives, with a focus on countries in Africa and countries in special situations. It will also support development cooperation with middle-income countries, in accordance with its mandate.
9.9 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Department contributes to building multi-stakeholder partnerships and capacity development in thematic areas, including forests, natural resources, water, energy, climate, the ocean, transport, science and technology, and special concerns of small island developing States.
9.10 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Department continues to support the quadrennial comprehensive policy review of operational activities for development of the United Nations system, in collaboration with United Nations system entities and the United Nations Sustainable Development Group. In collaboration with the Development Coordination Office, the Department facilitates structured engagement with resident coordinators strengthening delivery of capacity-building activities. These efforts help to translate global norms and policy frameworks into national action towards the 2030 Agenda and other internationally agreed objectives. Moreover, the Department, through the expanded Executive Committee on Economic and Social Affairs Plus, promotes common approaches and synergies that support the implementation of the 2030 Agenda, including through the voluntary national reviews and reporting on progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Furthermore, the Department continues to work with various agencies and stakeholders to improve policy analysis and knowledge products for Member States. To ensure coherence within and across topic areas, the Department continues to chair or co-chair inter-agency mechanisms for persons with disabilities, Indigenous Peoples, older persons and young people, legal identity, financing for development, statistics, and science, technology and innovation, among others. Moreover, the United Nations Economists’ Network continues to advance policy research on key current and emerging economic and financial issues, and their impact on sustainable development.
9.11 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Continued cooperation with policymakers and relevant national, regional and international stakeholders and entities on sustainable development issues in the various intergovernmental processes;
(b) Continued availability of up-to-date and accurate information, data and trends for analytical products;
(c) Recognition of the need for mitigation measures to address risks posed by growing policy uncertainty and fragmentation.
9.12 The Department integrates a gender perspective into its normative and analytical work and its support for intergovernmental bodies, including in its programme activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. It continues to apply gender analysis in its work and highlight issues related to gender equality in the substantive documentation and deliberations of intergovernmental bodies, as appropriate.
9.13 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Department promotes inclusive sustainable development for all, including persons with disabilities, and realizes the promise of the 2030 Agenda to leave no one behind. As secretariat to the Conference of States Parties to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, the Department facilitates global dialogue to address existing gaps in translating international commitments to persons with disabilities into development policies, programming and practices at the national and international levels. This includes the compilation and analysis of disability data and the highlighting of best practices for fostering more accessible, disability-inclusive societies.

9.24 The tenth anniversary of the 2030 Agenda was a critical juncture for Member States and stakeholders, who marked the occasion with productive and meaningful dialogue, engagement in intergovernmental decision-making and contributions to renewed political commitment for the Sustainable Development Goals. The subprogramme supported the Economic and Social Council, including its various segments and forums, and the high-level political forum on sustainable development. The subprogramme organized the 2025 high-level political forum, bringing together more than 6,000 participants, including more than 800 stakeholder representatives, reviewed progress and policy options for accelerating progress on the Goals under review (Goals 3, 5, 8, 14 and 17) and provided a platform for 35 voluntary national reviews.

9.43 The Madrid International Plan of Action on Ageing, adopted in 2002, provides a framework of commitments and policy approaches related to population ageing and older persons. Its implementation is reviewed every five years. Participation in that review ensures that national policies and strategies are evaluated through a bottom-up, participatory process involving older persons. By identifying policy gaps and priority actions, the review process supports more effective national responses that directly affect the well-being and quality of life of older persons. The subprogramme has supported Member States’ review of the Madrid Plan of Action through analytical work and capacity-building.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: Member States implement the System of National Accounts 2025
planned.narrative:
9.69 The Statistical Commission adopted the System of National Accounts 2025 as an international statistical standard, following four years of concerted efforts by the global statistical community to update the System of National Accounts 2008. The System of National Accounts 2025 reflects changes in the global economy and addresses user demands for better information about well-being and sustainability. In its resolution 2025/12, the Economic and Social Council recommended that Member States use the System of National Accounts 2025 in their international reporting, while the Statistical Commission endorsed its implementation strategy, with a 2029–2030 target date. The subprogramme will continue its support to Member States that have not yet implemented the System of National Accounts 2008, which is a prerequisite for the implementation of the System of National Accounts 2025. Given that countries that have not yet implemented the System of National Accounts 2008 face more significant challenges in doing so, supporting them will require more time and greater effort. As a result, it may not be possible to achieve implementation of the System of National Accounts 2008 in more than 17 countries in the reporting period.
Lessons learned and planned change
9.70 The lesson for the subprogramme was that the broad and intensive collaboration of all stakeholders enabled the successful updating of the System of National Accounts 2008. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will use its ability to bring together all stakeholders during the implementation of the System of National Accounts 2025, ensuring that Member States have the capacity to produce national accounts in line with the updated standard.

The subprogramme assisted Member States by developing online courses on the overlapping generations model and the climate, land, energy and water systems model, enhancing their ability to analyse complex interlinkages across macroeconomic, microeconomic and resource management frameworks. In addition, the subprogramme facilitated the use of the upgraded mobile application-based ePing alert system, which provides Governments and stakeholders with real-time notifications on trade-related measures. The Committee for Development Policy triennial review process, which identifies graduation eligibility, and the Committee’s enhanced monitoring mechanism for graduating and graduated countries provide a coherent and long-term framework for Member States to ensure sustainable graduation. The subprogramme has strengthened Member States’ knowledge on this topic and their policymaking capacity by improving data accuracy, enhancing economic analysis and fostering deeper engagement with the countries concerned.

9.96 The lesson for the subprogramme was that greater emphasis is needed on early engagement with potentially graduating countries and on tailoring analytical support to their specific development contexts and economic structures. This requires complex analysis of development data and processes, as well as meaningful dialogue with national stakeholders to ensure ownership and effective follow-up. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will continue to customize its approach to forecasting and its policy recommendations on structural transformation to the needs of graduating countries and will continue to support those countries in developing the skills to manage and analyse their own data for future analysis post-graduation.

performance.title: Supreme audit institutions assessed the implementation of Sustainable Development Goal 13 on climate action
performance.narrative:
9.102 Supreme audit institutions are uniquely positioned to strengthen climate action under Sustainable Development Goal 13 through independent audits and assessments. The subprogramme provided technical assistance to 18 supreme audit institutions, led by the Federal Court of Accounts of Brazil, to develop a standardized methodology and web-based tool, ClimateScanner, for assessing government actions and progress in addressing adverse impacts of climate change. This included peer learning among supreme audit institutions, experience-sharing on auditing climate action and discussions of the roll-out of these assessments, which involved auditors from several countries, including least developed countries and small island developing States. The assessments identified constraints, key risks and priority areas in governance, finance and public policy related to climate change. The findings are aimed at helping Governments to improve climate action and at accelerating the implementation of Goal 13 at the national level. The results were presented at the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change in 2024 and 2025.

2.36 The subprogramme planned and coordinated 17 major conferences and meetings held away from Headquarters in 2025, compared with 13 in 2024 and 12 in 2023. 2.37 The planning and coordination teams at the four conference-servicing duty stations collaborated closely to ensure effective and efficient resource allocation and service delivery. Dedicated sections for each conference away from Headquarters were created in the Journal of the United Nations in all official languages. These included information on side events and special events that facilitated multi-stakeholder engagement. The subprogramme also coordinated and facilitated many bilateral meetings among the Member States and other key stakeholders held on the margin of the conferences. The arrangement of such meetings was supported by the conference management systems developed and utilized by the subprogramme at all four duty stations, including the gMeets portal.

performance.title: Timely issuance of documentation sustained, notwithstanding constraints
performance.narrative:
2.50 The subprogramme faced exceptional challenges in 2025. Not only did the liquidity constraints prevent it from employing external capacity to supplement internal teams during workload surges, unexpected additional workload, such as the extra 340,000 words submitted in New York in relation to the revised estimates relating to the proposed programme budget for 2026 and support account for peacekeeping operations for the 2025/26 period and the 90,000 words associated with the new Intergovernmental Science-Policy Panel on Chemicals, Waste and Pollution established in Nairobi, significantly increased the pressure on documentation services at all duty stations.
2.51 The subprogramme responded by making every effort to maximize internal capacity, working closely with planning and coordination colleagues to determine processing priorities and proactively with author departments and submitting entities to clarify substantive or terminology matters, thus saving processing time. In Vienna, such efforts enabled six resolutions and seven decisions at the sixty-eighth session of the Commission on Narcotic Drugs to be delivered in time for the votes. Workload was also shared to the extent possible. The subprogramme in Geneva, for example, translated the pre-session documentation for the International Law Commission previously translated in New York.
2.52 These actions, together with the flexibility and professionalism of staff, ensured that, notwithstanding the liquidity constraints, Member States continued to receive high-quality documentation in a timely manner, with global timely issuance being 93 per cent in 2025, compared with 92 per cent in 2023 and 2024 (see figure 2.VI).

planned.title: equal treatment of official languages upheld
planned.narrative:
2.58 The simultaneous issuance of high-quality parliamentary documentation in the official languages is essential to support the intergovernmental process and uphold the Department’s multilingualism mandate. Given the challenges facing the language services, such as capacity imbalances stemming from uneven retirements that are compounded by the Organization’s financial situation, which limits the subprogramme’s ability to hire external capacity, simultaneous issuance has become increasingly difficult. In this regard, the Department has consistently leveraged new technologies, including neural machine translation, to increase efficiency while investing in staff and providing them with the necessary skills and tools, given that technologies in and of themselves cannot ensure the level of accuracy required of parliamentary documentation. The subprogramme therefore explored opportunities offered by cross-functional teams, contributing to the revision of generic job profiles, and implemented knowledge-sharing platforms, improved workload-sharing processes and adopted new internal working methods across the four duty stations. This work has helped to sustain quality and productivity, resolve bottlenecks during peak periods and ensure the simultaneous issuance of high-quality documentation.
Lessons learned and planned change
2.59 The lesson for the subprogramme was that, while technology improved efficiency, human expertise continued to be needed to ensure accuracy, completeness and correct terminology use. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will continue to implement upskilling programmes to enhance the ability to understand, use and evaluate artificial intelligence technologies, provide continuous learning opportunities and support operational and collaborative resilience in a context of continuous change, development and modernization.

performance.title: Quality maintained and efficiencies generated for meeting organizers through integrated global management of interpretation resources
performance.narrative:
2.65 The application of the proximity rule, whereby, to the extent possible, meeting services, including interpretation, are provided by the closest duty station to reduce the associated travel costs, plays a key role in reducing the outlays associated with meetings and conferences held away from Headquarters. The notional savings for the organizers of such events were $839,244 in 2023 and $1,057,063 in 2024, of which $705,426 and $1,013,393, respectively, corresponded to interpretation.
2.66 Effective integrated global planning and management of interpretation capacity at the four conference-servicing duty stations, in coordination with subprogramme 2, enabled the subprogramme to continue to support the application of the proximity rule. Staff also supported operational continuity by scheduling leave predominantly during off-peak periods, thereby helping to maintain adequate coverage during periods of high demand. Overall, those collective efforts enabled the subprogramme to sustain high-quality interpretation services across a demanding and geographically diverse meeting calendar and generate notional savings associated with interpretation of $754,200 in 2025.

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
28.2 The overall programme plan for 2027 reflects the Department’s strategy to strengthen support for the work and purposes of the United Nations by engaging with audiences and encouraging them to act, through impactful storytelling and a focus on solutions. The Department takes the following core approaches in its work: strategic planning by identifying communications goals and target audiences; maintaining close working relationships with stakeholders, offices of the Secretariat, entities of the United Nations system and other key partners; enhancing audience reach through multilingualism and the parity of all six official languages in the preparation of news and communications products, including content on United Nations websites and social media accounts; targeted use of social and digital media to deliver information directly and instantaneously to key audiences; and measuring the impact of campaigns in order to improve the Department’s work.
28.3 The Department delivers strategic communications campaigns to engage and inspire target audiences. It works through a global network of United Nations information centres, integrated with United Nations resident coordinator offices, to reach local audiences and provide content for global platforms. It produces accurate, objective and balanced multilingual news and communications products that convey authoritative information and solutions-based stories. It advocates on priority issues with Member States, civil society, academia, the media, young people and other partners. The Department contributes to the observance of international days and celebrations established by the General Assembly.
28.4 The Department also provides services to delegates and staff, including through the Dag Hammarskjöld Library, and promotes internal knowledge-sharing and communication by way of iSeek, the United Nations intranet.
28.5 The Department continues to place information integrity at the centre of its work and is committed to increasing access to relevant, reliable and accurate information and knowledge. In an age when misinformation, disinformation, hate speech and other content inciting harm are disseminated, the Department works towards advancing the United Nations Global Principles for Information Integrity and relevant commitments in the Pact for the Future and the Global Digital Compact throughout its work.
28.6 The Department will lead and coordinate crisis communications by strengthening the United Nations response through aligned messaging and mitigating risk by continuing to develop guidance on crisis communications.
28.7 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Department will leverage partnerships, including from the media, civil society, academia, the creative industry, the sports community and other representatives of the private sector, to enhance its ability to target and deliver information to an even wider community, with a focus on young people around the world.
28.8 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Department will strengthen the coordination of communications across the United Nations system, including through United Nations communications groups at the country and regional levels. Coordination will also be strengthened through the integration of United Nations information centres with resident coordinator offices and by streamlining processes and information-sharing. The Department will continue its work with the Development Coordination Office to provide strategic communications support to resident coordinators in countries without an information centre presence to ensure that information is widely disseminated.
28.9 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) All stakeholders and partners fulfil their responsibilities and obligations under service agreements and partnerships;
(b) Access by target audiences to programmes, products and services is not limited by communications technology, security or infrastructure conditions.
28.10 The Department integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. For example, the Department will promote the balanced presence of women and men in all its products, campaigns, events and activities.
28.11 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Department will use its network of focal points to help to develop a common and coordinated approach to making United Nations services and activities accessible for persons with disabilities. The focal points will provide communications support to the Strategy, including by setting accessibility standards for United Nations websites.

performance.title: Strengthened public engagement on United Nations priority issues
performance.narrative:
28.22 In its resolution 80/84 B, the General Assembly stressed the primary mission of the Department in providing accurate, impartial, comprehensive, balanced, timely, relevant and multilingual information to the public on the tasks and responsibilities of the United Nations in order to strengthen international support for the activities of the Organization. To diversify the United Nations presence on various social media platforms amid the changing social media landscape and to reach wider audiences, especially in countries and regions with lower Internet bandwidth, the subprogramme opened a pilot WhatsApp channel in French in May 2024 that provided information on global priority issues and the work of the United Nations. By the end of 2024, the channel had gained more than half a million followers. Building on that success, in 2025 the subprogramme established additional channels in Arabic, English, Hindi and Portuguese, almost quadrupling follower numbers to 2.1 million by the end of 2025. United Nations information centres played a pivotal role in amplifying the reach and impact of those channels by actively promoting them through their local networks. They leveraged their on-the-ground presence to help to engage communities on global priority issues such as climate action, sustainable development, human rights and peace and security through WhatsApp channels in five languages. That innovative approach strengthened public engagement and fostered greater understanding of the work of the United Nations among diverse audiences worldwide.

The subprogramme also continued to issue the Sustainable Development Goal “Goal of the Month” newsletter and the United Nations LinkedIn newsletter. During 2023 and 2024, the Sustainable Development Goal and LinkedIn newsletters built a combined subscriber base of more than 1.9 million, creating a strong foundation for direct engagement. performance.title: Increased public reach on United Nations news coverage
performance.narrative:
28.35 In 2025, UNifeed played a critical role in expanding global access to high-quality United Nations news content. As the video syndication service for more than 40 United Nations system partners, UNifeed supplied international broadcasters with timely coverage on climate action, peacekeeping, human rights, development issues and global economic and social conditions. It also provided essential reporting on major crises. UNifeed’s unique access to United Nations agencies and personnel on the ground enabled the production of exclusive material that became a primary content pipeline for leading global media organizations, further strengthened through its distribution partnerships with the Associated Press and Reuters. Beyond major broadcasters, UNifeed proved especially valuable for journalists and outlets with limited resources, offering free, reliable and ready-to-use video reporting that supported their ability to cover international developments. Outlets using UNifeed materials included major global networks such as Al Ghad Al Arabi, Al Jazeera, ABC Australia, BBC, CNN, CCTV, CNBC, Deutsche Welle, Euronews, France 24, Globo, RAI and TRT World, among many others, demonstrating both strong demand and extensive geographical reach. Monitoring data confirmed broad global distribution of usage by major media outlets, underscoring UNifeed’s continued role as a trusted, high-impact source of United Nations news content. The use of UNifeed material has been growing steadily in recent years. In 2025, the number of broadcasters using UNifeed material increased by 107 compared with the previous year, an increase of 5.35 per cent, and the largest annual increase over the past three years.

performance.title: Strengthened global support and action for the work of the United Nations
performance.narrative:
28.48 Under the theme “United for a Better Future”, the United Nations participated in Expo 2025 in Osaka, Japan, held from 13 April to 13 October 2025. The Department coordinated the United Nations pavilion, which showcased the work of 35 United Nations entities and 15 Secretariat departments and offices. Over six months, the United Nations pavilion welcomed 406,828 visitors and presented the Organization’s 80-year efforts in advancing peace and security, human rights, sustainable development and climate action. Through interactive installations, visitors also learned how the work of the Organization continued to benefit the Earth and populations around the world. As part of the visitor experience, a six-minute immersive film was screened that illustrated a vision for a peaceful, prosperous and sustainable future that can be achieved through collective action. In addition to the permanent exhibits, the pavilion also featured 24 rotating weekly exhibitions and 54 events across priority thematic areas, including the “United Nations Special Day”, on 22 August, with the participation of the Secretary-General. A visitor survey conducted at the pavilion, completed by more than 150,000 respondents, demonstrated a notable positive shift in visitors’ perceptions of the United Nations.

28.54 Guided tours at United Nations Headquarters educate the public on global issues, foster understanding of the Organization’s work and offer a unique, multilingual perspective on international cooperation. Thematic guided tours were introduced during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic to broaden the portfolio of offerings available at a time when schools were closed and educators required additional online resources to engage and inform students. During the suspension of in-person tour operations, tour guides and visitor services staff were able to devote increased time to the development of new content and visual materials. Initially launched in a virtual format, the thematic tours were subsequently adapted for in-person delivery when operations resumed in April 2022. The current thematic tour portfolio encompasses curated tours on art, architecture, the garden, women’s contributions to the work of the United Nations, Black history and a dedicated children’s tour. Since 2023, all thematic tours have recorded a steady increase in participation.
Lessons learned and planned change
28.55 The lesson for the subprogramme was that diversifying the guided tour portfolio not only attracted new audiences with specific thematic interests, but also promoted repeat visits from clients seeking a different United Nations experience. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will promote and grow the popular thematic tours and explore the introduction of additional thematic tours on new themes.

objectives: 29A.57 The objective, to which this component contributes, is to secure the financing of the Organization’s expenses, pursuant to Article 17 of the Charter of the United Nations, and to ensure sound, effective and efficient integrated financial management of and reporting on United Nations resources, supported by a strong internal control environment.

performance.title: Improved access to consolidated cost-recovery information for decision-making by Secretariat entities
performance.narrative:
29A.60 Cost-recovery activities across the Secretariat are recorded across multiple Umoja modules, including funds management, accounts receivable, general ledger, controlling, sales and distribution, and payroll. The absence of integrated reporting meant that entities relied on fragmented data sources and manual extraction, making it difficult to efficiently monitor fund balances, track revenue, assess receivables or evaluate performance. Following repeated recommendations from oversight bodies for strengthened monitoring, the component led a multi-year effort culminating in 2025 with the deployment of a cost-recovery dashboard in Umoja Analytics. The dashboard integrates data across six modules into a single platform, providing consolidated analysis of fund balance movements, revenue by client and cost-recovery method, receivables ageing and payment patterns, and budget consumption against revenue and cash collected. The Assistant Secretary-General for Programme Planning, Finance and Budget, Controller, as well as heads of entities, service providers and clients can now access streamlined, actionable cost-recovery insights from their own operational perspective, replacing what previously required consulting multiple disconnected reports.
29A.61 Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 29A.15).

performance.title: Addressing interpersonal, institutional, and systemic forms of racism in the Organization

29A.139 The subprogramme continued to implement the series of initiatives that had been launched to target interpersonal, institutional and systemic forms of racism within the Organization. The subprogramme convened the inaugural United Nations Conference on Addressing Racism and Promoting Dignity for All at the Secretariat in June 2025; continued entity-level engagement through dialogues, conversations and town hall meetings; and launched the Secretariat’s first online course entitled “Addressing racism and racial discrimination in the workplace” in English and French. The subprogramme made structural advances through the completion of a framework for the collection of race-related data, in line with General Assembly resolution 78/253. The subprogramme also worked to strengthen accountability mechanisms through progress on amending the Secretary-General’s bulletin on addressing discrimination, harassment, including sexual harassment, and abuse of authority (ST/SGB/2019/8), planned to be promulgated in 2026, to include racial discrimination as prohibited conduct.

priorities: Effective functioning of the organization

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
29B.2 In 2027, the Department will continue to support effective mandate implementation through the delivery of operational support. In executing its programme, the Department will partner with client entities to identify needs and jointly develop solutions, including in the areas of end-to-end supply chain management, support for uniformed personnel, human resources, a broad range of training services, business process improvement, medical and occupational health and safety, and information and communications technology services delivered through the Office of Information and Communications Technology. In exceptional circumstances, the Department will exercise delegated authority on behalf of client entities across the Secretariat. The Department will lead the implementation of the common administrative platform at Headquarters in New York, providing support to some 50 entities and their personnel in New York and, to various extents, their personnel located outside New York. The Department will also provide advisory support to guide the implementation of the common administrative platform in Bangkok and the establishment of additional common administrative platforms in Addis Ababa, Beirut, Geneva, Nairobi and Vienna.
29B.3 The Department will seek to strike an appropriate balance between direct service delivery and advisory support, adapting its approach to diverse client requirements and promoting a positive client experience. It will adapt its planning to anticipate and respond to changes in the operating environment, fostering a culture that is agile, responsive and forward-looking. The Department will also leverage technology, automation, innovation and high-quality data to simplify and streamline processes. In addition, it will assist relevant Secretariat actors in integrating positive legacy considerations into the planning and management of United Nations operations, including facilities, infrastructure and services, to maximize potential secondary benefits for host communities.
29B.4 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Department will strengthen collaboration with Member States and regional organizations, including through capacity-building initiatives, knowledge-sharing and functional arrangements across areas of operational support, with a view to achieving the scale and effectiveness required to address complex operational challenges.
29B.5 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Department will further advance its operating model for the provision of a comprehensive range of services within and beyond the United Nations Secretariat, guided by comparative advantage. In doing so, it will lead and coordinate a network of service providers, where the Department focuses its own efforts on enhancing service delivery and overall effectiveness.
29B.6 With regard to the external factors, the Department considered applicable risks identified in its risk register, and, accordingly, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) There is adequate support from relevant stakeholders to enable the delivery of effective operational support solutions in challenging operating environments;
(b) Requirements for crisis response and other special situations will not exceed the Department’s capacity to respond.
29B.7 The Department integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. For example, activities will include camp design methodologies, improvements in the area of women’s health, staffing initiatives such as the senior women talent pipeline, and advice to field entities, upon request, to enable them to meet targets related to gender parity. In order to encourage a more equitable approach to the Organization’s supply chain, the Department will continue to strengthen outreach and training for vendors, including women-owned businesses.
29B.8 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Department will support efforts to improve accessibility for persons with disabilities to the United Nations premises, to enable their full, meaningful and effective participation in the work of the United Nations, as outlined in result 3 under subprogramme 4. In addition, the Department will enhance accessibility for persons with disabilities to its training materials developed under subprogramme 1 component 2, and will further integrate disability inclusion across its global procurement activities, including through targeted outreach to disability-inclusive vendors under subprogramme 2, component 1.

planned.title: enhanced recruitment of gratis personnel
planned.narrative:
29B.26 The recruitment and nomination process for gratis personnel (gratis personnel type II and experts on non-reimbursable loan) relies on paper-based workflows, which create inefficiencies and lack transparency. Individual entities reach out to Member States separately by email, resulting in fragmented communication, limited visibility of opportunities and delays in processing nominations and resumes. The component has undertaken measures to streamline and modernize the process. Efforts have focused on identifying bottlenecks in the existing system and assessing digital solutions to strengthen coordination and transparency.
Lessons learned and planned change
29B.27 The lesson for the component was the need to establish a centralized and efficient system to prevent delays, increase the visibility of opportunities and reduce administrative burden. In applying the lesson, the component has developed an automated online workflow in Inspira that consolidates all opportunities in a dedicated portal. This will enable entities to publish vacancies centrally, allow Member States to submit nominations online and facilitate candidates’ direct application to vacancies. These enhancements will improve efficiency, accountability and equitable access to opportunities. The automated online workflow also allows managers to utilize existing screening tools in Inspira to review submitted applications in a more consistent, transparent and fair manner. The component will roll out the new workflow and provide training for entities and Member States’ representatives.
29B.28 Expected progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 29B.5).

29B.33 In 2025, the component launched the first centralized digital platform for language and communications learning in the six official languages of the United Nations. The United Nations languages website established a standardized and structured language and communications learning ecosystem with diverse assets that span language development courses, high-impact communication workshops, self-assessment tools and customized training solutions in the six official languages, expanding the multilingual skills of the workforce at the Organization. The new platform functions as a resource hub for accessible, inclusive and innovative programming aligned with the United Nations Language Framework and illustrative multimedia samples of all levels in the six official languages. Sustained outreach during enrolment periods alongside the component’s Secretariat-wide initiatives, including the flagship United Nations “Skills Fest”, significantly furthered the visibility of and engagement with the new platform. Beneficiaries across the world, including United Nations staff, Member States, job candidates and hiring managers, gained a deeper familiarity of opportunities to enhance their language and communication skills, support career mobility and enhance job function and professional development.

performance.title: Safe and timely repatriation of uniformed personnel in line with mission contingency plans
performance.narrative:
29B.59 The liquidity crisis faced by the Organization has entailed significant challenges for peacekeeping operations. In 2025, the Secretary-General requested that all peacekeeping missions funded under the peacekeeping budget implement their contingency plans for a 15 per cent reduction in expenditure. This has necessitated a reduction in the size of military and police units in peacekeeping operations and the repatriation of some uniformed personnel. The component worked closely with all field missions to ensure the safe and timely repatriation of uniformed personnel. This effort was far more complex than a routine repatriation because it required urgent, large-scale, contingency-driven movements under severe time, financial, logistical and diplomatic pressures that far exceeded normal rotational planning. The approach emphasized minimizing the impact on mandate delivery and personnel while maintaining strategic engagement with stakeholders. As a result of the effort, in close coordination with field missions 10,785 uniformed personnel were repatriated between 8 October and 31 December 2025, representing 74.1 per cent of the total number of uniformed personnel to be repatriated as part of the mission contingency plans.

29B.65 As part of the humanitarian reset, the component has been supporting a system-wide initiative to reprioritize resources and streamline operations in response to reduced humanitarian funding, with a view to enabling the United Nations to “deliver as one” through more efficient and integrated supply chain solutions. In collaboration with the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, the United Nations Children’s Fund and the World Food Programme, the component developed an integrated approach to delivering supply chain solutions in humanitarian and complex operational environments.
Lessons learned and planned change
29B.66 The lesson for the component was that fragmented, entity-specific arrangements limited the ability of the United Nations system to deliver in a coherent manner, reduce the efficiency and timeliness of support and increase operational burdens on field teams. In applying the lesson, the component will operationalize an integrated approach focused on three areas: (a) coordinated procurement of key items through demand aggregation, technical collaboration, joint market engagement and strategic contracting; (b) optimizing global freight by pooling access to optimized global logistics services and leveraging pre-negotiated contracts, established supplier networks and shared infrastructure; and (c) harmonized in-country logistics, including import processing, customs clearance, warehousing, inventory management and humanitarian fleet operations. This approach will improve the speed and reliability of international transport and upstream logistics, reduce burdens on field teams and enable the more efficient delivery of assistance. The integrated service offer will be provided as an opt-in model, with services provided on a transparent, full cost-recovery basis, enabling entities to reduce or phase out duplicative capacities, as appropriate, while respecting mandates.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: strengthened management of contingent-owned ammunition
planned.narrative:
29B.78 Effective ammunition management is critical to ensure operational readiness, accountability and safety, while minimizing risks of diversion, loss or accidental incidents. Managing ammunition inventory can help to ensure the accurate tracking, transparency and life-cycle monitoring of ammunition, enabling informed decision-making, timely reporting and oversight across field missions. The component manages the Uniformed Capabilities Management System, a platform that streamlines and enables end-to-end planning for uniformed capabilities management for troop- and police-contributing countries.
Lessons learned and planned change
29B.79 The lesson for the component was that the absence of a centralized repository for ammunition limited the ability of field missions and Headquarters to monitor ammunition status and plan for timely disposals and replenishments. In applying the lesson, the component developed, in close coordination with the Department of Peace Operations, field missions and the Office of Information and Communications Technology, a new module in the Uniformed Capabilities Management System to record, monitor and manage contingent-owned ammunition. This ammunition management module will standardize the ammunition inventory across all missions and enable field missions to generate inspections and record all transactions throughout the life cycle of the contingent-owned ammunition. This module will be further enriched to include performance analyses and data reporting, as well as additional functionalities related to ammunition claims and reimbursements.

performance.title: United Nations Support Office in Haiti established
performance.narrative:
29B.85 In 2025, the Security Council adopted resolution 2793 (2025), by which it requested the Secretary-General to establish the United Nations Support Office in Haiti (UNSOH) to provide support, primarily to the Gang Suppression Force, the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti, the Haitian National Police and the Haitian armed forces, on any joint operations with the Force, as well as technical support to the Organization of American States. planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: strengthened support partnership arrangements
planned.narrative:
29B.92 The Department has put in place a support partnership framework to facilitate an active approach to establishing and drawing on partnership arrangements within the Department and across the Secretariat. As part of this effort, the Department introduced support guidelines in reviewing and managing support partnership arrangements in a more consistent and coordinated manner, helping to clarify roles and streamline internal processes.
Lessons learned and planned change
29B.93 The lesson for the subprogramme was that, notwithstanding the establishment of a support partnership framework and related institutional partnership initiatives, gaps remained in translating partnership engagement into consistent practice. While initial scoping and relationship-building with designated focal points has helped to identify opportunities for cooperation with key partners, these efforts have not always progressed to formalized arrangements or sustained implementation. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will establish a departmental-wide governance mechanism to provide strategic direction for support partnerships, ensure alignment with operational priorities and support accountability for advancing partnerships from engagement to delivery. This will help to strengthen coherence, clarify roles and ownership and reinforce a more results-oriented approach to support partnerships.

performance.title: Rental cost recovery automated through payroll
performance.narrative:
29B.99 The rental obligations for leased buildings at Headquarters are funded from the regular budget, the peacekeeping support account and cost recovery for extrabudgetary positions. In previous years, the cost-recovery process required extensive engagement with all entities to review their extrabudgetary-funded positions based on Umoja staffing tables and to determine the total rental charge for each entity, taking into account the projected incumbency of each position for the year. Once an agreement was reached, cost-recovery transactions were processed manually, for each position or through a monthly batch process, depending on the availability of funding. This approach required continuous data reconciliation and the execution of thousands of manual transactions annually. In 2025, the subprogramme introduced a payroll-based cost-recovery mechanism, fully automating the process. This significantly reduced administrative overhead or burden and improved accuracy based on actual incumbency.

planned.title: increased accessibility of premises and facilities at United Nations Headquarters for persons with disabilities
planned.narrative:
29B.105 In 2018, the subprogramme commissioned a baseline accessibility assessment of the Headquarters premises. Following the initial assessment, the subprogramme implemented a three-year programme to upgrade the United Nations facilities and premises to meet basic accessibility levels, with a focus on the physical accessibility of United Nations buildings. By the end of 2023, the Department had implemented improvements, including the installation of automatic doors to several conference rooms, a wheelchair accessible exit gate at the staff entrance and wheelchair charging stations, and a lift in the General Assembly rostrum and an accessible ramp at the General Assembly 200 entrance, as well as modifications to a select portion of the floor seating in the General Assembly Hall and the modification of all curb cuts on campus to meet accessibility standards and provide safe, barrier-free access for persons with disabilities.
Lessons learned and planned change
29B.106 The lesson for the subprogramme was that further improvements could be made to enhance the accessibility of premises and facilities at United Nations Headquarters to go beyond meeting the minimum standards. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will implement a five-year programme, which commenced in 2025, to further upgrade the premises and facilities to enhance accessibility for persons with disabilities. Accordingly, the subprogramme completed the first phase of its second accessibility assessment focused on the routes used by delegates, staff and visitors. This assessment has and will continue to inform the implementation of further improvements to the premises and facilities. The second phase of this accessibility assessment is planned for 2027.

performance.title: Progress in the implementation of the 2019 Political Agreement for Peace and Reconciliation in the Central African Republic
performance.narrative:
5.I.18 With the subprogramme’s support, the United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) continued to implement its mandate in a comprehensive and strategic manner, contributing to further progress in the implementation of the 2019 Political Agreement for Peace and Reconciliation in the Central African Republic. In 2025, several signatory armed groups returned to the peace process and entered into the national disarmament, demobilization and reintegration programme. In this regard, MINUSCA supported 15 disarmament operations in 11 locations, resulting in the disarmament and demobilization of 1,263 ex-combatants, including 21 women, and the collection of 854 weapons, 135 grenades and 40,241 rounds of ammunition. In addition, with support from the subprogramme, MINUSCA provided extensive good offices, logistical, security and technical support for the organization of combined presidential, legislative, regional and municipal elections, which were held in a generally peaceful environment on 28 December 2025 across all prefectures. Municipal elections, which had not been held since 1988, were a significant outstanding provision of the Political Agreement.

5.I.24 The United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), with the subprogramme’s support, continues to implement its strategic priorities as outlined in Security Council resolution 2808 (2025) to contribute to: (a) the protection of civilians in its area of deployment; (b) the achievement of the objectives set by the Council in its resolution 2773 (2025); and (c) the stabilization and strengthening of State institutions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. As part of these efforts, MONUSCO intensified its support to disarmament, demobilization, repatriation, resettlement and reintegration processes and mechanisms, including by contributing to the disarmament, resettlement and repatriation of Forces démocratiques de libération du Rwanda (FDLR) combatants as part of the FDLR neutralization plan. Since January 2025, MONUSCO has facilitated the repatriation of 207 ex-combatants and their dependants from Goma to Rwanda.
Lessons learned and planned change
5.I.25 The lesson for the subprogramme was the need to ensure greater involvement of local communities in disarmament, demobilization, repatriation, resettlement and reintegration efforts, taking into consideration that FDLR combatants are often embedded within local communities, making disarmament and repatriation efforts more challenging. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will strengthen community awareness-raising initiatives to enhance awareness of such efforts and promote the greater involvement and cooperation of local communities in facilitating disarmament and repatriation efforts.

performance.title: Strengthened preparedness for the transition and withdrawal of United Nations peacekeeping missions
performance.narrative:
5.I.31 The Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations, in its 2024 report (A/78/19), stressed the importance of all peacekeeping missions having realistic and adaptable contingency plans that can address various scenarios and ensure the security of personnel. It also requested the Secretariat to ensure that every peacekeeping mission has appropriate contingency plans, including withdrawal plans, which implement relevant lessons learned and take into consideration the changing security environment. In response, the subprogramme continued to develop the exit concept of operations, which provides operational direction to the heads of military components for the development of detailed plans and directives related to the withdrawal of military personnel. These exit concepts of operations are designed to ensure the safe, secure and orderly extraction of peacekeepers and outline procedures for withdrawal under permissive, semi-permissive and non-permissive conditions in deteriorating security environments. In 2025, the subprogramme finalized three exit concepts of operations, for the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, MONUSCO and the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei, building on progress achieved in 2024, when the exit concept of operations for the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) was finalized.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: peace operations strengthen monitoring, analysis and response to misinformation, disinformation and hate speech
planned.narrative:
5.I.37 Peace operations continue to operate in increasingly complex environments characterized by both physical attacks and hostile activities in the information domain. In MONUSCO, for example, the proliferation of misinformation, disinformation and hate speech has affected the ability of the Mission to implement its mandate and exacerbated risks to United Nations personnel and assets. In response, the subprogramme has supported efforts to enhance monitoring and analysis of the information environment and to strengthen coordination between operational and public information components in MONUSCO. The Department, in collaboration with the Office of Information and Communications Technology, developed the Monitoring and Analysis of the Information Environment (MAIE) platform, which uses advanced analytics to track online discourse and identify disinformation and misinformation in peacekeeping settings, as well as Unite Wave, which analyses local FM radio broadcasts in several local languages.
Lessons learned and planned change
5.I.38 The lesson for the subprogramme was that improvements in military operations alone are insufficient to mitigate reputational and perception-based risks that may affect the safety and security of United Nations uniformed personnel. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will support the development of a more integrated approach to strengthening information integrity and addressing misinformation, disinformation and hate speech directed against peacekeeping operations and personnel. This will include enhanced monitoring and analysis of the information environment through the Monitoring and Analysis of the Information Environment platform; improved coordination between uniformed components and public information capacities; and the production of verified, field-based communication products aligned with operational realities, with a view to reducing anti-United Nations sentiment and mitigating associated risks to personnel, assets and mandate implementation.

performance.title: Strengthened national and regional capacities to mitigate the threats posed by improvised explosive devices
performance.narrative:
5.I.43 The increasing use of improvised explosive devices by non-State actors continues to pose a significant threat to international peace and security. Recognizing the widespread devastation caused by these devices, the General Assembly, in its resolution 79/53, urged all States, as well the United Nations system and other relevant organizations and institutions supporting affected States, to increase attention to prevention and capacity-building and to provide support to reduce the risks posed by such devices. In 2025, the subprogramme, in partnership with subprogramme 4, supported 17 national and regional training centres across Africa and Asia in delivering training on the mitigation of threats posed by improvised explosive devices, in accordance with United Nations standards. To this end, the subprogramme assisted training centres with curriculum assessment and alignment with United Nations standards and trained and certified instructors across training centres, which are pre-conditions for the centres to obtain formal training recognition. Through the subprogramme’s support, four additional training centres gained formal recognition in 2025. The four newly recognized training centres subsequently delivered threat mitigation training to national security personnel from their own and neighbouring countries, thereby building sustainable national and regional capacities and enhancing preparedness to prevent and respond to threats related to improvised explosive devices.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: increased accountability for crimes committed against United Nations personnel serving in peacekeeping operations
planned.narrative:
5.I.49 In its resolution 2589 (2021), the Security Council called for specific measures to ensure accountability for crimes committed against United Nations peacekeepers. Since 1948, 1,081 personnel serving in United Nations peacekeeping operations have been killed and more than 3,100 injured as a result of malicious acts. Of these, 289 peacekeepers serving in MINUSCA, the United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in Mali, MONUSCO and UNIFIL have been killed since 2013, accounting for 84 per cent of the 345 fatalities attributable to malicious acts during the period. The activities of the subprogramme in support of the implementation of resolution 2589 (2021) have therefore focused on these missions. Significant progress has been made since 2018 to ensure accountability for such crimes, with an increase in the number of alleged perpetrators identified and detained, an increase in the percentage of reported cases of crimes against peacekeepers resulting in confirmed national investigations and, since 2020, 103 convictions for a range of different offences related to the killing of 35 peacekeepers and two United Nations experts in the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Lebanon and Mali.
Lessons learned and planned change
5.I.50 The lesson for the subprogramme was the continued need to address both the political and operational aspects of supporting national authorities in their efforts to bring the perpetrators of such crimes to justice. In applying this lesson, the subprogramme will prioritize the following six key initiatives: (a) political advocacy and information-sharing to strengthen engagement with Member States; (b) reinforcement of support capacities in missions to facilitate the provision of capacity-building and technical assistance to host States for the investigation and prosecution of such crimes; (c) further operationalization of the database on accountability for crimes against peacekeepers; (d) support for the Group of Friends to Promote Accountability for Crimes Against Peacekeepers; (e) public information activities to enhance visibility and support; and (f) reinforcement of capacities at Headquarters to provide dedicated support with regard to these efforts.
5.I.51 Expected progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see figure 5.I.V).

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: strengthened prevention and response to conflict-related sexual violence in peacekeeping operations
planned.narrative:
5.I.62 Conflict-related sexual violence is recognized by the Security Council as a threat to international peace and security. United Nations peacekeeping operations play a critical role in preventing and responding to such violence, in line with Council resolutions and mission-specific mandates. Between 2023 and 2025, the subprogramme developed and conducted a global roll-out of a policy on conflict-related sexual violence and its associated handbook, which was jointly issued in collaboration with Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict. The roll-out was accompanied by awareness-raising campaigns, training activities and in-mission support from the subprogramme. These efforts strengthened understanding of responsibilities related to conflict-related sexual violence across civilian, military and police components. They also established the foundation for a more structured, mission-wide and tool-driven approach to institutionalizing prevention and response to such violence in 2027 and beyond, as required.
Lessons learned and planned change
5.I.63 The lesson for the subprogramme was that while awareness-raising and training activities have improved understanding of the conflict-related sexual violence mandate, the absence of standardized, user-friendly operational tools has limited the ability of missions to translate policy requirements into consistent practice. The lack of clarity regarding focal point roles, high staff turnover and uneven leadership engagement have further constrained the institutionalization of approaches for the prevention of and response to conflict-related sexual violence across mission components. These challenges have been compounded by the evolving operational and resource environment in recent years, including reductions in mission footprints and in specialized capacity. This context underscores the importance of an institutionalized approach that enables sustained implementation of the conflict-related sexual violence mandate beyond dedicated functions. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will transition from ad hoc support to a structured, tool-driven approach to integrate prevention and response to conflict-related sexual violence across mission components. The subprogramme will roll out a toolkit designed to strengthen the integration of the conflict-related sexual violence mandate across civilian, military and police components. This is expected to strengthen institutional ownership of conflict-related sexual violence responsibilities, reduce reliance on individual expertise and support more coherent, consistent and results-oriented implementation of the conflict-related sexual violence mandate across peacekeeping missions.
5.I.64 Expected progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 5.I.13).
