overview.name: Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs
strategy:
3.I.3 The Department has global responsibility for political and peacebuilding issues and manages a spectrum of tools and engagements across the conflict continuum to ensure a coherent and effective approach to conflict prevention and resolution, electoral assistance, peacebuilding and sustaining peace. Given its global mandate for conflict prevention and peacemaking, the Department will play a lead role within the United Nations in formulating and implementing comprehensive regional strategies that address cross-boundary issues, in cooperation with regional and subregional organizations.
3.I.4 In order to achieve these goals, the Department will rely on its expertise at Headquarters, including the single regional political-operational structure shared with the Department of Peace Operations, and its network of field presences, in particular, special political missions, regional offices and liaison presences with regional and other organizations. It will also draw on the capacities of the United Nations peace and security pillar, which was restructured in 2019 and further adjusted following the General Assembly’s approval of relevant proposals in the revised estimates relating to the proposed programme budget for 2026 (Assembly resolution 80/242).
3.I.5 The Department will continue to provide advice and substantive services to the Security Council, its subsidiary organs and the Military Staff Committee; assist and support the Peacebuilding Commission; provide advice and substantive support to the Special Committee on the Situation with regard to the Implementation of the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples, as well as to other relevant intergovernmental bodies; and continue to provide support to the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People.
3.I.6 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, under Chapter VIII of the Charter, the Department, through its special political missions and its liaison offices, will continue to strengthen partnerships with regional and other organizations in the field of peace and security, including with a view to supporting their role in diplomacy, mediation and the pacific settlement of disputes, in line with action 16 of the Pact for the Future. The Department will also expand its partnerships with other relevant actors, including civil society and local communities, in particular in support of women and young people.
3.I.7 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Department will continue to participate in the Executive Committee established by the Secretary-General and chair a number of inter-agency task forces aimed at enhancing the coherence of United Nations system engagement in specific countries, regions and thematic areas, in accordance with respective mandates. These coordination arrangements have contributed to more streamlined decision-making, reduced duplication of analytical and reporting products and clearer division of labour among entities, particularly in complex and protracted crisis settings. The Peacebuilding Fund, as a cross-pillar tool of financial support, will continue to work with and through agencies, funds and programmes in-country and at Headquarters. Under the United Nations-World Bank Partnership Framework for Crisis-Affected Situations, the Department will continue to strengthen partnerships with the World Bank and other international financial institutions to ensure that international engagement in crisis-affected situations is more coherent, effective and sustainable, in line with action 18 of the Pact for the Future. The Department will maintain the Partnership Facility to support field teams’ joint data, analysis and operational collaboration with the World Bank Group. The Department will also enhance collaboration with the Department of Peace Operations with a view to better linking cross-cutting functions across the two Departments, including in training, innovation, partnerships and information integrity, to provide more coherent support to missions.
3.I.8 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Unity among Member States, in particular the Security Council, including in critical situations in which the United Nations is engaged;
(b) Existence of entry points for United Nations engagement to mitigate tensions and prevent conflict;
(c) Commitment of the parties to a conflict to engaging in a process towards the peaceful settlement of disputes.
3.I.9 The Department integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. Through the newly established joint Gender Unit of the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and the Department of Peace Operations, the Department will enhance the implementation of the women and peace and security agenda to promote the meaningful participation of women in peacemaking, mediation, peace sustainment and peacebuilding efforts, as well as in electoral and political processes, consistent with relevant mandates, including action 19 of the Pact for the Future. Strengthened collaboration through the joint Gender Unit of the two Departments, and through close partnership with the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN-Women) and other relevant entities, will also enable more coherent support to missions and country teams. The Department will further support the efforts of the Peacebuilding Commission to integrate a gender perspective into all aspects of its work and prioritize women’s engagement through Peacebuilding Fund-supported programmes.
3.I.10 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Department will implement a joint Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs-Department of Peace Operations action plan for disability inclusion with a view to reinforcing an organizational culture that supports the inclusion of persons with disabilities and further advancing disability inclusion in strategic planning and management, knowledge and information management. The Department will also foster engagement with government counterparts and civil society organizations to promote the inclusivity of political processes, including in addressing the needs of persons with disabilities.

performance.title: Enhanced women’s leadership and participation in electoral and political processes
performance.narrative:
3.I.34 In 2025, the subprogramme strengthened Member States’ electoral and political processes by scaling up the Women’s Leadership Academy, implemented jointly with the United Nations Development Programme, into a global platform for senior women leaders from electoral management bodies, public institutions and civil society. The Academy aims to support women’s leadership and political participation by strengthening their digital skills, fostering peer networks and enabling knowledge exchange on common challenges. In 2023, the first edition of the Academy was held in Spain, with the participation of women leaders in the Arab region primarily from public institutions and civil society, with a view to piloting the Academy model and curriculum. In 2024, an expanded edition was held in Qatar with women leaders from Asia, Africa and the Arab region. Building on these previous regional editions, in 2025, a global edition of the Women’s Leadership Academy was held, with a strong emphasis placed on communication in the digital era, including the risks posed by misinformation and disinformation and the role of strategic communications. Through these efforts, the subprogramme enhanced the capacity of women leaders to engage effectively in electoral governance, public decision-making and political leadership in increasingly complex and polarized environments.

objectives: 3.I.57 The objective, to which this subprogramme contributes, is to promote the decolonization process in accordance with the Charter and relevant resolutions of the General Assembly of the 17 Non-Self-Governing Territories so as to bring about the complete eradication of colonialism.

performance.title: Strengthened public awareness of decolonization
performance.narrative:
3.I.60 In 2025, the subprogramme designed and implemented a dedicated digital awareness campaign highlighting key aspects of decolonization. This campaign was implemented alongside a high-level plenary meeting of the General Assembly held on 18 December 2025 to commemorate the sixty-fifth anniversary of the adoption of its resolution 1514 (XV), containing the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples, and to mark the first observance of the International Day against Colonialism in All Its Forms and Manifestations, established by the Assembly in its resolution 80/106. All campaign materials were produced in the six official languages of the United Nations and tailored for dissemination across various social media platforms. Launched on 6 December 2025, the campaign maintained consistent visibility and engagement across various digital and social media platforms and supported efforts to strengthen public awareness of United Nations efforts to advance the decolonization agenda.

objectives: 34.20 The objective, to which this subprogramme contributes, is to ensure a safe and secure environment for all United Nations personnel, delegates, dignitaries and other visitors while conducting activities at United Nations Headquarters, offices away from Headquarters and regional commissions and while attending special events hosted by the United Nations at external locations.
strategy:
34.21 To contribute to the objective, the subprogramme will provide strategic coordination and management of the security and safety services at eight duty stations, as well as operational guidance and technical supervision with regard to security risk management, physical security, close protection, crisis management, fire safety, recruitment, resilience, training and oversight of security and safety projects at those locations.
34.22 The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
(a) Safe, secure and efficient access of delegates, staff and visitors to United Nations premises and external special events;
(b) Effective delivery of United Nations mandates and programmes at United Nations premises and external special events.

performance.title: A safe and secure environment for all delegates and participants at the eightieth session of the General Assembly
performance.narrative:
34.23 The eightieth session of the General Assembly marked the Organization’s eightieth anniversary, and focused on renewing multilateralism under the theme “Better together: 80 years and more for peace, development and human rights”. This event saw an unprecedented level of security engagement and operational complexity at United Nations Headquarters. The subprogramme conducted an intensive planning exercise with host country law enforcement and emergency service partners and internal United Nations entities in preparing a safe and secure environment. Detailed risk assessments identified specific mitigation measures that were put in place to provide safety and security for the visiting Heads of State and Government and regular delegates. The subprogramme ensured seamless access control and safety procedures during the high-level week, and provided a safe and secure environment for all participants.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: improved safety and security decision-making
planned.narrative:
34.29 Effective decision-making depends on timely, accurate and comparable data across all duty stations. The subprogramme currently compiles weekly, monthly, quarterly and annual Excel-based reports on security operations, activities and emerging trends and developments from all Division of Headquarters Security and Safety Services duty stations. Security managers in all duty stations use this data for better planning and coordination of access control for delegates, staff and visitors, to enhance preparedness and governance to safeguard headquarters premises, to strengthen security support for high-level meetings, conferences and large-scale events and to identify trends for security resourcing and planning for future delegate and visitor support.
Lessons learned and planned change
34.30 The lesson for the subprogramme was that manual spreadsheet reporting limits data quality, slows analysis and constrains the ability to generate real-time insights that are essential for safety and security. To achieve more reliable and actionable information, the subprogramme will transition to digitized data-collection models that feed directly into Power BI dashboards. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will design standardized digital reporting tools, automate data flows and strengthen analytics capacity to best assist timely decision-making by security managers in consultation with senior leadership. The digitized reporting mechanisms and Power BI dashboards will provide security managers and senior leadership with access to real-time information, thereby enhancing security planning and service delivery and improving access to Headquarters premises, optimizing support for meetings and events and providing clearer trend analysis that ultimately improves safety and security.

The subprogramme undertook various operational and structural changes to strengthen the efficiency and resilience of security services in field locations. The subprogramme redeployed security personnel to priority locations, shifted analytical resources closer to field operations and created additional multi-country offices to ensure coverage with much-reduced resources. Regional desk structures were reformed to create efficiencies and better serve field operations.

planned.title: risk-informed safety and security decision-making
planned.narrative:
34.42 Security risk management is central to enabling United Nations security operations, as it provides a rigorous framework for the identification of security risks and mitigation measures and the residual risk after those mitigation measures have been implemented. This structured and standardized process allows security decision makers to analyse and manage safety and security risks in a consistent manner across diverse operational contexts. The subprogramme has worked on developing a quality assurance tool to identify where security risk management can be further improved and refined.
Lessons learned and planned change
34.43 The lesson for the subprogramme was that it was important to identify areas for improvement in the security risk management framework and the tool, based on inconsistencies and errors found through the collection and analysis of security risk management data. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will focus on improving the quality of security risk management outputs, simplifying the process and the tool and enhancing user experience and understanding, in order to make the security risk management framework not only easier for security decision makers and others to use but also even more impactful in identifying security threats to United Nations operations. Decision makers will be supported through targeted guidance and accompanying capacity-building activities.

performance.title: Strengthened debt management and sustainable financing strategies in small island developing States

18.22 Multiple global crises continue to severely impact developing countries, particularly small island developing States, by disrupting their economic activities and value chains, further exacerbating their fiscal vulnerabilities. The subprogramme provided support to Cabo Verde and the Comoros to address heightened fiscal constraints, compounded by limited access to external financing for their development priorities. The intervention aimed to strengthen debt management and external financing frameworks by enhancing the capacity of the two countries in designing their financing strategies. The subprogramme, in collaboration with UNCTAD, conducted debt sustainability analyses, risk and resilience assessments related to the impacts of climate change, and external financing diagnostics, to identify practical pathways to mobilize sustainable and affordable external financing while containing debt vulnerabilities in the countries. This led to the development of national financing strategies and corresponding implementation road maps to guide implementation in Cabo Verde and the Comoros.

performance.title: Enhanced readiness of Ethiopia to trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area
performance.narrative:
18.35 Ethiopia’s effective participation in the African Continental Free Trade Area is a strategic priority for accelerating export diversification, regional value chain integration, and private sector competitiveness. As a late entrant to preferential trade arrangements, Ethiopia faces specific structural, regulatory and institutional constraints that would need to be addressed to translate African Continental Free Trade Area commitments into tangible trading outcomes for firms, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises. To address these gaps, the subprogramme supported Ethiopia in strengthening its operational readiness to trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area by addressing policy, regulatory and implementation bottlenecks across goods and services trade. Key interventions focused on enhancing national coordination mechanisms, strengthening the understanding of the African Continental Free Trade Area among public and private stakeholders, and supporting evidence-based engagement in continental negotiations. Technical assistance and capacity-building activities helped national institutions to align domestic trade policies, customs procedures, and trade facilitation frameworks with African Continental Free Trade Area requirements, while targeted analytical work supported Ethiopia’s positioning in priority sectors with regional export potential. These interventions contributed to improved institutional preparedness and clearer national positions on African Continental Free Trade Area implementation and strengthened the capacity of Ethiopian trade officials and private sector actors to utilize African Continental Free Trade Area preferences effectively.

Although many member States and regional economic communities have made progress in aligning policies with African Continental Free Trade Area commitments, disparities persist in their ability to negotiate, articulate national and regional interests, and consistently operationalize agreed trade rules. These gaps affect the depth and effectiveness of participation in trade processes and limit the realization of integration gains.
Lessons learned and planned change
18.42 The lesson for the subprogramme was that, while analytical products, policy frameworks and regional-level engagements remain essential, their impact on observable change was greatest when complemented by more targeted, country-level and regional economic community-specific approaches. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will place greater emphasis on approaches tailored to the institutional readiness of beneficiaries, with increased focus on country- and regional economic community-level application of trade rules, negotiation scenarios and operational decision-making. Building on progress achieved in previous periods, the subprogramme will support members of ECA by increasing awareness of African Continental Free Trade Area provisions and providing tailored technical assistance towards institutional alignment with the African Continental Free Trade Area and strengthening policy frameworks through practical step-by-step trade guides.

performance.title: Member States have access to a tax policy simulation tool to support evidence-based policymaking for affordable connectivity, inclusive economic growth, and job creation in Africa
performance.narrative:
18.49 Digital connectivity is a key driver of economic growth, employment and social inclusion in Africa. However, many individuals and businesses still face barriers due to high access costs (continental average of 14.8 per cent of gross national income per capita, nearly five times the global average) and limited broadband investments. Cognizant of these challenges, the subprogramme developed a technical report on optimizing Africa’s ICT tax regimes towards economic growth and job creation to inform policymakers of the economic and fiscal impacts of ICT taxation and to provide evidence-based recommendations for digital transformation. Key findings from the subprogramme’s research include the finding that a 10 per cent increase in mobile broadband penetration yields growth in gross domestic product by approximately 2.5 per cent and in employment rates between 3.1 per cent and 13.2 per cent. In addition, the subprogramme developed the ICT Tax Impact Calculator, a practical policy tool that enables Governments to simulate country-specific ICT tax reform scenarios and assess their potential economic and fiscal impacts. In 2025, the tool was presented and validated to demonstrate that the reduction of sector-specific excise duties can boost aggregate tax receipts by expanding the tax base, with a view to supporting the adoption of evidence-based fiscal policies that promote digital inclusion, revenue generation and job creation.

performance.title: Members of ECA strengthen policy and institutional frameworks for climate-resilient agricultural value chains
performance.narrative:
18.75 Strengthening regional agricultural value chains and agro-industrial development is critical for improving agricultural productivity, expanding value addition, enhancing market connectivity, and advancing regional trade integration under the African Continental Free Trade Area. For countries such as Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, where cocoa and rice are strategic commodities, having a coherent and evidence-based framework is essential to guide policy alignment and unlock regionally integrated agricultural growth. In 2025, the subprogramme, through its analytical work and policy advice, and in collaboration with subprogramme 7, component 1, enabled Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana to review and validate a policy framework aimed at strengthening regional agricultural value chains and agro-industrial parks. The two countries reviewed the framework designed to improve agricultural productivity, increase value addition, strengthen market linkages, and promote regional trade integration within the agricultural sector. Through these efforts, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana aligned their policy and regulatory priorities towards the advancement of regional agricultural value chain development, ensuring that their national commitments reflect African Union guidelines and African Continental Free Trade Area objectives. This has reinforced the strategic conditions for coherent, regionally integrated and investment-ready agricultural value chains, enhancing both countries’ ability to drive sustained agricultural transformation and contribute more effectively to broader regional economic integration.

performance.title: Strengthened data collection, monitoring and reporting on gender equality and the empowerment of women
performance.narrative:
18.88 Significant gaps in the collection of sex-disaggregated data and gender statistics across Africa limit the ability of member States to effectively track progress towards national, regional and global commitments on gender equality and women’s empowerment. Coordination challenges between statistical offices, line ministries, and gender machineries further constrain the collection, integration and analysis of such data, undermining evidence-based policymaking and accountability. The Minimum Set of Gender Indicators for Africa provides guidance on the prioritization of indicators to be collected in Africa, acts as an important resource for the development of their own statistical frameworks and facilitates the harmonization of regional and sub-regional data collection. The subprogramme strengthened national capacities in Burundi and South Sudan for the collection of gender statistics. Through targeted technical assistance, capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder consultations, these member States assessed their monitoring and reporting systems, identified key gaps to guide improvements and adopted the Minimum Set of Gender Indicators for Africa. This enabled improved coordination, strengthened data systems, and enabled more systematic, policy-relevant reporting on gender equality and the empowerment of women.

performance.title: Members of ECA take action to increase sustainable finance
performance.narrative:
18.101 Africa faces mounting external debt and escalating debt service obligations that are increasingly crowding out resources for essential public services and investments. The component contributed to strengthening the capacity of African countries to advance sustainable finance practices. Through a regional advocacy platform, the component promoted regional peer learning and policy dialogue for 12 African countries by presenting their experiences and exchanging best practices on how to leverage innovative financing instruments such as green bonds, sustainability-linked bonds, and debt-for-purpose swaps. At the national level, the component contributed to enhancing public debt management through sustained advisory services, technical assistance and capacity-building programmes. These efforts led to the establishment of a Climate Finance Unit within the Public Debt Management Division in Sierra Leone in 2024, to mobilize and manage climate finance for sustainable national growth; and to the development, in 2025, of a national medium-term debt strategy in Egypt, which aims to reduce the country’s debt reliance. The strategy was adopted in January 2026.

performance.title: Members of ECA in West Africa integrate agricultural value chain analysis into planning frameworks
performance.narrative:
18.114 Developing competitive cross-border value chains is central to Africa’s regional integration agenda. By enabling specialization, scale, and value addition across borders, regional agricultural value chains can unlock higher productivity, increase export earnings, catalyse technology and skills transfer, create jobs and improve food security. In 2023, the component supported countries to conduct regional integration impact assessments, which enabled them to identify priority regional value chains to be promoted. In 2024, the component organized a training series for national experts on trade facilitation and regional integration, including integrating agriculture value chain analysis into planning frameworks. In 2025, the component, in collaboration with subprogramme 5, provided policy advice and technical assistance to Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana to identify policy, regulatory and institutional reforms needed to strengthen regional value chains integration under the African Continental Free Trade Area. It provided policymakers with evidence-based recommendations to reduce post-harvest losses, improve logistics and customs management, and enhance cross-border cooperation. Through this support, cross-border value chain analysis was integrated into national development planning processes of both countries.

performance.narrative:
18.141 The Agreement Establishing the African Continental Free Trade Area is a landmark agreement to boost intra-African trade and economic integration, while Somalia’s Centennial Vision 2060 outlines the country’s long-term development aspirations. The component advanced regional integration in Eastern Africa by supporting Somalia’s operationalization of the African Continental Free Trade Area and the development of its Centennial Vision 2060. Building on the validation of Somalia’s African Continental Free Trade Area National Implementation Strategy in November 2023, the component delivered targeted technical assistance and policy advice throughout 2024 and 2025, towards the alignment of trade priorities with long-term development objectives. These efforts strengthened institutional capacity and consensus on trade reforms, leading to Somalia’s historic accession to the East African Community in March 2024, the presidential launch of the Centennial Vision 2060 in June 2025, and the ratification of the Agreement by the Somali parliament in October 2025, providing a transformative framework for sustainable growth and regional integration.

performance.title: Members of ECA move from fragmented to integrated approaches to social protection through the development of national social protection strategies
performance.narrative:
18.167 Across Africa, fragmented social protection schemes have limited countries’ ability to effectively reach the most vulnerable. The subprogramme contributed to a major shift towards coherent national systems by strengthening regional capacities and supporting Member States to design integrated, fiscally sustainable and gender-sensitive social protection frameworks. In 2024, the subprogramme developed the curriculum for a bilingual regional course on social protection and the care economy in Africa, which was subsequently reviewed and validated by selected members of ECA. Following this, in 2025, the subprogramme delivered a bilingual regional course on social protection and the care economy in Africa, building the competencies of 1,138 policymakers from 48 members of ECA in system design, fiscal integration, targeting, labour market linkages and gender-sensitive planning. Participants created peer-learning networks that continued beyond the training, fostering cross-country learning and policy uptake. Building on this regional capacity base, the subprogramme provided targeted advisory services that led to the preparation of three draft national social protection strategies for Cameroon, Senegal and Zimbabwe. These strategies propose integrated frameworks to expand coverage for vulnerable groups, strengthen institutional coordination, align social protection with national development plans, embed considerations related to the care economy and ensure fiscal sustainability. Each strategy includes implementation road maps, governance arrangements and monitoring frameworks aligned with national priorities and the Sustainable Development Goals.

performance.title: Members of ECA established a common position for Africa on priorities for social development
performance.narrative:
18.180 Africa continues to face persistent social development challenges, including high income inequality and multidimensional poverty, limited access to decent jobs, and gaps in education and human capital development. Addressing these issues is critical to achieving the aspirations of Agenda 2063 and the 2030 Agenda. The World Summit for Social Development provides an important platform for African countries to influence global social development frameworks and ensure that Africa’s priorities are reflected in international commitments. The subprogramme, in collaboration with the African Union Commission, conducted an expert group meeting in preparation for the regional review of the Second World Summit for Social Development in September 2025. The meeting provided a platform for African experts, policymakers, and practitioners to deliberate upon and consolidate Africa’s perspectives and priorities, and to ensure that these were reflected in the global deliberations at the Second World Summit for Social Development. During the discussion, social development challenges in Africa were examined and consensus emerged around three interlinked priorities: (a) reduction of poverty and inequality; (b) promotion of decent jobs and youth employment; and (c) strengthening education and human capital development, which together form the foundation for inclusive and sustainable development across the continent. Participants highlighted concrete pathways for reform, calling for stronger institutions, better financing, and the deliberate inclusion of youth, women and the most vulnerable in policy design and delivery. The meeting led to the development of a common African position on social development priorities, which was adopted by members of ECA and guided their engagement at the Second World Summit for Social Development.

entities.name: Economic Commission for Europe
priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
20.3 The overall strategy and proposed programme of work of ECE is grounded in the shared vision and ambition of member States and the peoples of the ECE region for a just and prosperous future for all. It has been formulated in alignment with the commitments outlined in the Pact for the Future and remains anchored in multilateral frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda, the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, the Programme of Action for Landlocked Developing Countries for the Decade 2024–2034 and the New Urban Agenda set forth by Member States to address economic and social challenges through sustained, equitable and people-centred development.
20.4 The strategy of the programme integrates sustainable development approaches and builds on synergies and the expected results of its subprogrammes. It leverages cross-sectoral synergies of the 2030 Agenda and collaboration among the subprogrammes of the ECE secretariat, its intergovernmental architecture and broad expert community for multi-stakeholder engagement and action towards accelerating progress in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, including through the Regional Forum on Sustainable Development for the ECE Region and the United Nations Forum of Mayors. The programme will continue to provide support to its member States in addressing the economic and environmental challenges of achieving the Goals, with a focus on the demographic, digital and green transitions that have significant catalytic and multiplier effects.
20.5 The execution of the strategy will be realized through: (a) the facilitation of intergovernmental processes to promote consensus and cooperation, enable peer-to-peer exchanges of innovative policy solutions and good practices, and strengthen the existing and establish new norms and standards, as well as legal instruments and frameworks; (b) thought leadership and ensuring that member States have access to timely and quality evidence, including by supporting them in measuring their progress towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals, and foresight-based policy and technical advice and recommendations for informed decision-making; and (c) the strengthening of capacities of national institutions to implement norms and standards and commitments outlined in multilateral agreements and ECE legal instruments to which the member States are Parties.
20.6 In 2027, the Commission’s work will continue to focus on a range of issues in the ECE region pertaining to, among others, transboundary, subregional, intraregional and interregional cooperation on economic integration and trade; transport and mobility; environmental protection and the management of natural resources; forests and forest industry; affordable and clean energy; competitiveness and public-private partnerships for sustainable development; emerging social and demographic challenges; and land management.
20.7 ECE plans further strengthening of the secretariat’s operational model by enhancing internal coordination, streamlining internal workflows and processes and reinforcing data-driven and cross-sectoral approaches, in line with action 45 (a) of the Pact for the Future for more agile, timely and impactful support to its member States, and the UN80 Initiative.
20.8 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, ECE will build on its close cooperation with international and regional organizations and other regional actors to exchange knowledge, develop joint initiatives and enhance collective impact. Partnerships with the private sector and civil society organizations, think tanks and the academic sector will be strengthened to facilitate ECE policy dialogue and normative work and to engage them in the implementation of the 2030 Agenda by member States.
20.9 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, ECE will continue to lead inter-agency coordination in the region, co-chairing the Regional Collaborative Platform for Europe and Central Asia to strengthen joint action on cross-cutting policy issues at the regional level. Through its strategic partnerships and collaboration with United Nations entities and international financial institutions, including through initiatives such as the United Nations Special Programme for the Economies of Central Asia, ECE will continue to deliver integrated policy advice and regional perspectives globally. At the country level, ECE will collaborate with resident coordinators and United Nations country teams to support the implementation of joint programmes, aligned with national priorities and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. The programme will also foster interregional, South-South and triangular cooperation.
20.10 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) ECE member States continue to actively engage and support sustainable development initiatives and related intergovernmental processes and to prioritize regional and subregional cooperation and integration for shared development outcomes;
(b) All relevant stakeholders maintain the political will and commitment to multilateral cooperation and the implementation of ECE legal instruments, norms and standards;
(c) Sufficient resources are available for the implementation of planned activities.
20.11 Guided by its corporate policy and action plan on gender equality and the empowerment of women, ECE integrates a gender perspective into its results, deliverables and operational model that enables their delivery, as appropriate, as indicated, for example, in the programme performance for 2025 under subprogramme 6. In doing so, ECE aims to support member States in achieving commitments outlined under Sustainable Development Goal 5 and targets of other Goals relating to gender equality and women’s empowerment.
20.12 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, ECE will continue to ensure that disability inclusion is mainstreamed into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate.

planned.title: improved reporting of air emissions data
planned.narrative:
20.31 Reporting air emissions data is a prerequisite for assessing progress made by the Parties in meeting their commitments under the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution. Furthermore, the reported data support modelling efforts that allow for an assessment of the effectiveness of previously adopted measures and the strengthening of existing and development of new, ambitious policies, strategies and legal instruments pertaining to emissions reduction. The subprogramme has supported Parties in generating and improving the reporting of air emissions data, including by identifying gaps in inventories.
Lessons learned and planned change
20.32 The lesson for the subprogramme was that there were opportunities to further improve data quality and completeness to support the modelling and robustness of the evidence for environmental policymaking. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will enhance its assessments of the data submitted through informative inventory reports and evaluate the effectiveness and robustness of methodologies applied by Parties to collect and process data, with the aim of identifying gaps and challenges, as well as good practices and innovative solutions. Concurrently, it will provide technical advice to and strengthen capacities of the Parties to produce national reports on air emissions.

performance.title: Open-source software enables implementation of annex 11 of the Convention on International Transport of Goods under Cover of TIR Carnets
performance.narrative:
20.38 A lack of cost-effective and adaptable digital infrastructure has impeded the implementation of annex 11 of the TIR Convention, which governs the transition to fully electronic procedures in accordance with the Convention. To date, direct interconnection to the eTIR international system, the main data exchange hub of the electronic TIR procedure, requires investment of national resources and up to a year to complete. To enable access to the eTIR procedure, the subprogramme designed an open-source, technology-neutral, secure and scalable tool, the eTIR National Application, which can be installed and deployed within two weeks on existing national systems and allows countries with limited information technology capacity to implement paperless cross-border procedures, without the need to invest into costly and lengthy national system redesign. Subsequently, the subprogramme engaged with member States to build their capacity to roll out the tool.

performance.title: Strengthened cross-border cooperation on energy connectivity
performance.narrative:
20.77 Integrated and interconnected energy systems can enhance reliability, reduce costs and enable the deployment of renewable energy solutions at larger scales. In Central Asia, where national energy profiles and sources are often complementary, expanding cross-border electricity trade has been beneficial for advancing the energy transition, promoting economic diversification and creating jobs. Between 2023 and 2025, the subprogramme convened a series of policy dialogues and technical capacity-building workshops for policymakers, transition system operators and strategic energy planners from more than 20 member States on cross-border infrastructure development and renewable energy integration. The dialogues facilitated the exchange of best practices, the alignment of approaches and the identification of synergies across existing initiatives. To date, eight member States (Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Republic of Moldova, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Ukraine and Uzbekistan) have completed in-depth analyses on cross-border cooperation on energy connectivity and infrastructure. Subsequently, three member States in Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan) integrated cross-border cooperation measures into their national energy strategies, further strengthening the political commitment to expanding electricity trade across the region. Owing to the facilitated peer-to-peer engagements, the initiative has also gained traction beyond Central Asia, resulting in two member States (Georgia and Republic of Moldova) adopting new policies on cross-border energy connectivity.

entities.name: Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean
priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
21.2 The Commission will continue to support the development pillar of the United Nations, to foster economic integration at the subregional and regional levels, to support member States in the implementation of the 2030 Agenda and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals, the Pact for the Future, the Global Digital Compact and the international agreements stemming from the major summits and conferences in the development field, as well as to facilitate sustainable development by helping to bridge economic, social and environmental gaps within and among countries of the region and with other regions of the world. To that end, ECLAC will undertake applied research and evidence-based comparative analysis of development processes and provide normative and operational capacity-building, technical cooperation and advisory services in support of regional development efforts.
21.3 The Commission’s overall strategy for achieving the objectives of the programme is structured around 13 interdependent and complementary subprogrammes that are to be implemented using a multidisciplinary and integrated approach. The present proposed programme budget is also aimed at being responsive to the priorities, policy needs and emerging challenges of member States against a backdrop of increasing challenges and uncertainties.
21.4 To make progress towards more productive, inclusive and sustainable development and address the challenges faced by Latin America and the Caribbean, countries of the region would need to overcome three development traps: (a) low capacity for growth; (b) high inequality, low social mobility and weak social cohesion; and (c) weak institutional capacities and ineffective governance. For the region to achieve stronger growth, productive development policies for growth, investment, employment, productivity and more ample policy space are necessary, as well as strengthened governance and technical, operational, political and prospective capabilities of institutions. At the same time, evolving globalization trends and technological changes are transforming the production paradigm and impacting the implementation of the 2030 Agenda and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals in Latin American and Caribbean countries. A more ambitious approach can help to drive the structural transformations required to sustain the path towards the fulfilment of the 2030 Agenda and the Goals. To accelerate progress towards achieving the Goals, ECLAC will use key entry points, such as productive transformation policies, food systems, energy access and affordability, digital connectivity, education, jobs and social protection, and climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution.
21.5 At the fortieth session of the Commission, held in Lima in 2024, ECLAC presented to its member States the document Development Traps in Latin America and the Caribbean: Vital Transformations and How to Manage Them, in which it put forward a new proposal to analyse a number of transformations that can assist in the move towards a new development model, including: (a) productive transformation for higher, sustained, inclusive and sustainable growth; (b) transformation to reduce inequality and foster inclusion and social mobility; and (c) transformation to boost sustainability and combat climate change. The document includes various proposals for carrying out these transformations, taking into account developments in the global economy.
21.6 ECLAC will continue to offer its value proposition to member States by combining its think-tank and thought leadership role, its convening role through its intergovernmental platforms and subsidiary bodies, and its operational role by providing technical cooperation, peer learning, and advisory and capacity-building services, anchored in data and evidence-based analysis and understanding of the realities of the region. The Commission will continue to foster a multisectoral approach to development and to give a voice to countries in special situations, such as the one least developed country in the region, landlocked developing countries and Caribbean small island developing States and middle-income countries.
21.7 The Commission will continue to offer its intergovernmental architecture for consensus-building and regional dialogues, to analyse the key means of implementation of the 2030 Agenda and promote the exchange of best practices and lessons learned in its role as technical secretariat for the Committee of the Whole of ECLAC, the Caribbean Development and Cooperation Committee, the Regional Conference on Women in Latin America and the Caribbean, the Regional Council for Planning of the Latin American and Caribbean Institute for Economic and Social Planning, the Statistical Conference of the Americas of ECLAC, the Regional Conference on Population and Development in Latin America and the Caribbean, the Conference on Science, Innovation and Information and Communications Technologies, the Regional Conference on South-South Cooperation in Latin America and the Caribbean and the Regional Conference on Social Development in Latin America and the Caribbean, in addition to the Conference of the Parties to the Regional Agreement on Access to Information, Public Participation and Justice in Environmental Matters in Latin America and the Caribbean (Escazú Agreement), the Forum of Ministers and High-level Authorities on Housing and Urban Development of Latin America and the Caribbean, the Regional Intergovernmental Conference on Ageing and the Rights of Older Persons in Latin America and the Caribbean and the Ministerial Conference on the Information Society in Latin America and the Caribbean.
21.8 Furthermore, ECLAC will continue to provide integrated and comprehensive follow-up to world summits from a regional perspective and coordinate the region’s approach to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda. It will also continue to act as the secretariat of the Forum of the Countries of Latin America and the Caribbean on Sustainable Development, supporting the follow-up and review process of the implementation of the 2030 Agenda at the regional level, and the reporting by the Forum to the high-level political forum on sustainable development at the global level, thereby linking the national, regional and global dimensions of the process.
21.9 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, ECLAC will continue to work closely with the Governments of the region and other stakeholders, including the business community, academia and civil society, to reinforce links between national experiences and regional perspectives, comparability and exchange of good practices, and to provide effective technical cooperation services for transboundary issues. Furthermore, the Commission will continue its close coordination and collaboration with United Nations agencies, funds and programmes in the region and with the resident coordinator system, including through the Regional Collaborative Platform.
21.10 Collaboration will also continue with the Bretton Woods institutions, in particular the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, and with other relevant organizations, such as the Organization of American States, the Inter-American Development Bank, the Ibero-American General Secretariat and the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean. ECLAC will reinforce its close cooperation with various subregional integration mechanisms and strengthen its collaboration with private sector associations, non-governmental and civil society organizations, think tanks and academia to encourage policy dialogue and engagement in the implementation of the 2030 Agenda, which is driven primarily by member States. The Commission will continue its active participation to foster substantive global coordination among all participating entities in the United Nations Sustainable Development Group.
21.11 ECLAC will continue to enhance its bilateral and multilateral collaboration with partners within and outside the United Nations system, to strengthen its strategic partnerships and mobilize additional extrabudgetary resources to enhance the implementation of the programme of work and maximize its impact in beneficiary countries and at the regional level. The Commission will consolidate development partners’ trust and confidence by undertaking strategic dialogues with them on a regular basis, ensuring the efficient delivery of mandates, showing concrete achievements and providing comprehensive information on the use of their contributions.
21.12 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) The international community continues to be committed to implementing the 2030 Agenda and achieving the Sustainable Development Goals;
(b) The countries of Latin America and the Caribbean continue to support and attach high priority to multilateralism, regional and subregional cooperation and the gradual convergence of integration schemes with a view to broadening the opportunities for achieving economic, social and environmentally sustainable development;
(c) The regional and international communities support the member States of ECLAC and respond to their specific needs and concerns.
21.13 The Commission integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, and will continue to ensure that gender focal points (see General Assembly resolution 80/186) are consulted in programme formulation and that gender analysis (see Assembly resolution 79/223) is integrated into all areas under the Commission’s mandate.
21.14 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy and the ECLAC disability inclusion strategy (CEPALDIS), the Commission will continue to implement inclusive and comprehensive measures regarding accessibility, security and improvements in audiovisual technology in conference rooms, and reasonable adaptation of office spaces and furniture, to facilitate the full participation of persons with disabilities in the daily work of the Commission, with a view to further advancing their inclusion.

performance.title: A regional input-output table to inform evidence-based policymaking in Latin America and the Caribbean
performance.narrative:
21.25 In 2025, the subprogramme contributed to the strengthening of evidence-based policymaking in Latin America and the Caribbean by advancing analytical tools to support a deeper understanding of regional integration, productive structures and exposure to external shocks. Within this context, the subprogramme launched the regional input-output table for Latin America and the Caribbean, which connects the productive structures of 18 countries (10 from South America, 6 from Central America, Mexico and the Dominican Republic). The regional input-output table provides an instrument to conduct trade analysis in value-added terms, assess productive structures and value chains and estimate economic impacts under different demand and supply scenarios, directly supporting more informed public policy design. The subprogramme also undertook the joint construction of a multi-country table in collaboration with the statistics team of the European Commission Joint Research Centre and Eurostat. This collaboration enabled the interconnection of Latin America and the Caribbean with the European Union, the United States of America and Asia and the Pacific, helping to expand the scope and relevance of regional economic analysis.

planned.title: member States diversify their export basket through increased foreign sales of digitally delivered services
planned.narrative:
21.31 Exports of digitally delivered services represent an opportunity for Latin America and the Caribbean to tap into fast-growing global demand for computer services, as well as finance, insurance, business and creative services. However, their contribution to total exports remains relatively small in many countries, owing in part to limited capabilities in areas such as generation of statistics, the availability of specialized teams to promote services exports and attract foreign direct investment (FDI), understanding of trade barriers regarding digital services and the role of talent development. In this context, over the past two years the subprogramme has included analysis and policy recommendations in its annual flagship publication, has published specific research on the topic and has delivered capacity-building activities to raise awareness and support Governments to promote the development of this dynamic export sector.
Lessons learned and planned change
21.32 The lesson for the subprogramme was that promoting digitally delivered services exports would benefit from a holistic approach to the provision of technical support to member States in areas such as FDI attraction, trade regulations for digital services, skills development, statistics and coordination mechanisms. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will provide a holistic approach to technical support to help member States to make progress in all key areas to increase exports of digitally delivered services.

performance.title: Strengthened integration of a gender perspective into territorial productive development policies
performance.narrative:
21.39 Gender gaps are associated with challenges to inclusive and sustainable productive development, notably in value chains at the territorial level, with persistent occupational segregation and where women’s participation in decision-making roles remains limited. The subprogramme provided technical assistance to the government of Canelones, Uruguay, to strengthen the integration of a gender perspective into productive development policies, using the viticultural and vinicultural value chain as a pilot case. The subprogramme supported this process through analytical work, stakeholder engagement and capacity-building activities, including the development of a conceptual framework on gender-sensitive productive development policies, a gender analysis of the selected value chain and a set of policy recommendations aimed at addressing barriers to women’s full, equal and meaningful participation in territorial productive development. The subprogramme’s activities also facilitated dialogue and coordination with subnational authorities, contributing to the systematization of institutional interactions and supporting the translation of analytical findings into actionable policy inputs. As a result, the government strengthened its institutional capacities to integrate a gender perspective into productive development strategies and to advance coordinated actions across relevant departments.

The subprogramme supports countries by building capacities to evaluate and formulate resource mobilization policies. planned.narrative:
21.86 Care work can support social well-being, economic development and gender equality, yet it is disproportionately borne by women. As ageing and rising care demands intensify, public care services are an important policy lever for achieving gender equality. The subprogramme, in partnership with the International Labour Organization (ILO) and national stakeholders, is implementing a “simulator”, an online tool developed by ILO that ECLAC is tailoring to the region to provide data and analysis on the financial requirements for care policy investments and on the impacts on the labour force of care policies. To advance this work, ECLAC and ILO established a working group with stakeholders in Brazil (unions, the private sector and the Government).
Lessons learned and planned change
21.87 The lesson for the subprogramme was the importance of tailoring a global tool to the national context in countries where the online tool will be used, as shown in Brazil. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will engage policymakers to define scenarios and parameters based on national legislation and policies, enhancing the policy relevance of future assessments and continuing collaboration with ILO.

performance.title: Strengthened political dialogue and regional governance in the mining sector

21.120 The Conference of Mining Ministries of the Americas is a ministerial forum for discussing mining sector policies, sharing experiences, strengthening coordination among Governments and identifying opportunities for bilateral and regional cooperation that drive a productive and sustainable transformation in the region. The subprogramme provided technical support to the Conference in organizing its fifteenth meeting, a high-level, multisectoral dialogue, with the participation of authorities from 13 Latin American and Caribbean countries, plus Canada. As a result, the authorities approved new terms of reference for the Conference, strengthening its institutional framework, and agreed that ECLAC would assume the role of its technical secretariat. Together with the Conference’s coordinating committee, a biennial action plan is being prepared based on the themes prioritized at the meeting: productive development of the mining sector with added value, critical minerals, territorial development in mining, governance of mining operations and strengthening technical, operational and technological capacities in the mining sector.

performance.title: Adoption of the Regional Agenda on Governance of Planning and Public Management for Sustainable Development in Latin America and the Caribbean to guide long-term strategic planning
performance.narrative:
21.134 The Regional Council for Planning of the Latin American and Caribbean Institute for Economic and Social Planning, a subsidiary body of ECLAC, played an enabling role in promoting a broad, multi-stakeholder dialogue that helped identify regional progress, gaps and shared challenges. As a result of this collective and deliberative process – bringing together national planning authorities, academic experts and other key actors – the Regional Agenda on Governance of Planning and Public Management for Sustainable Development in Latin America and the Caribbean was adopted at the twentieth meeting of the Regional Council, held in October 2025 in Brazil. The agenda represents a substantive milestone and a collective commitment to guide long-term strategic planning, strengthen institutional capacities and consolidate more resilient, forward-looking and socially legitimate governance frameworks across the region, integrating four strategic areas: collaborative governance, foresight, coordination and evaluation. The new agenda will help align long-term planning instruments across different levels of government, support context-specific adaptations and foster more coherent, anticipatory and results-oriented development strategies throughout the region.

performance.title: Development of an integrative natural resources management approach for sargassum management in the Caribbean
performance.narrative:
21.174 Since 2011, large-scale sargassum seaweed influxes have posed significant environmental and socioeconomic challenges to Caribbean small island development States, posing a threat to tourism, fisheries, marine transportation, ecosystems, water salination and public health. In 2023, the Caribbean Development and Cooperation Committee specifically identified sargassum as a climate change-exacerbated threat. The subprogramme conducted data collection and research, which proposed an integrative natural resources management approach for sargassum management, incorporating case studies from Barbados, Saint Lucia, Trinidad and Tobago, and Guadeloupe, alongside insights, best practices and lessons on effective and sustained management from regional bodies, tertiary research institutions and the private sector, which led to the development of the public-led model for the sustainable management of sargassum blooms.

priorities: Effective functioning of the organization

overview.name: Ethics Office
objectives: The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to achieve and sustain an organizational culture of integrity, accountability and transparency, wherein all staff members observe and perform their functions consistent with the highest standards of integrity required under the Charter of the United Nations.

performance.title: Increased staff confidence in seeking advice on protection against retaliation
performance.narrative:
Ensuring that misconduct can be reported without fear of retaliation is essential for fostering integrity, transparency, and accountability across the Organization. The Office provides confidential advice, guidance and education on ethics-related matters, including issues concerning protection against retaliation. Over the years, the Office has observed a steady rise in requests related to protection against retaliation, especially requests for advice and preliminary reviews. These trends reflect several factors: the increasing complexity of operational environments; heightened global expectations around compliance and accountability; and shifts and uncertainty in staff work situations, which can be attributed to the ongoing management initiatives and resulting structural changes within the Organization. Early interventions, aimed at addressing concerns, preventing risks of retaliation, and redressing instances of retaliation, are critical for maintaining and strengthening trust among staff in the accountability framework of the Organization, and safeguarding its credibility. In 2025, the Office responded to 177 advice queries on retaliation, compared with 134 in 2024, reflecting an increase of 32 per cent and a continued upward trend since 2021. This sustained rise reflects growing staff confidence in seeking confidential advice and engaging with the Organization’s misconduct reporting framework at an early stage. Through targeted outreach aimed at strengthening staff knowledge of, and trust in, the Organization’s policy on protection against retaliation, the Office has supported staff in understanding and gaining confidence in the Organization’s misconduct reporting channels, contributing to a culture grounded in ethics, transparency, and accountability.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see figure 1.XXIX).

entities.name: Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific
priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
19.4 The programme strategy for 2027 is anchored in the principles and objectives of key global frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Pact for the Future and its Global Digital Compact, the Sevilla Commitment of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, the Doha Political Declaration of the “World Social Summit” under the title “the Second World Summit for Social Development” and the programmes of action and development agendas of the least developed countries, landlocked developing countries and small island developing States (countries in special situations). Together, these frameworks underpin the commitment of ESCAP to promoting multilateralism and international cooperation and advancing sustainable, people-centred and inclusive development in the region.
19.5 The Commission’s overall programme strategy is aimed at the balanced integration of the economic, social and environmental dimensions to advance sustainable development in Asia and the Pacific. It is implemented through nine subprogrammes, which collectively address the priorities of the region in areas such as macroeconomic policy and financing for development, trade facilitation and infrastructure connectivity, technology and innovation, sustainable management of natural resources and urban development, disaster risk reduction and resilience, social and demographic development and affordable and clean energy, while strengthening member States’ capacities to measure progress towards the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and their access to timely and quality evidence for informed policymaking. A central focus of the programme of work for 2027 remains on supporting countries in special situations by mainstreaming their needs as well as the relevant global programmes of action and agendas across all areas of work. The implementation of the programme of work is supported by the regular programme of technical cooperation and Development Account projects.
19.6 For 2027, the programme of work has been adjusted by strengthening the substantive linkages between the environment and issues related to disaster risk reduction, as reflected in the objective and strategy of subprogrammes 4 and 5 in line with an evaluation recommendation issued by the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS; see also para. 19.21). In consideration of the substantive proximity of environment, climate change and disaster-related issues and aiming to provide more integrated policy advice and effectively deliver on its mandates on environment and development and disaster risk reduction and management, ESCAP has aligned the structure of its programme of work with the thematic grouping of these issues in the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks of countries in the Asia-Pacific region.
19.7 To deliver on its mandates, ESCAP acts as a regional policy platform by convening intergovernmental and multi-stakeholder forums that foster dialogue and build consensus on regional and transboundary challenges. It also fulfils a normative function through the development and implementation of regional action programmes and framework agreements that guide policy alignment and cooperation among member States. Through its research, ESCAP delivers timely analytical work and innovative policy solutions, grounded in its suite of data-driven tools and knowledge repositories. These efforts are complemented by the Commission’s operational role, which focuses on providing evidence-based policy advice and demand-driven and context-specific technical assistance, enabling member States to translate regional commitments into tangible national outcomes. By offering capacity development initiatives and peer-to-peer exchanges, ESCAP also aims to strengthen institutional capacities and foster whole-of-government and whole-of-society approaches to accelerate progress towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.
19.8 In 2027, ESCAP will continue to convene the Asia-Pacific Forum on Sustainable Development as the central multi-stakeholder platform for the follow-up and review of the 2030 Agenda in the region. The Forum will provide an opportunity for countries to share experiences, identify regional priorities and develop policy recommendations that contribute to global discussions at the high-level political forum on sustainable development. ESCAP will also assist countries in preparing voluntary national reviews, including through the twinning programme and by enhancing policy coherence, data quality and stakeholder engagement in the process.
19.9 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the work of ESCAP will continue to be characterized by strong partnerships and collaboration across a broad and diverse range of stakeholders. The Commission collaborates with global, regional and subregional intergovernmental bodies and international organizations, as well as regional and local government associations, civil society networks and the private sector, in an open and transparent manner to promote durable solutions for regional and transboundary challenges and to advance the priorities of the Asia-Pacific region in global development processes. Building on its long-standing partnerships, ESCAP will pursue joint activities with, inter alia, international development banks and research institutes and will continue to promote North-South, South-South and triangular cooperation as key modalities for implementing its programme of work.
19.10 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, ESCAP works in close partnership with the other United Nations regional commissions and contributes to joint global analytical products and to projects implemented under the Development Account. It maintains close collaboration with the Office of the High Representative for the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries and Small Island Developing States to provide coordinated support to the countries in special situations in the region. ESCAP will provide secretariat services to the Regional Collaborative Platform for Asia and the Pacific, supporting issue-based coalitions, including co-leading two of the five issue-based coalitions, namely, the coalition on digital transformation with the International Telecommunication Union and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization and the coalition on raising ambitions on climate action and energy transition with the United Nations Environment Programme.
19.11 Through its subregional offices, ESCAP coordinates with resident coordinators and United Nations country teams, ensuring effective participation in common country assessments and United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks and coherence and complementarity between regional and national actions. It also promotes collaboration across the United Nations system that strengthens the integration of regional outcomes into national sustainable development strategies and reinforces the collective impact of the United Nations development system in the Asia-Pacific region.
19.12 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) National Governments maintain and strengthen their commitment to the Commission as the principal intergovernmental platform in the region for leveraging regional cooperation to meet transboundary and common challenges;
(b) Governments and other stakeholders continue to collaborate with the Commission in undertaking the proposed programme activities with the necessary capacity and resources;
(c) Extrabudgetary funding for technical cooperation continues to be available, and ESCAP is able to further mobilize voluntary contributions from State and non-State entities.
19.13 ESCAP integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as relevant and appropriate. Gender equality and the empowerment of women is a thematic area for subprogramme 6, while advancing the disaggregation of data, including disaggregation by sex, is a focus of subprogramme 7. In the 2027 programme plan, subprogrammes 2, 3, 6 and 7 and component 4 of subprogramme 8 specifically contribute results in this regard, while subprogrammes 2 to 9 mainstream gender equality and the empowerment of women in their respective strategies. In 2027, ESCAP will also continue to implement its gender equality policy and gender equality action plan to accelerate progress in gender equality through concerted actions across its programme of work.
19.14 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, ESCAP is committed to mainstreaming disability perspectives and ensuring the inclusion of persons with disabilities in all its work through its implementation of the ESCAP disability inclusion policy and its action plan. Subprogrammes 3, 5, 6 and 7 and component 4 of subprogramme 8 incorporate disability-specific interventions to support and empower persons with disabilities and, ultimately, to build disability-inclusive societies.

performance.title: Asia-Pacific countries’ priorities reflected in the global financing for development agenda
performance.narrative:
19.26 The Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, held in 2025, marked a critical milestone in advancing the global financing agenda through the adoption of the Sevilla Commitment. In preparation for the Conference, the subprogramme supported Asia-Pacific member States to channel regional perspectives into the process. This included organizing a high-level regional consultation on financing for development in Asia and the Pacific in December 2024, in collaboration with UNCTAD, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, which gathered 32 Governments, 27 international organizations, including United Nations entities, 29 civil society organizations and private sector representatives to shape common priorities.
19.27 To inform the regional consultation, the subprogramme prepared an issues paper entitled Strengthening Financing for Sustainable Development in Asia and the Pacific: a Discussion of Selected Policy Areas, which set out key regional challenges and policy options. The main messages of the regional consultation were summarized in the Chair’s summary and were shared with the co-facilitators of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development as perspectives from Asia and the Pacific. The subprogramme actively participated in the Conference, delivering statements in the plenary and the multi-stakeholder round tables to highlight Asia-Pacific priorities. It organized several side events with partners on select aspects of the implementation of the Sevilla Commitment, one jointly organized by all regional commissions. Many of the main messages were included in the Sevilla Commitment, which encourages enhanced regional follow-up processes, as part of the regional forums on sustainable development led by the regional economic commissions, with regular regional reporting on progress, regional committees and consultations on progress and priorities.

planned.narrative:
19.33 A transition to low-emission and climate-resilient economies has wide-ranging implications on macroeconomic resilience and development, while its success also relies on prudent and forward-looking macroeconomic policy choices that balance and find synergies across economic, social and environmental objectives. Supporting policy alignment between macroeconomic policy considerations and transformation strategies that enable sustainability and poverty reduction are thus a central component of the subprogramme’s work. The subprogramme has studied extensively the linkages between sustainable transformation and macroeconomic development and has been exploring economically viable paths of achieving such transitions.
Lessons learned and planned change
19.34 The lesson for the subprogramme was that operational guidelines and policy analysis tools, as well as a knowledge repository of practical policy options that have been tested in some countries, are essential for turning quality policy research into actual policy changes. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will develop such guidelines and tools, together with a repository of tested policy options, to support efforts by member States towards better alignment of macroeconomic policies with transformation needs for sustainability and poverty reduction.

19.41 The Trade Intelligence and Negotiation Adviser is an online tool designed to assist trade policymakers and researchers in carrying out analytical tasks commonly conducted as part of trade agreement negotiations. Since its launch in 2018, the subprogramme has gradually expanded the platform to include additional analytical features and cover an increasing number of economies. It has supported policymakers from more than 15 countries to strengthen their capacities in effectively using the tool to overcome challenges in trade negotiations.
19.42 Building on this foundation and at the request of the Government of Cambodia, the subprogramme developed the first dedicated national Trade Intelligence and Negotiation Adviser portal, featuring customized analytical modules for regional trade impact assessment, input-output simulation and market trends and analysis. Training for policymakers was conducted and enhanced national ownership and practical use of the tool. The new features, available on the national portal, also enabled the subprogramme to estimate sex-disaggregated labour impacts of trade measures. Following this pilot of nationalizing trade negotiation support, Bangladesh requested the development of a similar portal, demonstrating growing regional demand for support in strengthening trade negotiation capacities.
