19.49 The lesson for the subprogramme was that digital platforms for technology transfer must be complemented by active facilitation, strong institutional partnerships and structured follow-up to translate virtual collaboration into tangible adoption of technologies. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will strengthen the functionality of the Asia-Pacific technology transfer platform and the community of practice on climate technologies, and will operationalize the platform through regular engagement with technology providers, seekers, investors and policymakers. It will ensure that technology needs assessments shape platform content and services and will expand collaboration with international partners, academia and the private sector to enrich knowledge and mobilize financing for scale-up.

performance.title: Strengthened implementation of Early Warnings for All
performance.narrative:
19.83 The subprogramme strengthened the implementation of the Early Warnings for All initiative by scaling up regional cooperation to support the initiative and leveraged the ESCAP multi-donor trust fund for tsunami, disaster and climate preparedness. The subprogramme has delivered downscaled climate projection data and conducted training on impact-based forecasting to enhance capacities for anticipatory action in Cambodia, the Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Maldives, Nepal and Tajikistan, all of which are Early Warnings for All pilot countries. With the support of the trust fund, countries with an Indian Ocean coastline and countries with a Pacific Ocean coastline completed capacity assessments and adopted a standard methodology for measuring tsunami preparedness across ocean basins. Three additional strategic studies, namely, the 2025 evaluation of the trust fund, a 20-year cost-benefit analysis and a regional multi-hazard coastal vulnerability assessment, were also endorsed by the Advisory Council to the trust fund and informed the trust fund strategy for the period 2025–2030.

performance.title: Strengthened regional dialogue and engagement on and joint review of safe, orderly and regular migration in Asia and the Pacific

19.97 With international migration contributing significantly to socioeconomic development in Asia and the Pacific, the subprogramme, in close collaboration with the International Organization for Migration and other United Nations entities, guided a review process that culminated in the Asia-Pacific Regional Review of Implementation of the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration, convened in Bangkok from 4 to 6 February 2025. The intergovernmental meeting brought together 30 ESCAP member States, 20 international organizations and about 100 civil society organizations. The meeting provided an opportunity for Governments to assess implementation of the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration and exchange valuable lessons. Through stakeholder consultations and side events, the meeting ensured a whole-of-society and whole-of-government approach to the regional review.

performance.title: Leveraging data to drive progress in civil registration
performance.narrative:
19.110 The subprogramme has adopted an integrated approach to strengthening civil registration and vital statistics systems across the region by combining an intergovernmental process with joint analysis and targeted support for capacity-building in countries. The decade-long regional action framework on civil and vital registration has fostered collaboration among member States and provided a platform for sharing good practices. In 2025, the subprogramme serviced the Third Ministerial Conference on Civil Registration and Vital Statistics in Asia and the Pacific, which reflected growing political commitment and showcased the power of partnerships. It brought together member States, associate members, United Nations entities and civil society organizations to take concrete steps towards building more inclusive and resilient civil registration and vital statistics systems. Youth played a prominent role at the event, sharing their experiences and advocating for the importance of universal birth registration with senior policymakers. In addition, the subprogramme has strengthened national capacities in using demographic analysis to drive significant progress in birth registration in Asia and the Pacific. A key strategy of the subprogramme has been the use of civil registration and vital statistics inequality assessments, which identify disparities in registration by gender, geography and characteristics of parents and children. The assessments are essential for transforming the vision of universal civil registration and vital statistics into a reality and help to ensure that all individuals can access their rights and essential services.

performance.title: Strengthened capacity for integration of economic valuation of ecosystem goods and services into policy and planning by Pacific Governments
performance.narrative:
19.123 The 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, outlining key priorities of the Pacific and endorsed by the Pacific leaders in 2022, highlights valuing the Pacific region’s ecosystem goods and services as one of the key aspects of the sustainable management of resources. The component, in collaboration with the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat and the secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environmental Programme, and with support from the regular programme of technical cooperation, developed a user-friendly online guide to support Pacific Governments in utilizing the economic valuation of ecosystem goods and services for their policy decision-making, where appropriate. The mapping of existing assessments of the economic value of ecosystem goods and services in the Pacific was conducted and reviewed by two expert group meetings. A regional workshop on ecosystem valuation attended by Pacific government officials validated the utility of the online guide and served as a forum for peer-to-peer learning, including experiences from Asia.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: amplify the Pacific’s voice to advance a more tailored United Nations multidimensional vulnerability index
planned.narrative:
19.129 Pacific small island developing States face chronic debt stress and strongly advocated for the adoption of the United Nations multidimensional vulnerability index as a tool to capture the complex structural vulnerabilities of small island developing States. By moving beyond purely economic measures, the multidimensional vulnerability index also incorporates social and environmental dimensions, offering the potential to improve access to concessional finance and development support for the Pacific. The component supported Pacific small island developing States in assessing the relevance of the multidimensional vulnerability index and identifying ways to refine it to better capture their specific vulnerability challenges.
Lessons learned and planned change
19.130 The lesson for the component was that stronger collaboration among Pacific small island developing States is needed to link subregional experiences with global multidimensional vulnerability index initiatives. In applying the lesson, the component will support Pacific leaders to advocate for the formation of common positions to amplify the voices of Pacific small island developing States at the regional and global levels. It plans to strengthen the integration of Pacific insights into position briefs and prepare these briefs for high-level meetings to ensure that the index reflects small island developing States’ evolving vulnerabilities.

19.137 Reducing emissions in East and North-East Asia by the middle of the twenty-first century requires accelerated climate action at the local level. The component promoted local climate action by facilitating the exchange of knowledge, experiences and good practices among cities. At the annual International Forum on Low Carbon Cities, the component brings together national and city-level stakeholders to exchange policy practices and discuss innovations and technologies for sustainable urban solutions in the context of changing demographics and lifestyles. To strengthen local climate action, the component also issued a booklet on subregional cooperation and policy alignment for reducing urban greenhouse gas emissions through city networks in the subregion. To strengthen the priorities related to trade, trade facilitation and regional integration of the Awaza Programme of Action for Landlocked Developing Countries for the Decade 2024–2034, the component organized an expert group meeting with representatives of member States to develop recommendations on strengthening the subregion’s trade by developing mutually complementary trade digitalization and environmentally sustainable trade facilitation measures, as well as promoting regional trade initiatives in North and Central Asia.

19.164 The component has worked to explore the areas of knowledge exchange and cooperation on the water and climate change nexus, recognizing its critical importance for sustainable development in the subregion. Furthermore, the component convened two virtual subregional multi-stakeholder reviews of Sustainable Development Goal 6 on clean water and sanitation as part of its annual South and South-West Asia subregional forum on sustainable development. These reviews provided a platform for Governments, experts and civil society to assess progress, share lessons and explore integrated approaches to address the challenges relating to the water and climate nexus. These collective efforts supported the activities relating to ESCAP resolution 81/3 on strengthening cooperation on the water and climate change nexus for sustainable development in Asia and the Pacific, reaffirming the regional commitment to integrated action and positioning the component as a key contributor to advancing water-climate cooperation for sustainable development.

19.178 The ASEAN Multi-Stakeholder Forum on Sustainability was established in 2025 to integrate several key platforms aimed at advancing the Sustainable Development Goals in South-East Asia. These included the High-Level Brainstorming Dialogue, the ASEAN Forum on Sustainable Development Goals with national development planning agencies, and the South-East Asia Multi-Stakeholder Forum on Sustainable Development Goals implementation. The component has consolidated these initiatives to streamline efforts, optimize resource use and enhance audience engagement. A major milestone of this integrated approach was the inclusion, for the first time, of participants from ASEAN sectoral bodies, including senior officials from the political and sociocultural communities, as well as national development planning agencies. Notably, the Forum strengthened engagement between government officials and a broader range of stakeholders, including civil society organizations, the private sector, academia and youth groups, which are not typically involved in formal ASEAN processes. entities.name: Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia
priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
22.3 The Commission’s programme of work for 2027 remains guided by universal principles and rights, aligned with its mandates, and centred on tailored and timely support to member States in their efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. To deliver on this commitment, ESCWA will continue to provide evidence-based, novel policy options, underpinned by analysis made possible by its suite of interactive, data-driven modelling and policy simulation tools and knowledge repositories; to provide technical advice and enhance human and institutional capacities, including through peer-to-peer exchanges and the promotion of South-South and interregional collaboration; to leverage its convening role to promote inclusive dialogue, at the national and regional levels and forge consensus on viable development solutions; and to advocate for whole-of-government and whole-of-society approaches to accelerate progress against the Goals and their targets, while championing the region’s perspective through a global lens. The programme of work remains focused on high-impact interventions as a means of achieving inclusive and equitable development outcomes, which address the specific needs of groups in vulnerable situations, including women, young people, older persons and persons with disabilities; and the diverse and specific challenges of least developed and middle-income countries and countries in conflict, in line with the Doha Programme of Action for the Least Developed Countries for the Decade 2022–2031.
22.4 As defined by the objectives of the six subprogrammes, the Commission’s programme of work remains focused on areas such as climate action and the integrated management of water resources; the transition to new and renewable sources of energy, sustainable food systems and circular economy approaches; multidimensional poverty reduction and inclusive social protection; social and gender justice, women’s economic empowerment and improved access to labour markets, as part of the commitment to “leave no one behind”; macroeconomic, fiscal and trade policies, competitiveness of the business environment, and opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises; improved access to innovative sources of development finance and sustainable debt management; information technology and statistics; the transparency and accessibility of public institutions, including through digitization; innovation and digital transformation; and governance, the assessment and mitigation of transboundary risks, including conflict, and boosting the effectiveness and efficiency of public administration.
22.5 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, ESCWA will sustain its strategic partnership with the League of Arab States and other intergovernmental organizations, as well as the Islamic Development Bank, the Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development and other relevant financial institutions. It will also promote South-South and triangular cooperation and further enhance its outreach to academic institutions, think tanks, civil society organizations and the private sector. New partnership opportunities will also be pursued to enable the Commission to continue to deliver support to member States, including the production of knowledge products and the convening of policymakers and other stakeholders.
22.6 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, as outlined in General Assembly resolution 72/279, the Commission will continue to discharge its function of co-Vice Chair of the Regional Collaborative Platform for the Arab States and its subsidiary issue-based coalitions. It will also work closely with the Development Coordination Office, resident coordinator offices, United Nations country teams, other regional commissions, the World Bank, the Department of Economic and Social Affairs and the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development to ensure that any support that it provides to member States is relevant, timely and effective and fully aligned with the commitments outlined within the national United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks, while avoiding the duplication of interventions and gaps.
22.7 With regard to external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Sufficient opportunities for protecting and leveraging development gains for further progress towards the implementation of the 2030 Agenda exist, notwithstanding the increasingly volatile global, regional and national dynamics and increased need for urgent coordinated humanitarian action and peacebuilding efforts;
(b) Member States remain engaged and committed to collaborating on a range of sustainable development initiatives, with a specific focus on transboundary priorities and responses to emerging challenges;
(c) Development partners remain committed to collaboration on and joint implementation of development initiatives, including their prioritization, identification of innovative solutions and opportunities for specific contributions;
(d) The Commission’s operational preparedness and adaptive capacity enable it to maintain business continuity, even amid compromised safety and security emerging from conflict, political and social instability and/or natural disasters.
22.8 ESCWA integrates a gender perspective into its activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. This includes the provision of support to its member States in developing inclusive, gender-sensitive policy frameworks to address a wide range of economic and social issues and in enhancing the capacities of national institutions and actors, in addition to developing publications and technical materials specific to advancing gender equality and women’s economic empowerment in the region. The Commission’s commitment to gender equality remains in line with the United Nations global accountability framework and Economic and Social Council resolution 2023/11.
22.9 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, ESCWA will continue to make policy options available to member States and advocate in favour of the adoption of national frameworks that promote the greater inclusion and empowerment of persons with disabilities, including enhanced access to labour markets and basic social services.
22.10 ESCWA will integrate issues related to older persons and young people across its programme of work with the aim of augmenting their role as active contributors to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda. In this context, the Commission will: (a) promote their meaningful participation and inclusion in development dialogues; (b) generate and disseminate knowledge essential for developing policies that are responsive to the needs of young people and older persons; (c) facilitate peer-to-peer learning among member States within the region and beyond; and (d) support member States in the adoption and implementation of polices that protect the rights of young people and older persons.

performance.narrative:
22.21 As identified in the Doha Programme of Action, the least developed countries in the Arab region continue to face barriers to energy access, including a persistent lack of access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy, low electrification rates, a reliance on traditional biomass systems and limited access to finance. To address these barriers, the subprogramme, together with regional and international partners, developed financial instruments, business models and digital toolkits to mitigate risks and promote scalable energy solutions. Member States benefited from knowledge products on financing approaches and project models for small-scale initiatives, while policy options and investment frameworks were prepared to guide the effective use of financial instruments and to mobilize capital for sustainable energy projects. Those efforts were further strengthened through regional workshops and capacity-building activities. This enabled officials and local actors, including rural women entrepreneurs, to apply microfinance, cost-accounting and project-development tools.

performance.title: Young people in the Arab region are connected with employment opportunities
performance.narrative:
22.34 Arab labour markets face growing pressure as increasing numbers of educated young people enter the workforce amid an often-limited expansion of formal employment, leading to many young people entering low-paid or informal employment. To support the creation of an enabling environment that enhances the access of young people to decent employment, the subprogramme partnered with the Governments of Egypt, Jordan and Lebanon, 7 Arab universities and more than 30 private sector entities to launch an initiative targeting policymakers, businesses and young people. The subprogramme brought together all stakeholders to discuss labour market policies and presented policy recommendations. Young people were provided with free training in areas where there was a mismatch between skills available and skills needed in the labour market, in order to meet private sector labour demand, and were provided with private sector employment opportunities. Policymakers received tailored policy advice and recommendations and participated in South-South exchanges, and the private sector benefited from guidance on growth and youth employment strategies.

performance.title: Strengthened national accounts in the Arab region for evidence-based policymaking
performance.narrative:
22.60 Robust and reliable national accounts support informed, evidence-based policymaking and sound economic management in all countries, including in countries affected by armed conflict where data gaps may hinder recovery planning and investment decisions. The subprogramme supported Jordan and the Syrian Arab Republic in aligning their national accounts with the 2008 System of National Accounts, to help them to build institutional capacities, enhancing methodological rigour and ensuring international comparability. In the Syrian Arab Republic, the subprogramme coordinated with the planning and statistics authority and national stakeholders to compile gross domestic product data across the 17 core economic activities, in accordance with international statistical standards for national accounts, thereby restoring the country’s ability to produce internationally comparable macroeconomic statistics for the first time in recent years, enabling policymakers to ground recovery strategies and policy dialogue in reliable evidence. In Jordan, the subprogramme enhanced national accounts capacity by expanding coverage to priority areas, including the non-formal sector.

planned.title: policymakers use the integrated regional data platform for evidence-based policymaking
planned.narrative:
22.66 The adoption of modernized statistical systems and integrated regional data can help to meet today’s complex and fast-changing policy needs. By leveraging digital technologies, artificial intelligence and interoperable data platforms, countries can generate timely and comparable statistics to monitor progress made in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and address cross-border challenges such as climate change, migration and regional economic integration. In 2024, the Arab Development Portal was upgraded to harmonize statistical methodologies, integrate alternative data sources and link data with policy analysis through artificial intelligence-enabled data-processing and interoperability layers, enabling the subprogramme to support member States in enhancing statistical systems and integrating alternative data sources and digital solutions in order to support Goal monitoring and inform policymaking.
Lessons learned and planned change
22.67 The lesson for the subprogramme was that addressing individual statistical gaps in isolation might limit the ability of member States to generate integrated evidence for policymaking. In applying the lesson, and building on the 2024 upgrade, the subprogramme will further enhance the Arab Development Portal, transforming it into a regional data-policy integration system by embedding artificial intelligence-driven predictive analytics, geospatial modelling and policy scenario simulation tools to support interactive and forward-looking analysis. It will also strengthen member States’ capacity to generate disaggregated indicators and integrate alternative and big data sources into policy design and impact assessments using shared regional data frameworks, thereby promoting coordination and harmonization for comparable, policy-relevant data and statistics.

priorities: Maintenance of international peace and security

overview.name: Office of the Focal Point for Delisting
objectives: 207. The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to provide an independent review of delisting requests submitted by, or on behalf of, an individual, group, undertaking or entity designated on the lists of the sanctions committees established by the Security Council (the petitioner), excluding the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions Committee, in accordance with annex I to resolution 2744 (2024).
strategy:
208. To contribute to the objective, the Focal Point will carry out the tasks set out in the delisting procedures detailed in annex I to resolution 2744 (2024), which provides an outline of the process for information-gathering, dialogue and committee discussion and decision upon receipt of a delisting request, and in other relevant resolutions.
209. The above-mentioned work is expected to result in strengthened due process in Security Council sanctions regimes, through fair and clear delisting procedures, and the timely processing of requests for delisting, travel ban and asset freeze exemptions, as well as communications related to cases of false or mistaken identity and post-delisting challenges.
210. With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional and local levels, including in the context of information-sharing, the Focal Point will cooperate with Member States, such as members of the Security Council, and the designating State(s) and State(s) of residence and nationality or incorporation of the petitioners.
211. With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Focal Point will cooperate with any relevant sanctions committee’s groups or panels of experts or monitoring teams, as well as any relevant United Nations envoys engaged in negotiations and peace processes relevant to the sanctions. In the context of safety and security, information technology security and logistics, the Focal Point will also cooperate with the Department of Safety and Security, the Office of Information and Communications Technology and UNDP.
212. To improve the effectiveness of sanctions imposed by the Security Council, the Focal Point will, as requested, engage with the Informal Working Group of the Security Council on General United Nations Security Council Sanctions Issues established pursuant to resolution 2744 (2024).
213. With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Member States comply with the resolutions of the Security Council and cooperate with the mission;
(b) The security situation allows the mission to conduct missions, as needed;
(c) Petitioners and other relevant actors are aware of the new delisting procedure outlined in resolution 2744 (2024).

performance.title: Strengthen due process by ensuring fairer procedures for petitioners
performance.narrative:

The activities in 2025 focused on the recruitment of the Focal Point in coordination with the Office of Legal Affairs and in consultation with the Informal Working Group of the Security Council on General United Nations Security Council Sanctions Issues, on recruitment outreach activities to attract a wide pool of candidates, the review of all relevant sanctions committees’ guidelines on the Focal Point delisting procedures, and the establishment of the Office and its operational readiness.

planned.title: Strengthened due process through well-informed decision-making on delisting requests
planned.narrative:
217. While the Office of the Focal Point for Delisting has been established, the appointment was not completed in 2025, as a result of which the planned target was not met. The Secretariat undertook the recruitment of the Focal Point and presented additional candidates to the Informal Working Group of the Security Council on General United Nations Security Council Sanctions Issues for its consideration and approval. In addition, the Secretariat conducted substantial outreach activities to Member States, international and non-governmental organizations, providing briefings on the new delisting procedures and recruitment process of the Focal Point.
218. The Focal Point supports sanctions committees in their consideration of delisting requests. Upon receipt of a delisting request, the Focal Point verifies that the petition properly addresses the original designation criteria and engages with petitioners and relevant stakeholders to gather relevant information. The Focal Point then prepares a confidential comprehensive report articulating the principal arguments in respect of the delisting request. This report assists the relevant committee in its decision-making process, thereby contributing to the strengthening of due process. The Focal Point is also mandated to submit two biannual reports on its activities to the Informal Working Group of the Security Council on General United Nations Security Council Sanctions Issues and participates in various forums to raise awareness of the new delisting procedure.
Lessons learned and planned change
219. The lesson for the mission was the need for the Focal Point for De-listing, in consultation with the Security Council Informal Working Group on General Security Council Sanctions Issues to be appointed without further delay. In applying the lesson, the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs will intensify additional outreach efforts to identify suitable candidates for the Informal Working Group’s consideration.

performance.title: The establishment of the Technical Committee on Youth, together with other trust-building initiatives, strengthened dialogue, reduced tensions and raised hope among Cypriots, improving their situation vis-à-vis prospects for peace process
performance.narrative:
At the broader-format informal meeting with the guarantor powers on 17 and 18 March 2025, hosted by the Secretary-General, the parties agreed on six trust-building initiatives, including the establishment of a new technical committee on youth. A further broader-format meeting in July 2025 resulted in additional four initiatives agreed to build trust. The Secretary-General hosted the two leaders again in September 2025, and the United Nations facilitated meetings in November and December 2025 and as of May 2026, four additional leaders’ meetings were held. While the number of meetings with the leaders and their negotiating teams in 2025 remained comparable to 2024, the number of meetings and the outputs of the technical committees increased, including in quality, with projects that improved the daily lives of Cypriots.

planned.title: Furthering dialogue as a conflict management tool and an inclusive and sustainable peace process towards a negotiated settlement
planned.narrative:
In 2025, the mission’s work contributed to the holding of and support to 63 bilateral and joint meetings with the leaders and their representatives and 358 meetings of the technical committees, falling short of the planned target of 140 and 410 meetings, respectively. This shortfall stemmed primarily from the absence of active negotiations and the shift toward planning for the high-level meetings with the two sides and guarantor powers. In addition, no meetings at the level of the two leaders were held during the pre-election campaign period preceding the change in leadership in the Turkish Cypriot community in October 2025.
In 2027, the Mission will focus on the support to high-level meetings, trust-building activities, the work of the technical committees and the use of dialogue as an effective early warning and conflict prevention tool. Amid a persistent challenging regional landscape, additional trust-building measures to benefit Cypriots across the island for 2026 and 2027 will also be pursued.
Lessons learned and planned change
The lesson learned in 2025 was that despite tangible progress on trust building initiatives, including those delegated to the technical committees, public attention focused on measures not yet implemented, negatively impacting the atmosphere between the two communities. Considering its unique role in bridging divides, building trust and fostering cooperation in Cyprus, as underscored by the OIOS evaluation, the mission will strengthen its planning tools to improve effectiveness and responsiveness, particularly regarding the technical committees as trust-building bodies. Once trust-building initiatives have received the necessary political support for implementation, the mission will also help the technical committees shorten implementation timelines.

performance.title: A fair and equitable personal transitional allowance model
performance.narrative:
31.I.12 The personal transitional allowance was first introduced in 1992 to mitigate sudden decreases in the post adjustment multiplier upon the implementation of negative survey results. While the existing model had functioned adequately in most duty stations, the Commission identified shortcomings in cases involving exceptionally large personal transitional allowances, which resulted in prolonged payment periods and disparities between staff receiving the allowance and those who were not, creating tensions based on fairness and equity. For example, a personal transitional allowance promulgated in 2023 for Lebanon was projected to last until 2028. To address this, the Commission formed a focus group on extremely large personal transitional allowances to examine the issue and propose options to strengthen fairness and equity. The Commission considered the findings of the focus group and the application of revised parameters to existing allowances.

8.III.15 The end of the Assad regime in December 2024 presented an opportunity for the Mechanism to engage with the Government of the Syrian Arab Republic on accountability. The Mechanism supported Syrian-led transitional justice efforts by sharing knowledge and expertise related to aspects of the Mechanism’s mandate, including evidence preservation and analysis and insights from its engagement with competent jurisdictions, civil society, and victims and survivors. The Mechanism conducted regular diplomatic missions to Damascus, which included meetings with the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other justice actors. In July 2025, the Mechanism hosted members of the national committee on transitional justice in Geneva to discuss how the Mechanism could support the implementation of its mandate and participated in a forum on transitional justice with the same members and civil society convened by the International Center for Transitional Justice. The Mechanism also participated in various engagements in the Syrian Arab Republic, notably the day of dialogue hosted by the European Union in Damascus in close coordination with the Government of the Syrian Arab Republic and civil society, and an event on justice and accountability for chemical weapons use in the Syrian Arab Republic with Syrian justice actors.

objectives: 8.II.2 The objective, to which the Mechanism contributes, is to ensure the accountability of perpetrators and justice for victims of the most serious international crimes and violations of international law committed in Myanmar since 2011.

performance.title: Competent authorities have access to forensic analysis of open-source information
performance.narrative:
8.II.15 There is a significant volume of open-source information online and, more broadly, in the public domain regarding serious international crimes committed in Myanmar. Owing to the critical importance of promptly identifying and capturing such information, the Mechanism prioritized and integrated the collection and analysis of open-source information across all investigations. The Mechanism uses advanced methods that include the discovery, verification and authentication of large volumes of open-source materials, including videos, photographs, geospatial imagery, audio clips, public documents, official pronouncements and various databases and platforms. The Mechanism’s methodologies optimize the forensic value of open-source information to criminal prosecutions. For example, by using specialized tools, the Mechanism can identify where and when videos and images were taken, extract investigative leads from large data sets and enhance and authenticate videos, images and audio clips to detect “fake” content generated by artificial intelligence. In addition, the Mechanism can identify public statements by individuals that reveal their knowledge, intent or effective control over crimes to help to establish links between senior leaders and the crimes committed. The Mechanism analyses and cross-references open-source evidence with other evidence and prepares analysis that is available for sharing with competent authorities. Given the Mechanism’s lack of access to the crime scenes, open-source investigations are crucial to help to build cases for future prosecutions. Taking into account reduced extrabudgetary resources, the Mechanism prioritized the production of in-depth analysis, including incident reports, geolocation, chronolocation, data visualization and target profiles.

performance.title: Strengthened innovation, business and job opportunities in Africa and Latin America for youth start-ups and entrepreneurs
performance.narrative: 13.16 As global economies face rapid transformation due to digitalization, climate change and rising youth unemployment, fostering entrepreneurship among young people is critical for inclusive economic growth and sustainable job creation. ITC partnered with a development cooperation organization to jointly deliver the Youth Startup Academy. Anchored in co-creation, the Academy model combined the expertise of local business support organizations with the knowledge tools of ITC to incubate start-up businesses. Strong involvement of country-based institutions has set solid foundations for local ownership and sustainability. Following a successful roll-out in Uganda, the Academy was replicated in Colombia, adapted to its socioeconomic environment and mainly aimed at young people in less developed regions. Through ITC capacity-building support and tailored advisory solutions, young entrepreneurs seized new business opportunities with international investors and trade partners.

entities.name: Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
priorities: Effective coordination of humanitarian assistance efforts

overview.name: Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
strategy:
27.I.2 In 2025, overall humanitarian funding fell to its lowest levels in more than a decade, while nearly 117 million people were forcibly displaced by armed conflict and violence. Armed conflicts continued to take a heavy toll on civilians, protection services ceased in many areas for a vast majority of affected populations, and the impacts of climate change exacerbated humanitarian needs. The global food security crisis affected over 295 million people as acute hunger spread and intensified, marking a sixth consecutive annual increase. In addition, for the first time in this century, two famines unfolded simultaneously.
27.I.3 In the face of these challenges, the Office will continue to enhance the coordination of effective and efficient delivery of humanitarian assistance, together with humanitarian organizations. In line with the humanitarian reset, the Office will work to strengthen a humanitarian system that is locally led and globally supported, driven by communities’ expressed priorities and focused on the most severe needs. By simplifying coordination, reducing duplication and bureaucracy and transitioning to locally led responses, the Office, in collaboration with relevant United Nations entities and other humanitarian organizations, will deliver faster and more accountable humanitarian action.
27.I.4 The Office will continue to develop and promote a common policy on emerging issues and trends with significant humanitarian implications for the United Nations system and its partners; coordinate response to humanitarian emergencies; mobilize United Nations capacity to expedite the provision of humanitarian assistance; and strengthen anticipatory approaches and early warning early action systems, with special attention paid to those most affected by emergency situations and to the need to promote, fund and enable locally led humanitarian action. In addition, the Office will advocate and contribute to better preparedness for more timely humanitarian assistance in emergencies; advocate on humanitarian issues; and strengthen the analysis and availability of timely information on emergencies and natural disasters, in accordance with its mandate. The Office will also support the mobilization of resources for countries and communities facing humanitarian emergencies, including host communities, by scaling up timely and predictable funding, advancing innovative and anticipatory financing mechanisms and strengthening partnerships with development partners and international financial institutions to prevent, reduce and respond to humanitarian suffering. Furthermore, the Office will continue to advocate for safe and unhindered humanitarian access, the safety and security of humanitarian personnel, and respect for international humanitarian law.
27.I.5 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will continue to work with national and local governments, affected communities and other stakeholders, including regional disaster management and response organizations, other regional and subregional organizations, private sector actors and first responders, to promote principled, timely and effective humanitarian responses.
27.I.6 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will continue, through the Inter-Agency Standing Committee and its subsidiary bodies, to coordinate the development of guidance for the humanitarian system, including on operations policy development and advocacy and supporting implementation of the Secretary-General’s Action Agenda on Internal Displacement. The Office will provide and manage global platforms, such as the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination Team mechanism and the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group, to pool resources and facilitate a coordinated response to humanitarian crises. The Office’s country, regional and liaison offices are strategically located to work with governments and assist in humanitarian preparedness and response. The Office will also collaborate closely with United Nations agencies, funds and programmes, at both the Headquarters and country levels, to streamline the current guidance and indicators associated with thematic humanitarian issues and scale back the frequency and scope of updates to field guides, maps and other reference tools to enable core efforts to focus on contexts where humanitarian needs are greatest and event-driven updates. A humanitarian data collaborative will be established to prevent the siloing of information and encourage humanitarian partners to utilize and contribute to existing platforms rather than building new ones. This will enable effective and consistent system-wide response strategies that meet the humanitarian needs of people in vulnerable situations and minimize duplication and gaps in response efforts.
27.I.7 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) The impact of the global economic contraction, compounded by the impacts of natural disasters and armed conflicts, will continue to be felt and will increase the vulnerability of people;
(b) Natural disasters will continue to increase in frequency and magnitude, owing, among other things, to the adverse effects of climate change;
(c) Humanitarian needs and funding requirements will remain high, while humanitarian financing may continue to decline significantly.
27.I.8 The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, including by promoting the participation and leadership of women in decision-making.
27.I.9 Under the leadership of the Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs, as Chair of the Inter-Agency Standing Committee, the Office will continue to promote and operationalize system-wide commitments on protection from sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment across humanitarian coordination, advocacy and the humanitarian programme cycle. In 2027, the Office will support humanitarian coordinators and humanitarian country teams to sustain inter-agency networks, strengthen accountability frameworks by transitioning standard operating procedures into policy instructions, and reinforce risk management processes to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment across the humanitarian system.
27.I.10 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will strengthen efforts to ensure that humanitarian programming and response are inclusive of persons with disabilities, with a particular focus on integrating their needs into humanitarian data systems. Building on gaps identified during the previous implementation phase, the Office will develop a comprehensive action plan outlining the institutional and operational adjustments required to ensure disability inclusion.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: strengthened system-wide diplomacy to defend humanitarian principles, secure access and protect civilians
planned.narrative:
27.I.40 Humanitarian action is affected by political decisions, conflict dynamics and restrictions on humanitarian access. Diplomatic engagement in support of humanitarian action is a critical tool for defending humanitarian principles and addressing constraints that limit access to affected populations and the protection of civilians. Such engagement, consistent with General Assembly resolution 46/182 and the text contained in the annex thereto, entails engaging with decision-makers, parties to armed conflict and other relevant actors to secure and sustain humanitarian access, promote respect for international humanitarian law and safeguard the operating environment for humanitarian operations. These efforts are undertaken strictly within the Office’s humanitarian coordination mandate. In late 2025, the subprogramme began providing structured support to the principals of United Nations entities under the humanitarian pillar to enhance coordinated diplomatic engagement with Member States and other actors. This support is aimed at ensuring greater coherence, consistency and collective leverage in addressing structural impediments to humanitarian action.
Lessons learned and planned change
27.I.41 The lesson for the subprogramme, amid an increasingly challenging and polarized operating environment, was that collective diplomacy can be more effective in advancing humanitarian goals. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme supported the development of a pilot initiative by the Inter-Agency Standing Committee to strengthen collective diplomatic engagements to influence circumstances and actors restricting humanitarian access in several locations. The subprogramme will reinforce the coordination and support structures to operationalize this system-wide initiative.

27.I.47 Timely, well-coordinated international assistance is critical to saving lives and reducing suffering in sudden-onset emergencies and depends on common standards, interoperable procedures and predictable coordination arrangements among national authorities and international responders. In 2025, the subprogramme updated three key guidance documents: the United Nations Disaster Assessment and Coordination handbook, the International Search and Rescue Advisory Group guidelines and the United Nations humanitarian civil-military coordination handbook. These updates helped to ensure that Member State response mechanisms, international urban search and rescue teams and humanitarian civil-military coordination actors worked with harmonized procedures that reflect current operational practice, lessons from recent emergencies and the evolving role of local responders and private sector partners in the humanitarian programme cycle.

performance.title: Crisis-affected people received data-driven support from humanitarian actors
performance.narrative:
27.I.60 Each day, new information is produced about humanitarian crises around the world, yet critical warning signs can often go unnoticed. Humanitarians may sense that a crisis is worsening but lack the evidence needed to secure funding or to mobilize resources. Without timely, clear analysis, opportunities for intervention can be missed. To address these challenges, the Centre for Humanitarian Data of the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs developed the Humanitarian Data Exchange: signals, which monitors key humanitarian data sets and generates automated alerts when conditions deteriorate, enhancing resource allocation and response times. In addition to providing timely alerts, Signals offers historical trend analysis delivers crucial context for emerging crises, enabling the United Nations Central Emergency Response Fund to make informed funding decisions. For example, a Signal in January 2025 determined that armed conflict in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo had contributed to the displacement of more than 900,000 people over a period of several weeks. While the Central Emergency Response Fund was already considering an allocation of funding, Signals’ historical trend analysis indicated that was the largest displacement associated with armed conflict in more than five years. As a result, the Fund increased its allocation. Since the launch of Signals in June 2024, other organizations, including the International Rescue Committee and GOALPrime Nigeria have also used it to allocate funds, protect staff and save lives. For example, a Signal flagged severe disaster-driven displacement across Nigeria due to flooding from heavy rains, which enabled GOALPrime Nigeria to quickly plan and design a response and secure funding in record time.

performance.title: A global network for victims of terrorism to advocate for their rights, shape policy and access support
performance.narrative:
3.V.17 The United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy underscores the importance of protecting the rights and addressing the needs of victims of terrorism. The General Assembly, in its resolution 73/305, stressed the need to promote and protect the rights of victims of terrorism and the importance of providing them with proper support and assistance. In the same resolution, the Assembly recognized the role that victims of terrorism can play, including in criminal justice processes and countering the appeal of terrorism. In 2022, the United Nations Global Congress of Victims of Terrorism affirmed the need for victim-led platforms. In response, the Office supported the establishment of the Victims of Terrorism Associations Network, which unites victims of terrorism and victims’ associations from all backgrounds, recognizing the diversity of victims and the issues that are important to them, to drive collective action in favour of victims’ rights and promote the significant expertise and resilience of its members as advocates, educators and peacebuilders. Prior to its establishment, the Office undertook a year of consultations with victims and victims’ associations around the globe to reflect their priorities and needs in the Network. By facilitating collaboration and the sharing of best practices and amplifying the voices of victims, the Network seeks to strengthen victim-centred policy and programming on counter-terrorism and prevention of violent extremism conducive to terrorism and enable victims and victims’ associations to advocate with high-level decision makers. The Network was officially launched in April 2025 as the first and only global victim-led network of its kind, bringing together more than 120 victims and victims’ associations from over 50 Member States. Since its launch, members have collectively shaped the Network’s governance and priorities and have initiated the co-creation of victim-led initiatives.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: addressing emerging technologies in the area of lethal autonomous weapons systems
planned.narrative:
4.24 The open-ended Group of Governmental Experts on Emerging Technologies in the Area of Lethal Autonomous Weapons, convened within the framework of the Convention on Prohibitions or Restrictions on the Use of Certain Conventional Weapons Which May Be Deemed to Be Excessively Injurious or to Have Indiscriminate Effects, has considered issues related to emerging technologies in the area of lethal autonomous weapons systems. Since the establishment of the Group of Governmental Experts in 2016, the subprogramme has provided substantive and procedural support, including by facilitating the work of the Group, including its consideration and formulation of a set of elements of an instrument, without prejudging its nature, and other possible measures to address emerging technologies in the area of lethal autonomous weapons systems.
Lessons learned and planned change
4.25 The lesson for the subprogramme was that the continuity of substantive support to the Group of Governmental Experts on Emerging Technologies in the Area of Lethal Autonomous Weapons could help to support the advancement of deliberations for the formulation of a set of elements of an instrument and other possible measures to address emerging technologies in the area of lethal autonomous weapons systems. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will intensify efforts, including by facilitating the timely payment of assessed contributions for multilateral disarmament conventions, to support implementation of the consolidated financial measures agreed at the sixth Review Conference (CCW/CONF.VI/11, annex III), in order to ensure the operational continuity of the Convention on Prohibitions or Restrictions on the Use of Certain Conventional Weapons Which May Be Deemed to Be Excessively Injurious or to Have Indiscriminate Effect.

planned.title: Group of Scientific and Technical Experts on Nuclear Disarmament Verification advances understanding of technical challenges in and possible approaches to nuclear disarmament verification
planned.narrative:
4.37 To help to advance disarmament and the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons in all its aspects, the subprogramme convened three informal in-person meetings in 2025 on the technical challenges in and possible approaches to nuclear disarmament verification. The subprogramme also prepared a report of the Secretary-General to the General Assembly containing possible options for the establishment of a Group of Scientific and Technical Experts on Nuclear Disarmament Verification within the United Nations, taking into account the views submitted by Member States in writing and through the three informal in-person meetings as the basis for the subprogramme’s efforts to support the establishment and work of the Group, as mandated by the Assembly in its resolution 80/53. The subprogramme is also mandated, by this resolution, to provide all assistance necessary to the Group, including the provision of relevant documents.
Lessons learned and planned change
4.38 The lesson for the subprogramme, informed by previous experience of providing support to groups of experts, was the importance of establishing clear working methods and shared expectations at the outset of mandated activities of groups of experts. Early agreement on roles and responsibilities, decision-making modalities, timelines and communication channels contributes to more efficient deliberations, helps to reduce procedural delays and enables experts to focus on the substantive aspects of the mandate. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will support the development of standardized orientation briefings, model terms of reference for internal working methods and structured workplans aligned with mandated deliverables. The subprogramme will also facilitate early consultations among experts to foster a common understanding of objectives and outputs.

performance.title: Increased understanding of and proposals to mitigate the impact of the global increase in military expenditure on progress towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals
performance.narrative:
4.44 Through the Pact for the Future, Member States expressed concern about the potential impact that the global increase in military expenditure could have on investment in sustainable development and sustaining peace. To take this forward, the subprogramme, in collaboration with the Executive Office of the Secretary-General and the United Nations Development Programme, undertook consultations with relevant United Nations entities, international financial institutions, Member States, academia, experts and civil society. That input informed the report of the Secretary-General, The Security We Need: Rebalancing Military Spending for a Sustainable and Peaceful Future, which provided an analysis on the impact of the global increase in military expenditure on the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. The Secretary-General, in his report, articulated that higher levels of military expenditure did not always lead to greater stability or peace and that growing military expenditure was crowding out resources for sustainable development. The Secretary-General made the case for investing in peace and set out an agenda to mitigate the impact of the global increase in military expenditure on the progress towards the achievement of the Goals. To support broad dissemination of the research and the report, a dedicated outreach campaign and web page were launched to engage Member States and the wider public.

4.50 Since 2024, the subprogramme has designed, developed and helped to operationalize the small arms and light weapons fellowship training programme as a standing initiative to strengthen the technical and institutional capacity of Member States to implement the Programme of Action on Small Arms and Light Weapons and the International Tracing Instrument. Lessons learned and planned change
4.51 The lesson for the subprogramme was the importance of embedding structured mentorship and sustained post-training engagement within the programme design. While fellows actively participated and developed project proposals, follow-up mechanisms for implementation and reporting would benefit from more structured engagement and coaching. priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies
objectives: The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to ensure that cooperation on technology governance is advanced for a better future.
strategy:
To contribute to the objective, the Office will:
(a) Advise the senior leadership of the United Nations on key trends in technology, so as to guide the strategic approach taken by the Organization on such issues;
(b) Serve as an advocate and focal point for digital cooperation, through engagement with Member States, the technology industry, civil society and other stakeholders;
(c) Facilitate multi-stakeholder policy dialogue on digital and emerging technology issues;
(d) Strengthen system-wide coordination within and across the United Nations system on digital and emerging technology issues;
(e) Support the follow-up and implementation of the Global Digital Compact.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
(a) More inclusive and effective cooperation at all levels on digital and emerging technology issues;
(b) Strengthened coherence within and across the United Nations system on digital and emerging technology issues;
(c) Enhanced implementation of the Global Digital Compact.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following assumptions:
(a) Member States continue to engage in constructive dialogue and cooperation on digital and emerging technology issues at the global and regional levels;
(b) Adequate extrabudgetary resources are available to ensure meaningful engagement across the United Nations system, and with national, regional and global institutions and organizations.
With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will collaborate with global and regional organizations, such as the World Bank, the African Union, the European Union and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The Office will also prioritize the forging of new relationships and the strengthening of existing ones with relevant civil society organizations, academia and the private sector.
With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will strengthen system-wide coordination within and across the United Nations system on digital and emerging technology issues, promoting collective synergies and messaging on such issues, and reducing duplication for a more effective use of resources across the United Nations system. Such activities include serving as the coordinating entity for the Panel Secretariat supporting the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence; coordinating, as required, a joint secretariat supporting the United Nations Global Dialogue on Artificial Governance, separate from that supporting the Panel; serving as Co-Chair of the Working Group on Digital Technologies with the International Telecommunication Union; strengthening coordination within and between the processes for the implementation of the Global Digital Compact and the outcomes of the 20-year review of the World Summit on the Information Society, as well as other United Nations processes, such as the multi-stakeholder forum on science, technology and innovation for the Sustainable Development Goals, and coordination with the Technology Bank for the Least Developed Countries; and partnering with and connecting other United Nations system and non-United Nations entities through joint programming towards the Office’s objective. The Office will also advance engagement with the regional economic commissions, the Development Coordination Office and the resident coordinator system to provide guidance on best practices regarding digital transformation for use by Member States, and for connecting to regional, national and local networks in support of implementation of the Global Digital Compact.
The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, including by advocating for the meaningful participation of girls and young women in relevant United Nations processes, and by incorporating a gender perspective on digital and emerging technology issues in multi-stakeholder policy dialogues facilitated by the Office.
In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will advocate for the meaningful participation of persons with disabilities in relevant United Nations processes and incorporate the perspectives of persons with disabilities on digital and emerging technology issues in multi-stakeholder policy dialogues facilitated by the Office. The Office will aim to ensure accessibility for persons with disabilities to information produced and events organized by the Office, to the greatest extent possible.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative
The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the Office to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.
The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs.
Evaluation activities
The following evaluation completed in 2025 has guided the proposed programme plan for 2027:
(a) Self-evaluation of ODET’s capacity to support resident coordinators for an improved localised implementation of the Global Digital Compact.
In response to the results of the evaluation referenced above, the Office will continue providing guidance to resident coordinators to support the localized follow-up and implementation of the Global Digital Compact. In addition, the Office will seek to facilitate a workshop at the annual resident coordinators retreat.
A self-evaluation of the Office regarding its role in facilitating United Nations system-wide coordination on digital cooperation and digital and emerging technology issues is planned for 2027.
Programme performance in 2025
Progress on the Global Digital Compact becomes visible to all stakeholders
The commitments in the Global Digital Compact require significant collective action to achieve its ambitious goals. In 2025, the Office launched the UN Digital Cooperation Portal, which significantly enhanced the opportunities for all stakeholders to map digital initiatives, connect to global partners, and track progress on key priorities.
In line with ODET’s operational function to strengthen system-wide coordination, the portal brings together more than fifteen UN system entities and numerous stakeholders to present their progress across the five Global Digital Compact objectives. Besides showcasing UN system contributions, the portal has become a helpful tracker for external Compact implementation, making use of publicly available resources to show a global summary of initiatives by objective. The portal also offers an innovative suite of resources, compiled under an “AI Toolbox”. To increase alignment with the Global Digital Compact, the platform enables users to demonstrate how their initiatives integrate its objectives and to build a coherent narrative around it.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 1.187).

planned.narrative: Through the adoption of the Global Digital Compact (resolution 79/1, annex I) in September 2024, the General Assembly committed to establishing a multidisciplinary Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and initiating a Global Dialogue on AI Governance within the United Nations. Through its resolution 79/325 in August 2025 on the terms of reference and modalities for the establishment and functioning of this Panel and Dialogue, the Assembly established these mechanisms within the United Nations and requested the Secretary-General to facilitate appropriate Secretariat support for each, within existing mandates. In September 2025, the Office supported the high-level multi-stakeholder informal meeting to launch the Dialogue in the margins of high-level week. The Office also coordinated across the UN system and administered the implementation of the Secretary-General’s criteria-based open call to recommend a list of 40 members for the Panel for appointment by the General Assembly, alongside measures to safeguard the Panel’s scientific independence including administering the mandated conflict of interest disclosure procedure. planned.title: Enhanced organizational resilience and data protection and privacy-by-design maturity in the age of artificial intelligence
planned.narrative:
Effective data protection and privacy risk management is a core component of the Organization's data protection and privacy programme. The Office supports entities in the conduct of data impact assessments (DIA) to identify and mitigate risks, ensuring that these assessments are embedded in the design phase of personal data processing activities in line with the Data Protection and Privacy by Design (PbyD) principle. With the Organization’s growing reliance on technologies, including the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) projects – including under the UN80 digital workstreams – there is a heightened need to integrate this risk management process systematically and early across relevant workstreams.
Lessons learned and planned change
The lesson for the Office was that manual, entity-level support on privacy is not scalable for the rapid, decentralized deployment of AI technologies across the Secretariat. In applying the lesson, the Office will pivot to a systemic oversight model. This involves embedding PbyD as a core operating principle for the Organization and deploying a standardized DIA toolkit to ensure high-velocity, low-friction accountability at the engineering stage. This transition will strengthen compliance, improve the systematic and timely identification of data protection and privacy risks, and reinforce centralized oversight for more effective mitigation.

entities.name: Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
priorities: Promotion and protection of human rights

overview.name: Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
strategy:
24.4 In a global context affected by threats to the enjoyment of human rights by all, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) will continue to support the human rights mechanisms and to assist States in their efforts to comply with their human rights obligations. Increased support and cooperation in matters regarding human rights will be provided to requesting Member States through mutually agreed bilateral frameworks. Emphasis will be placed on highlighting the importance of human rights in international and national agendas; sustaining social development and social justice (as defined in General Assembly resolution 62/10) and countering discrimination on all grounds; advancing the rights of children and women; raising awareness of human rights; responding to the needs of the vulnerable for protection; and addressing situations of international concern as identified by the Assembly, the Human Rights Council and other competent intergovernmental organs.
24.5 The Office will continue to engage with Member States and all relevant actors to assist them in their efforts to promote and protect human rights, through the provision of technical assistance, support for human rights bodies and mechanisms and, where appropriate, the establishment or strengthening of regional or country presences. Consolidated organizational support will be provided to the Human Rights Council and its subsidiary bodies and mechanisms, the universal periodic review, the special procedures, the Human Rights Council Advisory Committee and the complaint procedure, as well as other relevant United Nations bodies. The United Nations treaty bodies will continue to be provided with services, support and advice.
24.6 It is proposed that the work of the Office of the Victims’ Rights Advocate (previously under section 1 of the proposed programme budget) be incorporated into the programme of work of OHCHR, specifically subprogramme 3, Advisory services, technical cooperation and field activities. Through the Victims’ Rights Advocate, the Office will ensure that the rights and dignity of victims of sexual exploitation and abuse are prioritized in all efforts of the United Nations system to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse by its personnel, uniformed or civilian, in peacekeeping, humanitarian and development settings and by non-United Nations personnel serving under a Security Council mandate.
24.7 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will use multi-stakeholder partnerships to support countries in the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals and its transformative promise of leaving no one behind. The Office will continue to engage with a wide range of stakeholders, including civil society actors, such as non-governmental organizations (NGOs). It will also continue to help victims of human rights violations by managing the humanitarian funds that provide financial assistance for support services, such as rehabilitation and redress for victims of torture and slavery.
24.8 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will help to ensure that human rights considerations are systematically integrated into United Nations policies and activities, including through the United Nations Human Rights Group, a system-wide internal coordination mechanism, led by the High Commissioner for Human Rights. The Office will continue to engage with the United Nations development system, both through participation in inter-agency forums and cooperation with United Nations country teams on the ground. The Office will continue to cooperate with missions with a human rights component supported by the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and the Department of Peace Operations. It will also continue its collaboration with all the United Nations agencies and programmes in crisis situations, such as humanitarian emergencies.
24.9 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) There is political will on the part of States to work with the programme;
(b) Extrabudgetary resources will continue to be provided for the programme.
24.10 The programme integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. For example, subprogramme 2 will deliver capacity-building activities on the follow-up to treaty body recommendations, including those related to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women.
24.11 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will integrate disability inclusion into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. For example, subprogramme 1 will provide expert advice on the development of standards on strengthening national human rights promotion and protection capacities as they relate to persons with disabilities.

subprogrammes.name: Human rights mainstreaming, right to development, and research and analysis

sections.name: Human rights mainstreaming
objectives: 24.19 The objective, to which this subprogramme contributes, is to advance the promotion and protection of all human rights through strengthened integration of all human rights into areas of work of the United Nations system.

performance.title: Integration of human rights norms and standards into common country analyses and United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks
performance.narrative:
24.22 In the Pact for the Future (General Assembly resolution 79/1), it was decided that the promotion and protection of human rights and the implementation of the 2030 Agenda would be recognized as interrelated and mutually reinforcing, with the recognition that the 2030 Agenda contained a pledge to leave no one behind and envisaged a world of universal respect for and promotion of human rights and human dignity, the rule of law, justice, equality and non-discrimination. To support this decision and Assembly resolution 79/226 on the quadrennial comprehensive policy review of operational activities for development of the United Nations system, the subprogramme provides system-wide leadership for the integration of human rights norms and standards into common country analyses and United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. A comparison of inter-agency reviews undertaken in 2022 and 2025 showed clear improvements in integrating human rights into United Nations analyses and planning, with 76.8 per cent of common country analysing who is left behind, up from 55 per cent in 2022, and 50 per cent of common country analyses reflecting recommendations from United Nations human rights mechanisms, up from 32 per cent. United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework programming that focused on reducing inequalities and discrimination grew from 50 to 62.7 per cent and programming that measurably contributed to implementing recommendations from United Nations human rights mechanisms increased from 27 to 43.4 per cent.
24.23 The subprogramme invested in joint guidance, practical tools and capacity-building and provided support through the provision of technical advice at the regional level, helping to ensure that economic policies supported the full realization of all human rights.

planned.title: Member States adopt counter-terrorism laws and implement measures that are consistent with and are applied in a manner that fully respects the rights enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and their obligations under international human rights law

24.29 To advance full compliance with Member States’ obligations under international law while countering terrorism, in particular international human rights law, the subprogramme has developed tools and guidance to support the integration of human rights norms and standards into counter-terrorism laws and implementing measures, to help to ensure respect for principles of legal certainty and legality and to ensure that counter-terrorism laws and measures do not hinder the work and safety of civil society organizations.
Lessons learned and planned change
24.30 The lesson for the subprogramme was that the utility of mandated reports, including reports of the Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism, could be complemented by concise checklists, operational tools, detailed guidance and targeted capacity-building that can be applied directly by policymakers and legislators, and that doing so would support report implementation. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will focus on producing and disseminating practical tools and conducting in-person training. For example, the subprogramme will provide tailored training for law enforcement officials, parliamentarians and members of the judiciary, delivered in collaboration with regional and country offices and other United Nations counter-terrorism entities.

In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will continue to deploy efforts to mainstream the right to development into international frameworks while also seeking opportunities to engage with regional and national stakeholders to address specific challenges and enhance the practical application of the right to development at the regional and national levels, including mainstreaming the right to development into relevant regional and national development frameworks.
