24.95 The subprogramme strives to improve the access of persons with disabilities to the work of the Human Rights Council. Through its sustained support for the work of the task force for accessibility for persons with disabilities, pursuant to Council resolution 16/21, the subprogramme has identified gaps and areas for improvements in the existing framework for the participation of persons with disabilities in the work of the Council. For example, the subprogramme was able to increase the accessibility of the online platforms used for inscriptions on lists of speakers for sessions of the Council, as well as for registrations to participate in the sessions.
Lessons learned and planned change
24.96 The lesson for the subprogramme was that persons with disabilities continued to face barriers to effective participation in the work of the United Nations human rights machinery. Identified barriers include limitations in physical access to Human Rights Council sessions, insufficient availability of easy-to-read versions of official documentation considered during sessions and only a limited number of Council meetings mandated to be accessible. In applying the lesson and to address these barriers, the subprogramme will strengthen its advocacy for an increase in the number of meetings mandated to be accessible during the regular sessions of the Council. This will include, among other, systematically recommending that mandated panel discussions be made accessible through the provision of live captioning and sign language interpretation. In addition, the subprogramme will collect feedback from persons with disabilities participating in Council sessions on their experience to support the collection the lessons learned to relevant United Nations counterparts to ensure that this informs decision-making on issues aiming at facilitating participation of persons with disabilities in meetings of the Council.

entities.name: Office of Information and Communications Technology
priorities: Effective functioning of the organization

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
29C.2 In 2027, the Office will continue to implement its programme of work in support of the achievement of the ICT strategic outcomes, ensuring an environment in which ICT enables coherent, efficient and integrated mandate implementation in the Organization and protects the Organization from rapidly escalating threats to ICT security.
29C.3 The Office will remain committed to providing resilient and secure global network and ICT systems, platforms and applications that enable collaboration and communication across the Secretariat and throughout the wider United Nations common system.
29C.4 The transformative potential of technology, including artificial intelligence and cloud-based platforms, enables United Nations personnel to collaborate and connect seamlessly. The Office will continue its strategic shift of leveraging hybrid cloud-based services and strengthen ICT security while maintaining enterprise on-premise solutions for legitimate business cases, such as compliance with specific resolutions and mandates. This hybrid multi-cloud approach strengthens operational resilience, supports business continuity and disaster recovery, mitigates single-vendor dependency and lock-in risks, and enables the Organization to balance central control with operational flexibility.
29C.5 In the context of ICT security, challenges are expected to continue to grow in scale, pervasiveness and complexity. The main risks foreseen for 2027 include threats amplified by artificial intelligence and increased vulnerabilities due to ageing equipment and infrastructure. In response, the Office will reinforce centralized ICT security capacity and enhance the use of shared services of proactive threat-hunting and vulnerability management capabilities. The centralization of ICT security services will strengthen internal capacity, while a clear focus is kept on United Nations global operations. Other key initiatives are also under way, including continuous improvements in networks, which are instrumental in containing threats and limiting the impact of successful attacks; the upgrade of various solutions to detect and prevent security issues and to protect end-user devices, digital identities and cloud-based services; and increased interactive security awareness campaigns.
29C.6 The Office will continue to support efforts to digitally transform the Organization into one that more effectively uses data and information to support decision-making and inform strategic direction. This work will be aligned with the ICT strategy (see A/77/489 and A/79/339) and the Data Strategy of the Secretary-General for Action by Everyone, Everywhere. The effective use of data across the Secretariat requires cross-cutting efforts. The Office will establish services and technology capacities that support the management and use of data. The Office will continue to leverage technology enablers that support the exchange, reconciliation, storage and governance of data. Analytics and data solutions will also continue to be implemented, and associated standards and architecture will be formulated to achieve a consistent approach to data. Further, the Office plans to support policy formulation and the governance of information management, including the use and adoption of artificial intelligence.
29C.7 In support of innovation, the Office will continue to provide access to technologies that can support a wide range of needs across the United Nations. Frontier technologies, in particular conversational artificial intelligence deployed in the productivity tools, will support the work of the Organization and more intuitive and efficient mandate delivery globally.
29C.8 The Office will further advance its work in digital transformation, strengthening business relationships between the Office’s service providers and United Nations Secretariat entities by facilitating clear communication, managing demands effectively and ensuring effective problem resolution. The Office will also continue to serve as a centralized function for global enterprise ICT project governance through the enterprise programme and portfolio management team, ensuring that projects comply with the project management methodology, achieve desired outcomes and are aligned with the approved objectives. It will also ensure that overall Secretariat ICT budget proposals are technically reviewed by the Office, leading to improved accountability of the Secretariat to Member States regarding the efficient use of ICT resources. The internal consolidation of the business relationship management and the enterprise programme and portfolio management functions will strengthen the Office’s oversight role in implementing the Organization’s ICT strategy, provide consistent and accountable mechanisms for engagement between entities and the Office of Information and Communications Technology, ensure effective project management and enhance Secretariat-wide coherence, transparency and prioritization in the planning, governance and execution of ICT initiatives.
29C.9 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will continue to collaborate with agencies, funds and programmes to agree on minimum standards of ICT security and promote the establishment of communities of practice in key ICT areas to discuss opportunities and challenges at the inter-agency level. This will be done through the United Nations System Chief Executives Board for Coordination Digital and Technology Network, which is co-chaired by the Assistant Secretary-General/Chief Information Technology Officer and serves as a mechanism to collaborate on, harmonize and explore possibilities for better use of shared ICT services. The Office will also continue to ensure access to Secretariat platforms for personnel from United Nations agencies, funds and programmes to facilitate collaboration and will strategize on the mitigation of cost increases and minimizing duplication across the United Nations common system to support coherence in mandate delivery.
29C.10 In line with the recent guidance provided by Member States, the Office will establish functional reporting between information and communications technology chiefs of United Nations entities and the Office, maintaining their existing administrative reporting lines while enhancing functional reporting and ensuring coherence, coordination and accountability across the ICT function without creating parallel or isolated structures. This functional reporting will strengthen enterprise-wide alignment and consistency in ICT governance and delivery, complement established reporting mechanisms and support implementation of the Organization’s ICT strategic direction, as reflected in the ICT strategy.
29C.11 The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. The Office will continue to promote women in technology within the Secretariat and to highlight the contributions of women in ICT.
29C.12 With regard to external factors, the Office considered applicable risks identified in its risk register. The proposed programme plan for 2027 is based on the planning assumption that there will be adequate voluntary contributions through effective partnering to complement regular budget resources to carry out the activities of the Office.
29C.13 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will strengthen digital accessibility to Secretariat digital platforms by coordinating outreach and awareness, providing technical capacity to conduct digital accessibility assessments and monitoring progress towards compliance with established standards. The Office will also improve physical accessibility at Headquarters by providing an audio-based navigation solution to help persons with visual impairments navigate designated indoor and outdoor areas.

performance.title: Improved information and security technology security awareness to safeguard the Secretariat
performance.narrative:
29C.21 As the United Nations becomes increasingly digitally interconnected, ICT security awareness remains essential to enabling personnel to respond effectively to continuously evolving threats, safeguarding ICT assets, including data, and ensuring business continuity. The subprogramme promotes awareness through the provision of specialized ICT security awareness sessions conducted during observations of ICT Security Awareness Month. Since 2019, these sessions have been offered to Secretariat personnel, covering key topics such as social engineering, digital hygiene practices, the backing up of data and systems, the use of strong passwords and multifactor authentication, and emerging artificial intelligence-enabled security threats. The subprogramme delivered four new virtual sessions and one in-person session. In addition, more than 30 new ICT security resources containing guidance for United Nations entities were developed and distributed for local use by such entities on specific topics to help raise awareness and develop practical skills. Over time, sustained awareness contributes to fostering the development of a stronger security culture in the Organization, reduces the likelihood and impact of ICT security incidents and supports the reliable delivery of the Organization’s mandates.

planned.title: reduced fragmentation and strengthened information and communications technology resilience, security and standardization of data centre infrastructure
planned.narrative:
29C.40 The consolidation of ICT infrastructure and hosting environments is critical to improving operational resilience, reducing duplication and containing operating costs across the Secretariat. Fragmented hosted environments increase complexity, elevate ICT security risks and limit the Organization’s ability to achieve economies of scale and standardized service delivery. The subprogramme has advanced the implementation of the hybrid multi-cloud strategy, including the migration of selected workloads from locally managed infrastructure to enterprise data centres, and approved cloud platforms. These efforts contributed to improved service reliability, strengthened disaster recovery arrangements, ensured more efficient use of shared enterprise infrastructure and allowed entities to reduce reliance on aged, underutilized and duplicative hosting environments.
Lessons learned and planned change
29C.41 The lesson for the subprogramme was that infrastructure consolidation delivers the greatest impact when supported by clear enterprise governance and early engagement with Secretariat entities to align operational goals, creating greater coherence in ICT across the Organization. Experience also confirms that phased migration and improved visibility of data centres and server rooms are critical to managing risk and minimizing disruption during consolidation activities. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will strengthen enterprise-level planning and coordination for data centre consolidation, which will be managed through a structured project and working closely with the entities to prioritize workload transitions to enterprise data centres or approved cloud platforms, supporting a more systematic, predictable and scalable approach to consolidation and enabling reduced fragmentation and operating costs.

entities.name: Office of Internal Oversight Services
priorities: Effective functioning of the organization

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
30.2 In support of the Secretary-General’s focus on building a more sustainable and inclusive future and on reforming the Organization to better deliver against this vision, the strategy for 2027 prioritizes internal oversight coverage of the work of the Organization in the following management areas: (a) implementation of the reforms of the management, peace and security, and development pillars; (b) strengthening of organizational culture; (c) procurement and supply chain management, including management of fraud and corruption risks; (d) management of mission drawdown or transition; and (e) strengthening of the protection against retaliation (whistle-blower) system. The Office will also continue to cover the programmes and strategies of the Organization, including cross-cutting areas such as the provision of support to Member States on the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals and the Pact for the Future, as well as the implementation of the Secretary-General’s strategies on gender equality, racial equality, environmental sustainability, disability inclusion and data.
30.3 Effective engagement with the senior leadership of the Organization will help the programme to identify risks to the Organization and provide timely assurance and advice on issues relating to the efficient, economical, effective and ethical management of the Organization’s resources.
30.4 The Office will strengthen the delivery of its mandated activities by: (a) strengthening the use of enterprise risk management in planning internal audit and evaluation and inspection activities (subprogrammes 1 and 2); (b) enhancing the methodology for measuring the impact of audit recommendations (subprogramme 1); (c) enhancing guidance for thematic and outcome evaluations of programmes (subprogramme 2); and (d) enhancing guidance on using data analytics to improve investigation planning and the timeliness of investigations (subprogramme 3).
30.5 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will consult closely on its programme of work with the Board of Auditors and the Joint Inspection Unit and liaise, as appropriate, with relevant offices involved in the internal justice system of the Organization.
30.6 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will share knowledge on good practices and innovations in oversight methodologies with the other internal oversight functions of the United Nations system through the meetings of the Representatives of Internal Audit Services of the United Nations Organizations, the United Nations Representatives of Investigative Services and the United Nations Evaluation Group.
30.7 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the planning assumption that the Office will have unimpeded access to the staff and records of the Organization and other required information.
30.8 The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. Subprogrammes 1 and 2 will cover the management of risks relating to mainstreaming a gender perspective. Subprogramme 3 will continue to integrate a gender perspective into its victim-centred methodology for all investigations, including sexual exploitation and abuse and workplace sexual harassment.
30.9 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will further advance disability inclusion by covering the management of risks relating to implementation of the Strategy.

30.45 The subprogramme responded to an increase in the number of allegations of misconduct reported to OIOS by opening and completing a corresponding higher number of investigations, which, in turn, informed subsequent corrective action taken by the Organization to protect its financial and human resources and hold its personnel accountable. In 2025, the subprogramme completed 641 investigations and opened 595 new investigations. In addition, the subprogramme referred 901 matters to responsible officials within and outside of the Secretariat, to enable the Organization to address reports of unsatisfactory conduct in the most appropriate and efficient way.

The target was not met owing to several factors, including a high volume of new investigations in 2025 and backlog from previous years, the complexity of investigations, which often required deoxyribonucleic acid forensic analysis, as well as delays in investigations conducted jointly with national authorities, whose procedures and timelines differ from those of the Organization.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: timely investigation of cases with a potential financial loss to the Organization
planned.narrative:
30.51 The timely handling of reports of possible misconduct that could entail financial losses to the Organization helps to safeguard its resources and enables the recovery of any accrued losses. Fraud and corruption remain the most frequent categories of misconduct investigated by OIOS, and such investigations are prioritized owing to the high risk posed by fraud and corruption to the Organization.
Lessons learned and planned change
30.52 The lesson for the subprogramme was that the timely handling of reports of misconduct with potential financial implications was important because, the longer cases remained open, the greater the risk that implicated individuals might leave the Organization or dissipate assets, making recovery increasingly difficult. This was recently illustrated by a cluster of interconnected insurance fraud cases linked to a broader scheme, in which timeliness was critical, given that unnecessary delays might have compromised the availability and integrity of financial and ICT evidence. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will prioritize investigations involving potential financial loss, recognizing that prompt action is essential to limit losses and strengthen recovery prospects. The subprogramme will adopt a new timeliness target: completion of at least 65 per cent of such investigations within 12 months in 2026, increasing to 80 per cent in 2027.

entities.name: Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria
priorities: Maintenance of international peace and security

overview.name: Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria
objectives: The objective of this mission is to advance the full implementation of all the relevant General Assembly and Security Council resolutions towards an inclusive, credible, comprehensive Syrian-owned and -led political solution to the conflict in the Syrian Arab Republic that meets the legitimate aspirations of the Syrian people for dignity, freedom and justice, based on the principles of equality and non-discrimination and with the full and meaningful participation of women.

performance.title: Constructive, coherent and comprehensive multilateral approach and continuous progress towards an inclusive, sustainable political solution in line with Security Council resolution 2254 (2015)
performance.narrative:
In 2025, the Special Envoy engaged with the caretaker authorities and the subsequently formed government, as well as the leadership of the Syrian Democratic Forces, leaders from the Druze, Alawite, Christian and other communities, a broad spectrum of Syrian civil society, and key regional and international partners, including through participation in international gatherings. Through these engagements, the Special Envoy helped maintain focus on a balanced, rights-based approach, emphasizing de-escalation, accountability, humanitarian access, reconstruction, detainees, and reconciliation, while promoting confidence-building and dialogue to address local concerns and safeguard Syria’s unity.
Overall, the Mission moved from a context of stalled mediation to active good offices engagement, advice and support. The value of this role lay in sustaining dialogue, promoting inclusivity, and aligning international efforts behind a Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political transition in line with the core elements of Security Council resolution 2254 (2015). At a critical juncture, this work helped preserve momentum and reinforced the principle that only negotiation, compromise, and broad participation - rather than rushed or exclusionary processes - can secure a durable and peaceful future for Syria. Steps so far on the institutional, constitutional, and governance front have been taken, and further progress is needed to ensure a fully inclusive and participatory transition.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 31).

planned.title: Progress towards institutional consolidation and reform in line with the principles of Security Council resolution 2254 (2015), supported by the widest possible spectrum of Syrian stakeholders and underpinned by strong international consensus
planned.narrative:
In 2025, the Mission’s work contributed to maintaining momentum around a Syrian-led and Syrian-owned political transition process, with improved alignment of national and international efforts in support of that process. It reinforced the principle that only dialogue, de-escalation, compromise, and broad participation can secure a durable and peaceful future for Syria. Despite these efforts, the planned targets for 2025 were not fully achieved, largely due to structural constraints and evolving realities on the ground.
In 2027, the Mission will continue to offer its good offices to advance a peaceful, orderly, transparent, and inclusive political transition, consistent with the principles of resolution 2254 (2015). The Mission seeks to become a trusted partner for the Syrian government and establish more systematic consultation and partnership, while also ensuring continued engagement with all other constituencies across the country.
Lessons learned and planned change
A key lesson for the Mission was the need to strengthen engagement on the ground and enhance accessibility to the Syrian government and the people it serves, in order to ensure closer alignment with evolving needs and realities and to better support the political transition process. In this regard, the potential establishment of small sub-offices in existing UN hubs outside Damascus, with the agreement of the Syrian government, will be evaluated as a means to improve operational outreach and deepen local engagement.

entities.name: Office of Legal Affairs
priorities: Promotion of international justice and law

overview.name: Office of Legal Affairs
strategy:
8.I.3 The Office supports international law as the foundation for Member States to interact and cooperate in achieving their common goals. The Office will continue to respond to the needs of its stakeholders and beneficiaries with a specialized legal skill set, institutional memory, credibility and neutrality, while delivering on a diverse and complex mandate.
8.I.4 The Office will respond to the increasing demands for legal services from United Nations organs, including through the provision of advice on questions relating to the interpretation and application of international law instruments and on general questions of public international law, to ensure that legal considerations are an integral part of the Organization’s operations and the effective functioning of its principal and subsidiary organs. The Office will defend and protect the privileges and immunities of the United Nations in accordance with the Charter and the relevant conventions, including in national and international courts.
8.I.5 The Office will contribute to international justice and accountability, including through support for United Nations-assisted criminal tribunals and their oversight bodies, and other international accountability mechanisms.
8.I.6 The Office will continue to promote the wider appreciation and understanding of international law through its capacity-building activities, including those related to ocean affairs and the law of the sea, the United Nations Programme of Assistance in the Teaching, Study, Dissemination and Wider Appreciation of International Law and special initiatives such as subregional workshops on international law, workshops on treaty law and practice and those related to continuing to advance awareness and understanding of UNCITRAL texts, among others.
8.I.7 To further the progressive harmonization, modernization and unification of the law of international trade, the Office will ensure the widespread adoption and use of harmonized and modernized substantive private law rules to govern international commercial transactions, strengthen technical cooperation and promote the participation of developing countries in the law-making activities of UNCITRAL. The Office will support Member States in the preparation of universally acceptable legislative and non-legislative texts.
8.I.8 The Office will continue its role in supporting the Organization’s efforts to strengthen its response to allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse and to hold accountable those who have engaged in such behaviour. The Office will also support the legal aspects relating to the implementation of the Secretary-General’s strategic action plan on addressing racism and promoting dignity for all in the Secretariat.
8.I.9 The Office will support the initiatives of the Secretary-General envisioned to increase the Organization’s capacity, including by providing guidance on the legal aspects, to achieve a more agile, responsive and resilient United Nations, in particular by enhancing the Organization’s capabilities in innovation, data analytics, digital transformation, strategic foresight and behavioural science, in order to better support Member States and deliver on the Office’s mandates, in accordance with the Pact to the Future. In the context of the UN80 Initiative, the Office will continue to provide legal and procedural advice to address questions arising out of structural changes with a view to protecting the Organization from legal risks and liabilities and ensuring that reform is done in accordance with international law and the internal rules and regulations of the Organization.
8.I.10 With regard to the general legal services provided to United Nations organs and programmes, the Office will provide those services with a view to maximizing the protection of the legal interests of the Organization and minimizing its legal liabilities. The Office will advise on the legal aspects arising from United Nations institutional and operational activities and provide legal services for resolving disputes of a private law character involving the operations of the Organization, its subsidiary bodies and organs, and its separately administered funds and programmes.
8.I.11 The Office will also support the progressive development and codification of international law and the conclusion of legal instruments resulting in the promotion of universal respect for international law, including by continuing to serve as the secretariats of the Sixth Committee, the International Law Commission, the Special Committee on the Charter of the United Nations and on the Strengthening of the Role of the Organization, other special or ad hoc committees and diplomatic conferences convened to consider and formulate legal instruments. The Office will disseminate materials on international law through the United Nations Audiovisual Library of International Law and major legal publications.
8.I.12 The Office will engage in processes relating to oceans and the law of the sea to support the increased participation of States in and the effective implementation and application of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and its implementing agreements. The Office will provide secretariat functions to oceans-related processes of the General Assembly and the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, as well as temporary secretariat functions related to the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction. It will support the implementation and promotion of the Sustainable Development Goals, in particular Goal 14. The Office will also continue to deliver capacity-building activities on that topic, including for developing countries.
8.I.13 The Office will intensify the use of technological tools and other means to enhance the custody, registration and publication of treaties, including the registration of treaties and treaty actions in line with Article 102 of the Charter, and fulfil the depositary functions of the Secretary-General. The Office will continue to provide legal assistance and advice to States, specialized agencies, United Nations programmes and offices, treaty bodies and other entities on the law of treaties. The Office will also promote and ensure wider knowledge of the law of treaties, including through capacity-building activities and workshops, thereby preventing issues of interpretation and implementation of treaty provisions by contracting States.
8.I.14 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will continue to enable the International Law Commission to exchange knowledge, experience and ideas with the President of the International Court of Justice, the African Union Commission on International Law, the Inter-American Juridical Committee, the Asian-African Legal Consultative Organization and the Committee of Legal Advisers on Public International Law of the Council of Europe. The Office will also continue to cooperate with States and bodies established under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. In the fields of the law of the sea and ocean governance and of international trade law, the Office will continue to cooperate with international financial institutions, donor agencies, intergovernmental organizations, non-governmental organizations and relevant communities, including Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
8.I.15 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Legal Counsel, as the focal point for UN-Oceans, will continue to coordinate the delivery of UN-Oceans outputs and promote cross-sectoral and integrated activities with the United Nations system, in particular with respect to capacity-building and in relation to the Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction. In addition, the Office will coordinate the work of organizations dealing with international trade law and promote the use of online resources, including those provided by other institutions, in the light of the closing of the dedicated trade law library. The Office will continue to foster and strengthen the networks of legal advisers of United Nations agencies, funds and programmes.
8.I.16 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Extrabudgetary resources are available to complement the programme budget, allowing the Office to respond to the increased demand for its services;
(b) Principal and subsidiary organs of the United Nations continue to request legal advice as a main component of the decision-making process;
(c) Specific mandates relating to international trade law, oceans and law of the sea and others are renewed or confirmed by the competent intergovernmental bodies.
8.I.17 The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. The Office will continue to promote gender equality and the empowerment of women throughout all its subprogrammes in the context of the Office’s capacity-building programmes and other related aspects.
8.I.18 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will integrate disability inclusion in its work, as appropriate. The Office will continue to take the steps necessary to ensure that, in the committees it services, delegates with disabilities are provided with the materials needed to facilitate their participation.

performance.title: Legal frameworks for establishing a new United Nations field operation in Haiti and support for the multinational Gang Suppression Force in Haiti
performance.narrative:
8.I.27 The Security Council, in its resolution 2793 (2025), authorized Member States to establish a Gang Suppression Force mandated to neutralize, isolate, and deter gangs in Haiti and to support the Haitian National Police, the Haitian armed forces and national institutions. The Council also established the United Nations Support Office in Haiti to provide logistical and operational support, primarily to the Gang Suppression Force, as well as the United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti, the Haitian National Police and the Haitian armed forces, and, as required, technical support to the Organization of American States.
8.I.28 The subprogramme provided legal advice to inform the development of the planning directive for the new field mission. This included the preparation, review and clearance of operational documents of a legal nature and legal instruments relating to the grant, occupancy and use of land and premises, reimbursement frameworks for contingent-owned equipment in relation to the Gang Suppression Force, and the formulation of a draft agreement detailing the status, privileges, immunities and facilities applicable to the United Nations Support Office in Haiti and its personnel. The complexity of interaction between the United Nations field mission, the ad hoc multinational force and national security and military institutions requires comprehensive adjustments to the standard United Nations legal instruments for missions and adapting some practices of the Organization, including in relation to legal and financial liability. The subprogramme will continue to assist in these issues, as well as matters related to the implementation of the agreement, once concluded.

planned.title: advancement of organizational reforms and institutional transitions
planned.narrative:
8.I.34 As the central legal service of the United Nations, the subprogramme provides legal advice on applicable rules and procedures, in particular on procedural and institutional law and privileges and immunities of the United Nations. The subprogramme supports the Organization through periods of transformation and reform initiatives, including within the framework of the UN80 Initiative. The subprogramme’s involvement is multifaceted, encompassing, among others, the provision of expert legal and procedural advice to address structural changes and institutional transitions. The subprogramme also offers critical guidance on complex legal challenges, in particular related to the safeguarding of the Organization’s interests and legal frameworks, including on privileges and immunities. The subprogramme will also support the implementation of any relevant decisions taken by legislative bodies, in connection with such changes and transitions.
Lessons learned and planned change
8.I.35 The lesson for the subprogramme was the importance of early and sustained engagement in reform processes. As organizational reforms and institutional transitions, including those under the UN80 Initiative, advanced, the subprogramme faced a continuous and significantly higher-than-anticipated demand for legal advice. The demand related to highly complex legal issues pertaining to, among others, procedural and institutional law and privileges and immunities of the United Nations. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme is refining the scope and nature of its engagement in organizational reforms and institutional transitions, thereby enhancing services by placing a greater emphasis on taking proactive steps to liaise closely with the relevant Secretariat departments and offices, to anticipate legal issues and to provide legal advice in a timely manner.

performance.title: Strengthened judicial capacity in applying guidance provided in United Nations Commission on International Trade Law insolvency law texts
performance.narrative:
8.I.80 Improved knowledge of the UNCITRAL insolvency law texts can support the more effective handling of domestic insolvency cases. On the basis of a request by UNCITRAL, the subprogramme, in partnership with the World Bank Group, has implemented the biennial online Judicial Capacity-Building Initiative on International Best Practices in the Area of Insolvency Law since 2021. Building on the previous editions, the third edition, in 2025, continued to provide a global platform for judicial engagement on using UNCITRAL insolvency law texts. For the first time, interpretation was available in all six United Nations official languages, broadening accessibility across diverse linguistic and legal environments, which attracted significant worldwide interest, with participants attending from 55 jurisdictions, an increase from 30 in 2023.
8.I.81 Sustained participation across editions reflected continued demand for practical guidance on the interpretation of UNCITRAL insolvency law frameworks. In 2025, participants strengthened their understanding of international best practices, contributing to the more effective handling of domestic cases and reinforcing dialogue and cooperation among various jurisdictions.

objectives: 153. The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to provide an independent review of delisting requests of individuals, entities and undertakings on the ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida sanctions list. In doing so, it ensures that listed individuals, entities and undertakings have access to fair and clear procedures for the administration of requests for removal (delisting) from the sanctions list.
strategy:
154. To contribute to the objective, the Office will fairly and expeditiously consider and process all requests for delisting and travel to interview each petitioner in person, whenever possible, in the petitioner’s country of residence.
155. The above-mentioned work is expected to result in informed decision-making by the Committee on the Ombudsperson’s analysis and recommendation on the delisting request contained in a comprehensive report on each case.
156. With regard to cooperation with other entities, including in the context of information-sharing, the Office cooperates with, among others, Member States, the European Union, academic institutions, think tanks and international law associations.
157. With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office cooperates with, among others, UNDP, OHCHR, the Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate, the Office of Counter-Terrorism, the Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism, and the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team pursuant to resolutions 1526 (2004) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da’esh), Al-Qaida and the Taliban and associated individuals and entities. In the context of safety and security, information technology security and logistics, the Office cooperates with the Department of Safety and Security, the Office of Information and Communications Technology and UNDP.
158. With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Member States comply with the resolutions of the Security Council and cooperate with the Office;
(b) The security situation allows the Office to conduct missions, as needed.

performance.title: Enhanced planning and preparedness for potentially hazardous near-Earth objects
performance.narrative:
6.15 Recognizing the growing risk posed by high-impact natural hazards from space and the need for advance preparedness, the programme facilitated multi-stakeholder engagement on potentially hazardous near-Earth objects at the international Planetary Defense Conference held in 2025 in South Africa. The engagement included a hands-on simulation exercise of a hypothetical asteroid impact scenario, bringing together experts from space agencies, national authorities and regional and international organizations in Southern Africa. It introduced disaster managers and responders to internationally established early warning and information-sharing mechanisms and protocols. The need for planning for cross-border and cascading impacts, coordination and decision-making across national boundaries was emphasized, and the exercise focused on detection, uncertainty management, civil protection actions and post-impact responses.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: increased use of space-based technology and data for disaster management and emergency response
planned.narrative:
6.21 The use of digital technologies for disaster management and building resilience is an important resource for Member States in responding to and recovering from natural disasters and extreme weather events. The programme has supported Member States in this area through high-impact technical assistance, notably the 2024 pilot in Tonga, which utilized satellite-based models for sea level rise simulation. This work expanded in 2025 to Ghana and Trinidad and Tobago, where artificial intelligence-driven three-dimensional models were deployed to visualize urban flood risks and infrastructure vulnerability, demonstrating the practical utility of space data in national preparedness.
Lessons learned and planned change
6.22 The lesson for the programme was that traditional disaster mapping tools often lack the predictive depth required for complex scenarios, leading to high demand among Member States for more sophisticated, integrative technologies. In applying the lesson, the programme will facilitate the development and delivery to requesting Member States of virtual three-dimensional replicas of geographic regions vulnerable to natural disasters. Pilot projects have demonstrated that real-time virtual replicas, often referred to as “digital twin models”, can better support disaster preparedness, as they allow for dynamic “what-if” simulations that two-dimensional data cannot provide. The programme will also facilitate the integration of satellite-based data and simulation videos to support the inclusion of these models into national preparedness processes in order to support early warning and risk management. To ensure sustainability, the programme will integrate standardized data protocols and simulation workflows by embedding them directly into the standard operating procedures of national disaster management authorities, upon request. This systematic integration will enable Member States to move beyond experimental use towards the autonomous, long-term application of three-dimensional virtual replicas for national early warning and disaster risk reduction.

performance.title: African policymakers applied integrated analytical approaches to promote long-term peace and development outcomes
performance.narrative:
11.17 In 2025, the subprogramme highlighted how long-term peace and development outcomes in Africa depend on a specific sequence of policy conditions, particularly sustainable financing and effective governance and strong institutions. To address persistent structural constraints, the subprogramme developed and operationalized an integrated analytical framework that clarifies how progress in peace, development, financing and governance is interdependent and why policy action must be interlinked to achieve durable results. Building on analytical work initiated in 2023, the framework was operationalized through an online training course launched in 2024, which equipped 100 policymakers and practitioners with practical skills to apply this analysis in their professional work. An assessment conducted in 2025 showed that 78 per cent of participants had applied the approach to their professional work nine months after course completion.

11.23 Africa faces a converging challenge: food insecurity driven by adverse impacts of climate change is coinciding with a large proportion of youth who lack the skills needed to participate in productive, resilient livelihoods. Approximately 23 per cent of African youth are not in education, employment or training, limiting countries’ ability to develop sustainable food systems and to adapt to adverse impacts of climate change. Without targeted interventions, this convergence threatens long-term food security, economic development and the capacity of communities to respond to future risks. The subprogramme has laid analytical foundations to address this challenge in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 analytical reports. Together, these reports provide the building blocks to connect youth skills development, climate resilience and food systems, guiding Member States on coherent policy design and intervention planning.
Lessons learned and planned change
11.24 The lesson for the subprogramme was that siloed policy approaches addressing education, climate or food security in isolation achieve limited impact. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will employ its policy, advisory and advocacy capacities to promote integrated policy solutions that position education, human capital development and agricultural technology at the core of policies to promote climate resilience. The subprogramme will work with African Member States, the African Union Commission and education partners to promote technical and vocational training in climate resilience and sustainable agriculture, enhance digital literacy and advocate for and support policies that strengthen science, technology, engineering and mathematics education, as well as science, technology and innovation systems.

performance.title: Domestic resource mobilization strategy adopted to finance the second 10-year implementation plan of Agenda 2063
performance.narrative:
11.30 Agenda 2063 sets out Africa’s long-term vision for inclusive growth and sustainable development, which can be realized only through robust and sustainable financing. Domestic resource mobilization is central to this vision, as it provides the financial foundation needed to translate continental aspirations into concrete results at the national and regional levels. As a member of the Agenda 2063 technical working group, the subprogramme provided technical and advisory advice and facilitated inclusive, multi-stakeholder consultations with an emphasis on sustainable financing, innovation and inclusion. These efforts culminated in the development and validation in 2025 of the Domestic Resource Mobilization Strategy for the second 10-year implementation plan of Agenda 2063. The strategy was subsequently endorsed by the Executive Council of the African Union at the 2025 mid-year coordination meeting, marking a significant milestone in advancing the objectives of Agenda 2063.

objectives: 11.40 The objective, to which this subprogramme contributes, is to achieve the informed understanding and engagement of a global audience in support of the economic, political and social development of Africa.

performance.title: Media partnership with a reach of 130 million highlights African perspectives on artificial intelligence and digital employment
performance.narrative:
11.43 In September 2025, on the sidelines of the General Assembly high-level week, the subprogramme collaborated with African and global media partners to organize high-level discussions on themes relevant to the African continent. The week culminated in a televised town hall on artificial intelligence and the future of jobs in Africa, which was produced in collaboration with British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) News Africa and was broadcast on BBC World and BBC domestic and online channels, which together reach an estimated 130 million people across the African continent. The broadcast explored how artificial intelligence, technology and digitization can drive job creation, skills development and economic empowerment for young people in Africa, helping them to thrive in an increasingly competitive global marketplace. The town hall built on a successful partnership with BBC Africa, which was first developed on the sidelines of the Summit of the Future in 2024. Through this media partnership, youth representatives from the continent, ministers and United Nations officials worked together to discuss employment opportunities for African youth in the digital age.

performance.title: Expanded Integration of Protection Measures in Country Cooperation Frameworks
performance.narrative:
Sexual exploitation and abuse are inherent risks across all United Nations system entities, regardless of context. In 2025, the Office worked with relevant actors to help ensure that those served by, and serving alongside, United Nations personnel can trust the Organization and remain safe. To support this effort, the Office further strengthened its strategic role in key coordination forums, enhanced outreach initiatives, and deepened collaboration with both internal and external stakeholders, including government counterparts to reinforce common standards. This included continued advocacy for the integration of a model clause on protection from sexual exploitation and abuse in United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks, as part of broader efforts to promote joint action, build national capacity and mainstream protection into government systems.

performance.title: Strengthened coherence between regional and international peace efforts
performance.narrative:
Following the capture of Goma and Bukavu in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Special Envoy intensified engagements with regional and international stakeholders to help prevent a regional spill-over of the conflict and help maintain coherence and complementarity among the concurrent peace initiatives. Through sustained outreach, the Special Envoy helped ensure that African-led efforts were consistent with ongoing efforts under the Washington and Doha processes.
The Mission supported preparations for a coordination meeting in Lomé between the African Union mediator between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda and the Panel of Facilitators, which clarified the way forward and the respective roles of the Facilitators. Throughout this period, the Special Envoy had regular contacts with African Union senior officials to strengthen coordination and collaboration.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 43).

planned.title: A revitalized Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework better addresses the root causes of recurrent crises in the Great Lakes region
planned.narrative:
In 2025, the mission met the target by supporting the revitalization of the Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework. The twelfth high-level meeting of the Regional Oversight Mechanism (ROM) adopted an Action Plan and the 39th meeting of the Technical Support Committee (TSC) reviewed progress in its implementation. On 21 December, a Joint Ad Hoc Summit of the ROM and ICGLR was convened to address crises, strengthen alignment with the Washington and Doha processes and enhance coherence between the Framework and the ICGLR Pact. The mission co-organized, together with ICGLR and the Kimberley Process Secretariat, a workshop to strengthen the ICGLR Regional Initiative on Natural Resources. The mission also facilitated the development of regional standard operating procedures for Disarmament, Demobilization, Repatriation, Reintegration, and Resettlement (DDR/RR) by the Contact and Coordination Group on non-military measures.
In 2027, the mission will continue to support the Framework and strengthen synergies between African-led and international mediation efforts in a gender-sensitive manner.
Lessons learned and planned change
Despite sustained peace efforts, military offensives continued in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, increasing the risk of regional spill-over. This underscores the urgency of tackling the root causes of the conflict and advancing inclusive political solutions.

performance.title: Strengthened regional coherence and coordinated preventive action in the Horn of Africa
performance.narrative:
In 2025, the mission played a central role in advancing preventive diplomacy and confidence-building amid regional tensions. Through sustained political engagement, the Special Envoy worked with regional leaders, neighbouring States and partners to promote dialogue. A key achievement was the establishment of structured engagement platforms, including the Friends of the Horn of Africa forum, which brings together permanent members of the Security Council and influential regional actors to align messaging and reduce fragmentation among external initiatives.
The mission also strengthened regional UN coordination through joint regional analysis, shared risk assessments, prioritizing collective action, leading to more effective information-sharing, consistent messaging and better sequencing of diplomatic interventions in contexts marked by political transitions and protracted crises.

planned.title: Enhanced collective action in implementing the prevention agenda in the Horn of Africa
planned.narrative:
In 2025, the mission’s work contributed to strengthened regional coherence in preventive engagement across the Horn of Africa. Through the Secretary-General’s good offices and closer collaboration with regional organizations and stakeholders, the mission supported enhanced information-sharing and consistent messaging and improved the sequencing of engagement. Joint Regional Analyses and coordination mechanisms under the Regional Strategy fostered a shared understanding of risks and entry points for collective action, reinforcing regional ownership of prevention efforts.
In 2027, the mission will support political and peace processes in the region, by working with the AU, IGAD, Member States and regional actors. Leveraging the UN’s convening power, the mission will promote trust-building, dialogue on regional issues and unified action by key stakeholders. These efforts aim to strengthen crises prevention. The mission will also coordinate the implementation of the Regional Strategy, ensuring a coherent One-UN approach across the peace and security, development and human rights pillars.
Lessons learned and planned change
The lesson for the mission was that preventive engagement through regional coordination is most effective when used to inform decision-making and the sequencing of political engagement based on shared analysis and clearly identified risks. In applying this lesson, the mission will focus on prioritizing high-impact actions, collective messaging with regional partners, and targeted joint efforts to reduce fragmentation and prevent escalation.

performance.title: Cessation of violence and progress toward a Myanmar-led political solution to the crisis, including creating conditions conducive to the return of refugees
performance.narrative:
In 2025, the Special Envoy engaged Myanmar stakeholders, Member States and civil society to explore pathways toward a Myanmar-led political solution to the country’s multidimensional crisis and its regional implications. During her visits to Myanmar, the Special Envoy underscored the opportunity for the country to unite in response to the March 2025 earthquakes and for building momentum toward a cessation of hostilities and an inclusive political process. While several armed actors declared unilateral ceasefires to allow for rescue and recovery efforts, these were ultimately not sustained, and violence continued. Through continuous engagement, including participation in the General Assembly High-level Conference on the Situation of Rohingya Muslims and other Minorities in Myanmar, the Special Envoy helped renew international attention to the Rohingya crisis and generate new funding pledges for the response. Strong coordination with the ASEAN Special Envoy and advancing UN-ASEAN cooperation, including joint women, peace and security initiatives, helped amplify the voices of Myanmar women. The Special Envoy also continued efforts to promote system-wide coherence, and safeguard the operating space of the United Nations country team in Myanmar.

priorities: Maintenance of international peace and security

overview.name: Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen
objectives: The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to achieve a negotiated political settlement between the parties to end the conflict in Yemen and enable the resumption of a peaceful, inclusive, orderly, Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political transition that will lead Yemenis towards a path of sustainable peace.

performance.title: The multitrack UN-led mediation process advanced
performance.narrative:
In 2025, the mission advanced efforts in support of the United Nations-facilitated political process. On the political track, the mission regularly engaged with the conflict parties, as well as regional and international actors. The mission also held political consultations with diverse Yemeni political actors, women, media, youth and civil society across multiple governorates. Despite tensions in the region, the Red Sea, and parts of southern Yemen, front lines within Yemen remained broadly stable, with the mission’s proactive and broad engagement contributing to preserving space for continued dialogue. The mission also co-convened, with the International Committee of the Red Cross, a meeting of the Supervisory Committee on the implementation of the detainees’ agreement in Muscat, which resulted in an initial agreement that marked a step forward for the potential release of thousands of conflict-related detainees.
On the economic track, the mission engaged with senior Government of Yemen and Houthi-affiliated officials, as well as with key and senior private sector actors to better understand key economic developments, issues and pressure points impacting the conflict; and to identify viable entry points, with a focus on confidence-building measures and developing concrete solutions, for example, overcoming the bifurcation of the Central Bank and the currency. On the military/security track, the mission convened six meetings with delegations of the Military Coordination Committee to discuss and plan for a national ceasefire and transitional security arrangements.

overview.name: Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict
objectives: The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to eradicate the six grave violations committed against children in situations of armed conflict through strengthened mechanisms for the protection of children used in armed conflict, prevent these violations from occurring in the first place, and improve measures to better protect children in situations of armed conflict, including by ensuring that children are placed at the centre of peace negotiations and securing optimal conditions for the release and reintegration of children, thereby avoiding re-recruitment and contributing to sustainable peace.

performance.title: Decrease in the verified number of children in detention
performance.narrative:
As stipulated in article 37 (b) of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the detention of children should only be used as a measure of last resort and for the shortest appropriate period of time. While it is not one of the six grave violations against children in armed conflict, the number of children deprived of liberty for alleged or actual association with parties to conflict remains a significant concern, as detention may expose children to further protection risks, impede their recovery and reintegration and undermine efforts to treat children associated with parties to conflict primarily as victims entitled to protection and reintegration support, in line with Security Council resolution 2427 (2018). The Office has engaged in sustained advocacy with Member States and with parties to conflict to adopt specific measures to end and prevent the detention of children for association with parties to conflict, such as the establishment of handover protocols to civilian child protection actors. In contexts like Haiti and Yemen, for example, the adoption and implementation of handover protocol for the transfer of children allegedly associated with armed groups led to the actual release of dozens of detained children to civilian actors. In the DRC, Nigeria, and Somalia, engagement with the authorities led to the transfer of children to civilian actors for reintegration purposes. The Office also monitors and reports on the number of children deprived of liberty for alleged or actual association with parties to conflict. After a sharp increase in 2024 due to the emergence of new conflicts and the intensification of existing conflict situations, the verified number of children in detention declined in 2025, notwithstanding deteriorating political and security conditions across several situations on the children and armed conflict agenda.

overview.name: Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict
objectives: The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to prevent and eradicate sexual violence as a tactic of war and terrorism and improve the provision of multisectoral services for survivors and the delivery of justice and accountability for such crimes.

performance.title: Strengthened national ownership to prevent conflict-related sexual violence and deliver justice for survivors: the case of Ukraine
performance.narrative:
Since 2022, in response to allegations of conflict-related sexual violence in Ukraine, the Office led the development and implementation of a comprehensive victim-centered system-wide strategy to prevent and respond to conflict-related sexual violence in Ukraine. The early advocacy, mobilisation of United Nations entities and Member States political and financial support and the early deployment of specialised technical advice and expertise resulted in a unique pioneering model that brought together national authorities, the United Nations, survivor networks, and partner organizations. A framework of cooperation was signed between the Special Representative, on behalf of the United Nations system, and the government of Ukraine in May 2022. The Framework’s Implementation Plan was subsequently rapidly developed over a period of two months through extensive co-led consultations and comprehensive stakeholder participation as a unified roadmap across five priority areas: accountability, trafficking, services, reparations, and reform of the security sector. Through its advocacy, the Office mobilized Member States’ support and voluntary funding to deploy specialized expertise to operationalize commitments under the framework. This included the rapid deployment of: (i) specialized capacity to document and verify allegations, (ii) a Senior Women Protection Adviser to the office of the Resident Coordinator to support coordination and oversee the monitoring and reporting arrangements; (iii) specialized coordination and programmatic capacity to the United Nations Country Team; and (iv) international and national experts within key ministries to strengthen national capacity and support the implementation of the Framework’s commitments. The Team of Experts supported the development of a survivor-centered, trauma-informed strategy to national investigations and prosecutions, set up national specialized units, and delivered training, mentoring, and technical guidance. Since 2022, more than 650 prosecutors, investigators, judges, and legal aid providers built specialized skills, including in strategic case-building and trauma-informed interviewing, through scenario-based skills training. In addition, the United Nations Action against Sexual Violence in Conflict network spearheaded a catalytic project bringing together six United Nations entities that delivered multisectoral services to more than 2,200 survivors and supported the creation of Survivor Relief Centres across the country. In 2025, nationwide evaluations and consultations to assess progress on the implementation of the Framework were co-led by the Office with the Office of the Gender Commissioner and resulted in an updated implementation plan for 2026–2027.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 1.75).

objectives: The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to accelerate action to end all forms of violence against children by 2030.

performance.title: Strengthened commitment of the private sector to protect children from violence in the context of travel and tourism
performance.narrative:
Many child protection challenges emerge in the context of travel and tourism, whether as a result of offenders moving within or between States, technology-facilitated abuse, or as an unintended result of the activities and operations of the sector itself. As the travel and tourism industry was rebuilding after the COVID-19 pandemic, the Special Representative determined that it was a strategic moment to re-engage the sector and put child protection at the core of its sustainability agenda. The Special Representative consequently focused her 2023 annual report to the General Assembly on this theme and re-engaged the industry. She supported the creation of a working group of the World Travel and Tourism Council, leading industry representatives and civil society to identify and share good practices and develop a joint advocacy strategy. Following sustained advocacy by the Special Representative, the World Travel and Tourism Council included child protection as an explicit priority in its social impact work at its annual meeting in October 2024. Another important milestone was the World Travel and Tourism Council Summit in September 2025, during which participating chief executive officers committed to incorporate child protection as a key dimension in their companies’ sustainability strategies.

overview.name: Office of the Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Sudan
objectives: The objective to which this mission contributes, is to seek an immediate cessation of hostilities, leading to a sustainable resolution to the Sudan conflict, and to advance a lasting peace through dialogue and an inclusive and comprehensive Sudanese-led political process that reflects the aspirations of the Sudanese people.

performance.title: De-escalation and an inclusive political process
performance.narrative:
In 2025, against an increasingly fragmented and volatile political environment marked by continued hostilities, heightened risks to civilians and competing political trajectories, the Office of the Personal Envoy intensified its good offices with the conflict parties to maintain direct engagement, incentivizing dialogue and de-escalation, maintaining channels active with the parties, and raising attention on the violence and its impact on the civilians. Extensive consultations took place between the Office and Sudanese civilian and political actors across the spectrum, including women and youth, underscoring a shared demand for an immediate ceasefire, interim measures to protect civilians and a civilian-led transition anchored in an inclusive Sudanese owned political process.
In parallel, the Office played a facilitating role in strengthening coordination among mediation actors. These efforts resulted in enhanced common messaging, further clarity on partners’ roles and greater complementarity of effort. The Office also began preparatory work to strengthen the political track, including comparative analysis of political visions and road maps articulated by Sudanese stakeholders, to contribute to shared understanding and preparedness for structured consultations in support of an inclusive Sudanese owned political process.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 61).

planned.title: Increased coherence of mediation initiatives in support of peace and of the launch of an inclusive political process
planned.narrative:
In 2025, the mission focused on aligning mediation initiatives, sustaining good offices with the parties and supporting inclusive political engagement. The mission supported the Consultative Meetings on Enhancing Coordination of Peace Initiatives, including the fourth meeting in June 2025, facilitated the operationalisation of a technical-level Task Force in January 2025, and reinforced multilateral coordination through the consolidation of the Quintet framework. The mission also conducted consultations with Sudanese civilians and advanced analytical and preparatory work, including comparative analysis of political visions and road maps, to inform structured political engagements.
In 2027, the mission will continue to promote coherent and complementary mediation, sustain good offices with the conflict parties to encourage confidence-building and de-escalation, and advance inclusive civilian engagement and preparatory political work toward an inclusive, Sudanese-owned political process. This will include support to the Quad’s de-escalation efforts and coordination within the Quintet to facilitate structured engagement of Sudanese stakeholders toward a credible political process.
Lessons learned and planned change
The mission’s experience in 2025 confirmed that stronger coordination at multiple levels is one of the Mission’s most effective tools to reduce fragmentation, discourage disparate peace efforts, and promote convergence around a coherent political process. In applying these lessons, the mission will prioritize structured coordination through established mechanisms, including the Consultative Meetings and the Quintet framework, and focus on sequenced consultations, supported by analytical and preparatory work, while expanding the use of virtual and hybrid modalities to sustain inclusive participation.

overview.name: Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Western Sahara
objectives: The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to advance the parties’ efforts to achieve a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution, which will provide for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara.
strategy:
To contribute to the objective, the mission will:
Encourage the parties to continue the discussion on the question of Western Sahara in order to identify elements of convergence, through bilateral consultations, including with the neighbouring countries of Algeria and Mauritania, conduct visits to the region to meet with key interlocutors and engage in shuttle diplomacy and other activities deemed useful in that regard;
Consult with members of the Security Council and the Group of Friends on Western Sahara, both in their capitals and in New York, as well as with regional organizations, towards a solution;
Facilitate two international meetings bringing together all concerned on Western Sahara.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
Additional trust built and strengthened involvement by the parties in the political process;
Maintained support by the international community for the political process.
With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission regularly meets with regional organizations and other relevant stakeholders to exchange views on the United Nations-led political process.
With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission receives support for visits and information on developments in Western Sahara from the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara. It also coordinates and liaises with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees on visits to the refugee camps and on confidence-building measures and maintains contact with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in Geneva on issues related to the human rights situation.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
All concerned show willingness to meet for direct negotiations;
The security situation remains conducive to the mission’s objective for the region.
The mission integrates a gender perspective into its activities. It ensures that women and representatives of women’s organizations are included in meetings with civil society and will encourage delegations to include women in political meetings.
In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the mission will include consultations with persons with disabilities on their inclusion in meetings.

In this context, the Personal Envoy continued his efforts to engage all concerned and undertook broadened consultations on the issue of Western Sahara with a view to constructively advancing the political process. The consultations focused on exploring constructive suggestions for the people of Western Sahara to attain a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution that provides for their self-determination. The adoption of Security Council resolution 2797 on 31 October 2025, provided new impetus to efforts to resolve the conflict based on renewed international engagement in support of the political process. These developments contributed to a readiness of all concerned to engage with a view to resolving the protracted situation and meet the aspirations of the people of Western Sahara to find a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution that provides for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara.

objectives: 50. strategy:
51. To contribute to the objective, the mission will continue to support the work of the Security Council and the Committee in relation to the implementation of the sanctions regime with regard to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.
52. The above-mentioned work is expected to result in an enhanced capacity of the Security Council and the Committee conducive to overseeing and promoting the full implementation of the Council sanctions measures.
53. With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission will continue to cooperate with the Resident Coordinator’s Office and the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs and other United Nations agencies carrying out humanitarian assistance and relief activities in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, including the Food and Agriculture Organization, UNDP, the United Nations Population Fund, the United Nations Children’s Fund, WFP and the World Health Organization, as well as other non-United Nations agencies carrying out related activities. The mission will continue to facilitate the work of the United Nations agencies through regular and ad hoc briefings to the United Nations country team in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, and assist those agencies with the Committee’s humanitarian exemption application process. The mission will also continue to guide relevant entities through the sanctions measures and exemption procedures to ensure sanctions compliance. In the context of safety and security, information technology security and logistics, the mission cooperates with the Department of Safety and Security and the Office of Information and Communications Technology.
54. With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

57. The above-mentioned work contributed to the Security Council’s and the Committee’s ability to oversee the implementation of sanctions as the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea persisted in carrying out prohibited activities, including ballistic missile launches.

overview.name: Resident coordinator system
objectives: The objective, to which the resident coordinator system contributes, is to accelerate Member States’ progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals through leadership of the strengthened United Nations development support, robust coordination mechanisms, tools and frameworks, the effective management of joint resources and improved transparency of results to improve the impact, efficiency and effectiveness of operational activities for development at the country, regional and global levels.

performance.title: National Governments advanced integrated policy approaches to Sustainable Development Goal acceleration
performance.narrative:
Resident coordinators lead United Nations system-wide support to host governments in ensuring integrated policy formulation at the national level to advance progress across the SDGs. In 2025, resident coordinators worked with host Governments to support their preparations of the new Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement, ahead of the 30th Conference of Parties of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP30). Resident coordinators supported 107 host Governments in the formulation effort of the NDCs, helping ensure the adoption of an economy-wide approach to support SDG acceleration synergistically with climate action. Through their convening leadership, resident coordinators harnessed the expertise of 30 United Nations entities to support Governments in this effort, helping ensure that new NDCs act as vehicles for integrated policies and financing spanning key sectors and SDGs such as agriculture and food systems (SDG2), energy (SDG7), buildings and transport (SDG 11), waste management (SDG12), and biodiversity (SDGs 14 and 15). Significant emphasis was also placed on situating the NDCs as entry points to reduce inequalities (SDG10) and advance gender equality (SDG5), in line with national needs and priorities and within the context of their cooperation frameworks.

planned.narrative: ILO estimates indicate that 3.8 billion people globally lack access to any form of social protection, while closing this gap would require an additional US$1.4 trillion in public financing. At the same time, the global jobs gap—people willing to work but unable to find employment—is projected to reach 400–408 million by 2026.
