objectives: The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to advance national, regional and international efforts to protect populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity and their incitement.

performance.title: Strengthened genocide prevention capacities of regional organizations, governments, non-governmental organizations and civil society organizations
performance.narrative:
In 2025, the mission supported the Uganda National Committee for the Prevention of Genocide and Other Mass Atrocities, enabling a two-day workshop to revitalize the Committee after two years of inactivity and prepare an action plan ahead of the January 2026 elections in Uganda. The workshop facilitated the Committee’s election of its new leadership bureau and enhanced members’ capacity to assess and respond to risks of genocide and other atrocity crimes. As a result, new leaders were elected, members received targeted training on prevention, and a practical action plan was developed to guide the Committee’s work during and after the elections. During the elections, the Committee deployed observers and produced a report with recommendations to mitigate election-related violence, which the Special Adviser shared with relevant UN entities. This experience highlights the value of the mission’s support in strengthening national mechanisms for genocide and atrocity-crime prevention.
Building on sustained technical engagement, the mission also strengthened its prevention framework through the development and adoption of three policy documents and training manuals in 2025. Focused on countering hate speech and enhancing genocide prevention, these resources provide communities, non-governmental organizations (NGO), and civil society organizations with tools for risk identification and response. As a result, vulnerable communities benefit from stronger risk analysis, more coordinated prevention strategies, and increased resilience to genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. Combined with increased advocacy following General Assembly resolution 78/282 on the Srebrenica genocide commemoration, these advances reinforce global prevention efforts and support healing processes for affected communities.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 9).

planned.title: Enhanced protection from atrocity crimes through improved awareness and prevention mechanisms and better risk identification capabilities for Member States and regional organizations
planned.narrative:
In 2025, the mission advanced national, regional and international efforts to protect populations from genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, and met the planned target of 20 follow-up actions taken by Member States and regional organizations to address risks of such crimes. A special emphasis was placed on supporting the revitalization of prevention of genocide work within the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR), reinforcing regional commitment to early warning and coordinated prevention efforts.
Lessons learned and planned change
The lesson for the mission was that collaborating with United Nations field entities, NGOs and civil society organizations proved essential in improving outreach and strengthening the quality of risk assessments. Joint development of context-specific action plans enhanced partners’ capacity to detect and respond to hate-speech trends, while memorandums of understanding with civil society organizations improved access to timely community-level information. Going forward, the mission will deepen collaboration, information-sharing and joint analysis with community level and regional partners to strengthen the assessment of risks related to genocide and other atrocity crimes.
At the same time, to respond to evolving risks of genocide and other atrocity crimes, the mission adjusted its delivery modalities by shifting from predominantly knowledge-product outputs to more practice-oriented workshops, strengthening engagement with United Nations country teams, and expanding the use of virtual platforms, thereby enhancing reach, responsiveness, and impact in support of its prevention objectives.
Expected progress towards the objective and the target for 2027 are presented in the performance measure below (see figure III).

planned.title: Advancing implementation of resolution 1540 (2004) through needs-based assistance and enhanced regional cooperation
planned.narrative:
257. In 2025, the mission contributed to the enhanced implementation of resolution 1540 by implementing multiple awareness-raising and capacity-building activities including regional and national workshops and through facilitation of strengthened regional cooperation. Among those activities, four regional workshops were conducted, including the first training course for resolution 1540 points of contact in the Latin America and Caribbean region in ten years, which exceeded the planned target of three workshops. These activities enhanced Member States’ knowledge and capacity, led to higher rates of 1540 points of contact nominations and engagement, and enhanced regional collaboration and coordination for the implementation of resolution 1540 (2004). Building on progress achieved to date, the Mission plans to conduct three regional workshops and four national workshops in 2027 to sustain momentum and further enhance implementation while adapting to changes arising from the UN80 initiative.
Lessons learned and planned change
258. An important lesson learned for the mission was that the sustainable implementation of resolution 1540 requires a nationally driven process aligned with national priorities. Applying this lesson, the mission will promote a nationally owned approach that aligns national priorities with efforts to implement resolution 1540 (2004). The mission will also strengthen its partnerships with regional and subregional organizations to build synergies and enhance collaboration. entities.name: United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women
priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
17.3 The UN-Women strategic plan 2026–2029 guides the Entity’s direction, objectives and approaches to advancing gender equality, the empowerment of all women and girls and the full realization of their human rights. It comes at a pivotal moment, with four years remaining to achieve the 2030 Agenda. The triple mandate of UN-Women – normative support, United Nations system coordination and operational activities – provides a unique opportunity for driving integrated, systemic change by connecting global norms, United Nations system-wide accountability and country-level implementation in a coherent and mutually reinforcing manner.
17.4 The strategic plan draws from comprehensive analysis of the rapidly evolving context and builds on an extensive consultative process, lessons from the midterm review of the 2022–2025 Strategic Plan, findings from audits, evaluations and assessments and the 30-year review of the implementation of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (Beijing+30).
17.5 It will advance gender equality, empowerment and rights for all women and girls through four impact areas: (a) women’s leadership and decision-making; (b) women’s economic empowerment in resilient economies; (c) women and girls free from violence; and (d) women and peace and security and humanitarian action.
17.6 Across these thematic impact areas, UN-Women will pursue three cross-cutting systemic outcomes that address the root causes of inequality and drive systems change: (a) norms and standards that uphold the rights of all women and girls are protected, strengthened and implemented in laws and policies; (b) institutions are accountable to all women and girls, with financing, data and practices that advance equality; and (c) more women and girls can exercise their agency and have equitable access to quality services, resources and assets.
17.7 These outcomes underpin the two subprogrammes by linking global norm-setting and United Nations system coordination with country-level policy advice and programming support. As a knowledge hub and thought leader, UN-Women will generate evidence, data and analysis to inform intergovernmental processes and to support Member States, upon their request, to develop and implement gender-responsive laws, policies and budgets.
17.8 UN-Women is rejuvenating its business model to drive agile, efficient and forward-looking performance. Its organizational effectiveness and efficiency framework integrates and reflects the UN-Women contributions to United Nations system-wide transformation initiatives. It will apply a balanced scorecard methodology and a quarterly business review process that support continuous, integrated performance management across five areas: accountability and performance; resource partnerships and communications; business transformation and innovation; empowered people; and programme effectiveness through results-based management. These efforts collectively reinforce results-orientation, accountability, transparency and value for money.
17.9 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, UN-Women will continue to work with and through wide-ranging partnerships, encompassing Member States, the United Nations system, civil society (including grass-roots and women’s rights organizations), the private sector, international financial institutions, philanthropy, youth and men and boys. UN-Women will leverage multi-stakeholder initiatives to promote institutional change, positive social norms and collective action, working with and through others to extend reach and impact.
17.10 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, UN-Women plays a crucial role in ensuring that gender equality remains at the centre of the ongoing reform processes. UN-Women will leverage its United Nations coordination mandate on gender equality through system-wide accountability frameworks, including the United Nations System-wide Action Plan on Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women and the United Nations country team System-wide Action Plan gender equality scorecard, gender marker and gender parity, as well as by setting norms and standards to accelerate progress on gender equality at the global, regional and country levels. UN-Women will continue to support the leadership of resident coordinators in integrating gender equality into United Nations country team planning processes, including common country analyses, Cooperation Frameworks and humanitarian response plans. UN-Women will also co-lead gender theme groups, advance joint programming and, at the regional level, co-lead issue-based coalitions on gender equality, to strengthen United Nations system programming and resource mobilization for gender equality to deliver results for women and girls.
17.11 With regard to external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Sustained political commitment of Member States to the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action and to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda, with adequate resources allocated to gender equality;
(b) Continued availability of voluntary contributions and expanded partnerships to address a challenging funding landscape;
(c) Coherence and collaboration across the United Nations system to advance gender mainstreaming and support Member States;
(d) An enabling environment for civil society and organizations promoting women’s rights to participate in intergovernmental processes and policy dialogue.
17.12 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the UN-Women global strategy on the empowerment of women and girls with disabilities, and the entity’s Disability Inclusion Policy, UN-Women will accelerate the effective mainstreaming of disability inclusion and promote accessibility in its institutional processes, programming and joint initiatives in partnership with Member States, organizations of persons with disabilities and other partners. UN-Women will continue to chair the United Nations Inter-agency Group on Gender Equality and Disability Inclusion. Where it has a presence, UN-Women will facilitate an intersectional approach to disability inclusion by leveraging operational and programming collaboration with United Nations country teams.

17.24 In the context of the thirtieth anniversary of the Fourth World Conference on Women, UN-Women led a global advocacy effort with Governments, the United Nations system, civil society and women and girls to secure national commitments to close gaps in implementing the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action and achieve lasting progress for all women and girls.
17.25 Drawing on the evidence from the thirtieth anniversary review of progress in the implementation of the Beijing Platform for Action, 159 Member State reports and the political declaration adopted by the Commission on the Status of Women at its sixty-ninth session, on 10 March 2025, the subprogramme defined the Beijing+30 Action Agenda: for all women and girls to advance efforts to achieve the full, effective and accelerated implementation of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action. At the high-level meeting of the General Assembly marking the thirtieth anniversary of the Fourth World Conference on Women, held on 22 September 2025, Member States from all regions reaffirmed their commitment to the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, as well as to the full empowerment and realization of the rights of all women and girls. These high-level political commitments demonstrated strong political will to take action to advance the effective and accelerated implementation of the Beijing Platform for Action.

planned.title: Enhanced gender mainstreaming through the United Nations System-wide Action Plan on Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women 3.0
planned.narrative:
17.31 The United Nations System-wide Action Plan on Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women is the system-wide accountability framework for promoting gender equality and the empowerment of women. Its new iteration, the United Nations System-wide Action Plan on Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women 3.0 (2025–2030), responds to Member States’ calls under Economic and Social Council resolution 2025/4 and General Assembly resolution 79/226 for stronger institutional accountability and measurable progress on gender equality. The subprogramme led its design and roll-out, coordinating 75 United Nations entities and ensuring alignment with system-wide frameworks. It provided technical guidance, help desk support, digital reporting tools and training to enhance the quality, consistency and use of gender data for planning and results reporting. The System-wide Action Plan 3.0 strengthens the capacity of United Nations entities to mainstream a gender perspective into all policies and programmes, supports results-based analysis and informs intergovernmental dialogue and collective accountability.
Lessons learned and planned change
17.32 The lesson for the subprogramme was that, while entities’ institutional capacity has improved, gaps persist in translating system-wide progress into results on the ground. Experience demonstrated that institutional gender mainstreaming can be more directly linked to entities’ results frameworks. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will reinforce results-based approaches, strengthen the analytical use of data from the System-wide Action Plan and build targeted capacities of United Nations entities and inter-agency mechanisms to contribute to gender equality and women’s empowerment outcomes in line with system-wide and national priorities.

performance.title: Member States use time-use data to inform evidence-based policies to recognize, reduce and redistribute unpaid care work
performance.narrative:
17.39 Women and girls perform an estimated three quarters of unpaid care and domestic work globally. This disproportionate responsibility can constrain women’s and girls’ participation in formal employment, education and leisure, underscoring the growing recognition among Governments of the need to recognize, reduce and redistribute unpaid care and domestic work. Time-use surveys shine a light on how women and men spend their time and are used to inform evidence-based policies to support and redistribute unpaid care work, including through the development of household satellite accounts that measure the economic value of unpaid work. The subprogramme, during 2025, provided support to six Member States, at their request, to design and conduct time-use surveys and use the results for decision-making. Time-use surveys conducted with the support of UN-Women in previous years informed care-related policy development, including the first national care policy of Kenya and the integration of unpaid care work into national development planning in Bangladesh, Georgia and Senegal.

entities.name: United Nations Human Settlements Programme
priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
15.3 UN-Habitat operates in a world that will continue to urbanize over the coming three decades. Approximately 90 per cent of urban growth is taking place in less developed regions, where unplanned growth is driving urban sprawl, and where lack of adequate and affordable housing exacerbates poverty and inequalities, which manifest in the rise of informal settlements, slums and homelessness. By contrast, many cities in other parts of the world are facing negative growth and shrinking populations. The global housing challenge is intensifying, with the demand for affordable and adequate housing outpacing supply in urban areas, further deepening inequality and vulnerability. Globally, more than 2.8 billion people live in inadequate housing, a figure that includes over 1.12 billion who reside in slums and informal settlements. Additionally, there are 304 million international migrants, most of whom live in urban areas, and 75.9 million internally displaced people.
15.4 The proposed programme plan for 2027 is guided by the UN-Habitat strategic plan for 2026–2029, which was approved by the UN-Habitat Assembly in May 2025. The proposed programme structure is informed by the strategic focus and means of implementation. The programme of work centres on access to adequate housing, land and basic services for all, including the transformation of informal settlements and slums to help drive sustainable urbanization. This focus responds directly to the scale and urgency of global housing shortages and recognizes adequate housing as central for addressing broader development challenges, including poverty, inequality and vulnerability to the adverse impacts of climate change.
15.5 The programme structure distinguishes between the substantive programmatic areas through which UN-Habitat contributes directly to development outcomes and the enabling areas that strengthen the policy, knowledge and partnership ecosystems required to achieve sustainable urban development at scale. This structure also responds to lessons learned from the implementation and midterm evaluation of the previous strategic plan, which highlighted the need for greater strategic prioritization, clearer programmatic focus and improved coherence across the organization’s normative and operational activities.
15.6 Subprogramme 1, Housing, land, basic services and urban environment, advances the central focus of the strategic plan on access to adequate housing, land and basic services for all, including the transformation of informal settlements and slums. Through this subprogramme, UN-Habitat will support Member States and local authorities in expanding access to adequate housing and basic services, strengthening land governance and promoting environmentally sustainable urban development, thereby contributing directly to improved living conditions, inclusive prosperity and resilient cities and human settlements.
15.7 Subprogramme 2, Planning, finance policy, localization and governance, operationalizes the first two means of implementation identified in the strategic plan, namely, integrated urban and territorial planning, management, investment and finance, and participatory multilevel governance and localization of the Sustainable Development Goals. Through this subprogramme, UN-Habitat will strengthen policy, planning and governance frameworks that enable sustainable urbanization, support the development of integrated planning systems and sustainable urban finance mechanisms and advance participatory governance processes that accelerate the localization and implementation of the Goals.
15.8 Subprogramme 3, Knowledge, data, digitalization and capacity development, operationalizes the third means of implementation, with a focus on strengthening knowledge systems and institutional capacities to support evidence-based policymaking and effective implementation of sustainable urban development policies and programmes. Through this subprogramme, UN-Habitat will advance the generation, collection and analysis of urban data and knowledge, promote digital and smart city approaches that support improved urban management and strengthen the capacities of national and local governments and other stakeholders, including monitoring of Sustainable Development Goal 11 and the implementation of the New Urban Agenda.
15.9 Subprogramme 4, Partnerships, coalitions, advocacy and communication, a fourth means of implementation, recognizes that achieving impact at scale requires strengthened collaboration among Member States, local and regional governments, international organizations, civil society, academia and the private sector, among others. Through this subprogramme, UN-Habitat will promote strategic partnerships, facilitate global and regional coalitions for sustainable urban development and strengthen advocacy and communication on the importance of adequate housing, land and basic services as drivers of sustainable development. It will also leverage the organization’s convening role through global platforms and partnerships to mobilize action, share knowledge and enhance the visibility and impact of sustainable urban development within the broader multilateral system.
15.10 Taken together, the four subprogrammes provide a coherent and mutually reinforcing structure that aligns programmatic delivery, enabling policy frameworks, knowledge generation and partnerships in support of the strategic focus of the strategic plan. The structure ensures that UN-Habitat can effectively deliver normative guidance, technical cooperation and knowledge products while mobilizing partnerships and strengthening institutional capacities across levels of government and among stakeholders.
15.11 The programme of work of UN-Habitat is presented under the new structure, with subprogrammes 1 to 4 of the proposed programme plan for 2026 reorganized and integrated across the new subprogrammes with an annex reporting against programme performance for additional deliverables and results from the proposed programme plan for 2026 (see annex to part A below).
15.12 Across regions, subprogramme implementation will be tailored to diverse development contexts – with particular attention to countries in vulnerable and crisis-affected contexts, including least development countries, landlocked developing countries and small island developing States, as well as middle-income and economies in transition – using context-specific thematic entry points and delivery approaches that reflect varying priorities, capacities and pathways to impact under each subprogramme.
15.13 Cities are hotspots for environmental challenges, accounting for approximately 75 per cent of global energy consumption, 70 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions and more than 70 per cent of resource use. In the Pact for the Future (General Assembly resolution 79/1), Member States reiterated their commitment to ensuring access for all to adequate, safe and affordable housing and supporting developing countries in planning and implementing just, safe, healthy, accessible, resilient and sustainable cities. In that context UN-Habitat will support national, regional and local governments in integrating urban and territorial planning, management, and investment and finance aspects and will support them in developing sustainable construction value chains and policies, supported by innovations and technology, that help to overcome inequalities and build resilience.
15.14 The deterioration in progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and implementing the Paris Agreement in the context of interrelated global crises calls for more transformative multilevel action. UN-Habitat will continue to fast-track integration between its normative and operational work, scaling up and accelerating the impact of the organization. UN-Habitat recognizes that rapid urban growth requires bold, forward-looking and collective action to shape cities in ways that address the most pressing urban challenges. As a global advocate for urban development, UN-Habitat will support countries in navigating complex housing issues, including by supporting the open-ended intergovernmental expert working group on adequate housing for all, by providing evidence-based policy advice, capacity development and technical support, and by driving urban programmes to address complex housing issues.
15.15 In line with its capacity-building strategy for the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the New Urban Agenda, UN-Habitat will continue to localize the Sustainable Development Goals and to respond to local challenges by identifying and targeting specific capacity gaps while raising awareness and building skills in transformative solutions. UN-Habitat will strengthen capacity development as a cross-cutting function across its operations, through the continued digitalization and dissemination of knowledge and tools, supported by strategic partnerships for innovation, knowledge and learning across practices.
15.16 In its catalytic role as a knowledge hub and partner convenor, UN-Habitat will carry out advocacy, communication and outreach activities and mobilize broad-based support for the implementation of the New Urban Agenda. It will operationalize stronger stakeholder engagement and collaboration with universities and centres of knowledge and research in order to continue to leverage advocacy and knowledge platforms, including the thirteenth session of the World Urban Forum, the Urban Agenda Platform, coalitions, global corporate events, regional ministerial conferences, the ministerial meeting on urbanization and climate change and the intersessional activities of the open-ended intergovernmental expert working group on adequate housing for all.
15.17 Furthermore, UN-Habitat will continue to monitor and report on global trends and provide evidence for policymaking, including through the enhanced use of technologies for data collection and analysis, data visualization and management of information. It will continue to expand the roll-out of the Global Urban Monitoring Framework and its support for Member States and other stakeholders in monitoring and reporting on the progress in the implementation of the New Urban Agenda and other global agendas and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.
15.18 Regarding cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, UN-Habitat will continue its close cooperation with international and regional organizations, such as the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the World Bank, the European Union and regional development banks and explore deepened partnerships with relevant institutions from the global South. UN-Habitat will maintain its focus on partnerships with local authorities and their associations and city networks, grass-roots organizations, foundations, international financial institutions, the private sector and academia to promote participatory and multilevel governance and support municipal efforts in the localization of the Sustainable Development Goals and will continue to serve as the secretariat and co-Chair of the Local2030 coalition.
15.19 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, UN-Habitat will continue to collaborate with the United Nations programmes and funds as well as specialized agencies, the Department of Economic and Social Affairs and the United Nations regional economic and social commissions, and strengthen its strategic inter-agency partnerships, building on the United Nations system-wide strategy on sustainable urban development and agency-specific collaborative frameworks. Additionally, UN-Habitat will continue to advance the goals of the United Nations reform aimed at increasing sustainable development impacts at the country level with a focus on regional collaboration achieved through the regional development cooperation platforms and issue-based coalitions. UN-Habitat will also deepen its collaboration with the Development Coordination Office to strengthen the United Nations system-wide impact on sustainable development by providing technical guidance, contributing to the revision of system-wide guidance, helping to build capacity for the use of innovative diagnostic and planning methodologies, and working with the resident coordinator system and United Nations country teams to mainstream sustainable urbanization across common country analyses and United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks.
15.20 To pursue stronger integration of environmental, social and economic sustainability and the protection of biodiversity into urban development, UN-Habitat will continue to strengthen its collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme through the Greener Cities Partnership, in serving as the secretariat for the Secretary-General’s Advisory Board of Eminent Persons on Zero Waste and as a partner in the Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction, which is led by the United Nations Environment Programme. UN-Habitat will also lead a new Issue Management Group on Urbanization and the Environment as part of the Environment Management Group; strengthen collaboration with the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Road Safety; and continue to collaborate with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the United Nations Development Programme, the International Organization for Migration, the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, the World Food Programme and all relevant United Nations entities and international actors to integrate sustainable urban development into resilience, humanitarian response, solutions to forced displacement and urban recovery.
15.21 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Adequate unearmarked extrabudgetary resources are available to implement the planned work and produce the deliverables;
(b) Countries remain committed to the New Urban Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development;
(c) National, regional and local governments continue to request policy advice and technical assistance from UN-Habitat in the development and implementation of their urban legislation, policies, plans and strategies;
(d) Urban indicators, data and information are used to formulate policies, with adequate mechanisms available for impact monitoring and performance assessments;
(e) Countries in which UN-Habitat delivers large programmes maintain political, economic and social conditions that allow for the implementation of programmes and projects.
15.22 UN-Habitat will continue to mainstream social inclusion to address cross-cutting issues affecting women, older persons, persons with disabilities, and children and young people. UN-Habitat will also continue to implement and participate in mechanisms that strengthen the meaningful participation of young people in sustainable urban development, such as the UN-Habitat Youth Advisory Board and the Global Alliance Cities4Children. Furthermore, it will develop critical programmes to promote urban liveability, such as the Youth 2030 Cities programme and the Young Gamechangers initiative.
15.23 UN-Habitat integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, through its gender policy and action plan. Furthermore, the Advisory Group on Gender Issues advises the Executive Director on how to promote gender equality and women’s empowerment in sustainable urban development. UN-Habitat, in collaboration with the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN-Women), will continue to support Member States with policy, legislation, planning and financing instruments to achieve integrated, inclusive and participatory results. For example, UN-Habitat will continue to promote land and housing policies that incorporate a gender perspective and improve tenure security for all, especially women.
15.24 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, UN-Habitat will continue to work with its partners, including the International Disability Alliance, the Global Disability Fund, World Blind Union, World Enabled and the Global Disability Innovation Hub, to provide support on disability-inclusive urban development. It will develop a dedicated action plan to mainstream disability inclusion across its programmatic work and internal operations, highlighting best practices while identifying critical needs in capacity development and technical assistance. This plan will supplement the established environmental and social safeguards applied to all projects.

subprogrammes.name: Housing, land, basic services and urban environment

objectives: 15.32 The objective, to which this subprogramme contributes, is to ensure access to adequate housing, land and basic services for all, transforming informal settlements and slums with access to clean, safe, affordable and equitable basic services that lead to the creation of low-carbon, resilient, inclusive, healthy and economically vibrant cities and neighbourhoods.

performance.title: Integrated sustainable mobility and transit-supportive housing to expand equitable access to safe, equitable public transport in cities, particularly city peripheries
performance.narrative:
15.36 To support access to public transport, especially in city peripheries, which, owing to urban sprawl, is often where low- and middle-income households reside, the subprogramme supported Member States in integrating sustainable mobility and transit-supportive housing to expand access to livelihoods, education and essential services. Sustainable mobility initiatives were implemented in 29 cities across 21 countries, advancing safer, more inclusive and climate-responsive transport systems. Concrete implementation projects – focused on improving pedestrian and cycling infrastructure around public transport corridors and school zones – were carried out in Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda, expanding access to safe, equitable public transport to 816,000 people. This work also contributed to the roll-out of the Pan-African Action Plan for Active Mobility in five countries and supported the expansion of activities to more than 50 cities under the Global Alliance of Cities for Road Safety.

subprogrammes.name: Planning, finance policy, localization and governance

objectives: 15.46 The objective, to which this subprogramme contributes, is to advance integrated urban planning, financing mechanisms, evidence-based policy frameworks, effective legislation and participatory multilevel governance systems for equitable access to adequate housing, land and basic services, taking into consideration the localization of the Sustainable Development Goals and mainstreaming gender equality and women’s empowerment.

performance.title: Planning law reforms strengthen multilevel governance for resilient and sustainable cities
performance.narrative:
15.50 Rapid urbanization and climate change are placing growing pressure on cities, exacerbating fragmented planning systems, unclear institutional mandates and weak coordination between national and local authorities. Addressing these challenges is essential to ensure that climate and urban development commitments translate into effective local action. The subprogramme supported Member States through analysis of legal and institutional frameworks, capacity development and comparative research to strengthen urban legislation as a foundation for resilient and sustainable development, focusing on clarifying institutional roles and responsibilities, improving legal coherence and reinforcing multilevel governance. For example, in 2025, stakeholder consultations and a UN-Habitat review of the Zimbabwe Climate Change Management Bill were undertaken to enhance national ownership of the proposed law and ensure broader institutional and community engagement in its implementation. Moreover, in Sierra Leone, the enactment of the Town and Country Planning Act (2025) strengthened decentralized urban governance by empowering local councils to lead spatial planning and development control, enhancing vertical coordination and integrated territorial planning. Also in 2025, Botswana initiated reforms to the 2013 Planning Law, informed by legal gap analyses, international comparative case studies and inclusive stakeholder consultations, modernizing the planning framework with effective governance mechanisms.
15.51 Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see figure 15.V).

15.54 The subprogramme advances system change and territorial transformation through Sustainable Development Goals localization and multilevel governance, translating global goals and national policies into local action. It supports sustainable urban development by strengthening institutional capacity, mobilizing partners and stakeholders, leveraging finance for local solutions and building the capacities of the United Nations System on Goals localization.
Lessons learned and planned change
15.55 The lesson for the subprogramme was that there were further opportunities to advance territorial transformation and the translation of global goals and national policies into local plans and impact through localization and multilevel governance. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will enhance its guidance and toolkits for Sustainable Development Goals localization, targeting the United Nations System and its partners, to demonstrate in practical terms how to translate global goals into local tangible outcomes. The subprogramme will consolidate technical assistance efforts into integrated support packages and facilitate the use of common methodologies, shared data platforms and coordinated capacity-development approaches. The subprogramme will promote regular knowledge-sharing across regional and global partners and will align its work more systematically with United Nations country teams to ensure coherent system-wide delivery.

subprogrammes.name: Knowledge, data, digitalization and capacity development

objectives: 15.58 The objective, to which this subprogramme contributes, is to advance inclusive, evidence-based and digitally enabled knowledge systems to ensure access to adequate housing, land and basic services.

performance.title: Urban practitioners have open access to practical knowledge and guidance in multiple languages to help accelerate the implementation of the New Urban Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals
performance.narrative:
15.62 Building the capacities of urban practitioners across the globe with adequate skills, knowledge and tools can be supported by developing and scaling digital learning solutions. The subprogramme leverages the potential of knowledge digitalization to enhance outreach and accessibility of learning on critical skills and capabilities. Starting in 2020, UN-Habitat piloted the creation of its first self-paced online courses based on the New Urban Agenda illustrated handbook. This marked the creation of the UN-Habitat Learn platform and the development of an instructional design function at UN-Habitat. The UN-Habitat Learn platform has helped with both scaling up and localizing the organization’s practical knowledge and guidance, with more than 25 different courses to date, providing practical guidance to advance the New Urban Agenda and the Goals, free and accessible to all. The platform offers content in eight languages over 126 hours of learning. It also provides space for digital classrooms supporting hybrid or in-person training programmes. The platform’s course offering presents guidance and methodologies illustrating the main findings of normative and operational work, often capitalizing on multi-year, multi-partner and multi-country initiatives. This knowledge is integrated into learning pathways through an iterative co-creation process across UN-Habitat teams. In some cases, courses have been translated into non-official languages for further replication at the local level.

entities.name: Office of the High Representative for the Least Developed Countries, Landlocked Developing Countries and Small Island Developing States
priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
10.3 Building on the national, regional and thematic preparatory process scheduled to be undertaken in 2026, the least developed countries and their development partners are expected to agree on a new global strategy at the comprehensive high-level midterm review, to be held in Qatar in 2027, to fully and efficiently implement the Doha Programme of Action for the Least Developed Countries. In this context, the Office will support preparatory and follow-up processes, including by strengthening partnerships, supporting coordination among stakeholders and facilitating the mobilization of resources and knowledge to boost progress towards implementation of the 2030 Agenda, leave no one behind and contribute to accelerated implementation of the Doha Programme of Action, including its five deliverables, by the least developed countries and their development partners, through the mobilization of commensurate resources and knowledge in support of accelerating their sustainable development and enhanced monitoring and accountability.
10.4 In 2027, the central task ahead for the landlocked developing countries and their development partners is to strengthen partnerships to intensify efforts to operationalize the objectives and key deliverables of the Awaza Programme of Action for Landlocked Developing Countries. In this regard, the Office will help with the mobilization of adequate financial, technical and capacity-building resources, undertake efforts to strengthen partnerships and support countries with integrating the Programme of Action into national development plans and relevant global frameworks, with a view to addressing the specific vulnerabilities of landlocked developing countries. These measures will contribute to accelerating progress towards implementation of the 2030 Agenda through structural transformation, resilience-building and sustainable development in the landlocked developing countries.
10.5 In 2027, small island developing States and their development partners will advance implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Small Island Developing States, guided by its monitoring and evaluation framework to prioritize action and to track delivery and report results, and fully operationalize the small island developing States centre of excellence. The Office will actively advocate for the strengthening of global partnerships, including through the Small Island Developing States Global Business Network, utilization of the multidimensional vulnerability index, enhanced access to concessional and climate financing, and strengthening the capacity of small island developing States’ national focal points to integrate the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda into national development plans. In parallel, the Office will support the Small Island Developing States Partnership Framework to catalyse accountable results-driven partnerships and engage international financial institutions to drive financing that enable structural transformation and resilience-building. These efforts are intended to deliver early, tangible results under the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda that address the unique challenges and special needs of these States.
10.6 The Office will utilize its strategic position in directly supporting the three groups of countries to respond to current evolving development issues of potential concern, in particular those of a regional or global nature, such as climate change, food security and digital divides. In this regard, the newly established subprogramme 4, on advocacy, outreach and analysis, will enable a more coordinated implementation of the programmes of action, while improving the Office’s capacity to produce analysis across regions and groups of countries, strengthen its research and data management capabilities and ensure more effective advocacy on shared development challenges.
10.7 The Office will continue to mobilize resources to ensure that the least developed countries, landlocked developing countries and small island developing States have their voices heard in global deliberations. Resource mobilization efforts will also have an increased focus on joint initiatives, which can amplify impact across the three groups of countries. Furthermore, representatives of the most vulnerable countries will benefit from capacity-building activities, peer learning and the exchange of best practices all on thematic areas relevant to the Sustainable Development Goals and to building resilience to future crises.
10.8 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will convene the inter-agency consultative groups for the least developed countries, landlocked developing countries and small island developing States. These groups will enable United Nations entities, funds and programmes and other international organizations to exchange information on their work, strengthen coordination of their activities and mount joint inter-agency activities. At the national level, the Office will cooperate with the networks of national focal points, which act as interfaces between global, regional and national processes. The national focal points will promote coherence and coordination on issues relevant to the three groups of countries and facilitate policy formulation, implementation, follow-up and review of their programmes of action, ensuring full alignment with the 2030 Agenda and other global frameworks.
10.9 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will work closely with resident coordinators to promote the integration of the programmes of action into the United Nations strategic plans and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks and to act as an interface with Member States on the ground supporting the mainstreaming of the programmes of action into national strategies.
10.10 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) The security and political situation in the least developed countries, landlocked developing countries and small island developing States and in their surrounding regions is conducive to the implementation of the three programmes of action;
(b) Continued international support measures in the areas of development finance, market access, technology and technical assistance are made available by development partners.
10.11 The Office will further explore the ways of cooperation, support and participation in the global efforts towards the implementation of the 2030 Agenda and the Pact of the Future, with special attention given to the needs of those in vulnerable situations, women, young people, persons with disabilities and older persons.
10.12 The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. The Office will implement its gender equality strategy for the period 2025–2029 and mainstream a gender perspective into its programme of work. In addition, as part of its monitoring and reporting work, the Office will include sex-disaggregated data and analysis across its reports for the three groups of countries.
10.13 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will focus on strengthening knowledge management, learning and capacity for promoting disability inclusion in all aspects of the Office’s work programme, including monitoring, reporting and advocacy activities, in accordance with its mandate. For example, the Office will continue to advocate for the inclusion of language and references to disability inclusion in intergovernmental deliberations, as appropriate and in accordance with its mandates.

In 2025, the subprogramme further supported the use of these tools through targeted outreach and training to least developed countries, guidance on integration into national development plans and United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks, the facilitation of exchanges among national focal points, United Nations country teams and other stakeholders on alignment with midterm milestones and review, and a training workshop for African least developed countries on the monitoring framework and its integration into national review reports of the Doha Programme of Action.

10.30 As more least developed countries meet the graduation thresholds, the General Assembly has underlined that graduation must not lead to setbacks in sustainable development. The subprogramme has operationalized the Sustainable Graduation Support Facility to respond to growing country requests for tailored support in the design and implementation of incentive-based smooth transition strategies.
Lessons learned and planned change
10.31 The lesson for the subprogramme was that support for least developed countries too often prioritized meeting statistical thresholds over building resilient postgraduation trajectories grounded in vulnerability-responsive international support measures and nationally owned transition strategies. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will place a greater emphasis on: (a) country-tailored diagnostics of graduation readiness; (b) systematic use of the Sustainable Graduation Support Facility as a platform for integrated, cross-pillar support; and (c) structured engagement with providers of international support measures to promote incentives-based, time-bound and predictable transition arrangements that reduce the risk of reversal and make graduation a springboard for sustained implementation of the Doha Programme of Action for the Least Developed Countries.

The Office played a central role in supporting the preparation, organization and successful outcome of the third United Nations Conference on Landlocked Developing Countries. The Office supported the development of background documentation, analytical input and draft outcome elements, ensuring that the Political Declaration was informed by evidence, reflected emerging global challenges and responded to the priorities articulated by landlocked developing countries. overview.name: United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan
objectives: The objective, to which the Mission contributes, is to create the conditions for peace and stability, with foundations established for the promotion of inclusive and responsive governance and functioning and accountable institutions, as well as a coherent and sustainable path towards the economic and social conditions for self-reliance.

performance.title: Afghans retain access to dialogue and coordinated assistance
performance.narrative:
In 2025, amid heightened human rights, political, civic and economic constraints, the Mission undertook efforts to maintain a space (even though limited) for dialogue among Afghan stakeholders and between them and UNAMA and the international community. Despite persistent restrictions on media freedoms, civic space and Afghans’ enjoyment of their human rights, most acutely affecting women, Afghans retained access to channels to express concerns and communicate priority needs, enabling their voices to inform discussions on the protection of human rights, including the rights of women and girls, and advocacy for a coherent socio-economic, political and policy agenda.
Through various engagement modalities facilitated by UNAMA, Afghan stakeholders conveyed the impacts of these constraints on rights, livelihoods, social cohesion and economic conditions. Their perspectives informed international advocacy and dialogue on the country’s political trajectory, including the implications of continued constraints for Afghanistan’s reintegration into the international system. In parallel, the High-Level Coordination Forum and the Technical Level Coordination Forum with de facto line ministries, facilitated by UNAMA, enabled an assessment of how the United Nations could complement the implementation of the Afghanistan National Development Strategy 2025-2030 adopted by the de facto authorities.
Based on the areas of common interest for targeted action identified by UNAMA, information gathered from Afghan stakeholders supported more coordinated responses to growing economic pressures, climate-related shocks and limitations on private sector activity. The Mission promoted joint engagement and tangible actions to address the challenges faced by the Afghan population through the Counternarcotics and Private Sector Working Groups under the Doha Process, improved the coherence and predictability of assistance, contributing to a shift from emergency relief toward basic human needs support.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 69).

planned.title: Advancement in the efforts by the international community and the de facto authorities toward the full reintegration of the Afghan State into the international community
planned.narrative:
The international community, the de facto authorities and relevant stakeholders engaged in more coherent and structured direct dialogue, shaping conditions for Afghanistan to advance its reintegration into the international community and meet its international obligations.
Increased direct engagement was undertaken through the United Nations-facilitated efforts of the Comprehensive Approach. The contours of a political roadmap (“Mosaic”) consolidated and identified feasible initial steps to address six key issues affecting prospects for reintegration, including inclusive governance and human rights. The Counternarcotics and Private Sector Working Groups focused on practical measures to address challenges facing the Afghan people. Technical engagement progressed on access to finance, women’s economic empowerment and trade facilitation in support of private sector development. Practical cooperation also expanded on counter-narcotics priorities, including financial and in-kind support for alternative livelihoods, technical dialogue on drug-related health issues and strengthened cross-border and regional engagement. Enhanced coordination and expert exchanges, including Afghan women, contributed to increased information-sharing, more coherent resource mobilization and sustainable support for the Afghan population, while fostering incremental confidence-building to sustain continued engagement.
The Mission will continue to facilitate structured engagement among the international community, the de facto authorities and relevant Afghan stakeholders through the Comprehensive Approach, while promoting dialogue among Afghan stakeholders.

planned.label: Result 2
planned.title: Strengthened economic and social resilience in Afghanistan
planned.narrative:
In 2025, the United Nations country team mobilized $1.76 billion for basic human needs assistance to the people of Afghanistan. At least 26.2 million Afghans accessed health care services; 2.5 million Afghans benefited from short-term employment and improved livelihoods through cash-based interventions; 545,360 Afghans enrolled in and/or accessed informal and non-formal education services and training; 29,256 teachers were trained; 105 business associations and chambers strengthened, including women’s business associations; and 3,650 loans disbursed to Afghan private sector through financial institutions. These results were possible through the implementation of basic human needs programmatic activities under the United Nations Strategic Framework for Afghanistan, which the Mission supported through coordination of United Nations agencies and resource mobilization with donors.
The Mission will continue to strengthen basic human needs programming in support of Afghan community resilience through coordination and resource mobilization, while maintaining advocacy to continue resourcing critical humanitarian needs with Member States, donors and the de facto authorities as the main duty bearers of the Afghan people. Furthermore, it will continue dialogue with the de facto authorities to promote a more conducive regulatory and operational environment for the private sector and aid organizations.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: Strengthened human rights awareness
planned.narrative:
Strengthening human rights awareness in Afghanistan is essential to protecting civilians, promoting respect for human rights and accountability for violations, and upholding the country’s international obligations. UNAMA contributes by gathering credible information, raising awareness of international human rights standards and recommending concrete measures to enhance the protection and fulfilment of the rights of all Afghans, including through thematic public reports and periodic updates on the situation in the country. These efforts help ensure that human rights concerns remain visible nationally and internationally.
The Mission will continue its engagement and advocacy through monitoring, verification and engagement with relevant actors to promote respect for the rights of all Afghans. This will support tangible improvements in specific cases, including harm mitigation, prevention of further violations and facilitation of corrective actions. The Mission will also continue supporting awareness-raising initiatives at the subnational level with the de facto authorities and other individuals.
Lessons learned and planned change
A lesson for the Mission was that traditional field-based monitoring, while essential, cannot be the sole method for documenting and verifying violations in Afghanistan’s current context. Underreporting, fear of reprisals and shrinking civic space require UNAMA to adapt its methodologies through the safe use of locally available technology to keep its human rights work credible, comprehensive and safe for those engaging with the Mission. In applying the lesson, the Mission will diversify and strengthen its approaches to monitoring and verification where direct access is limited, and communities face heightened risks in sharing information.

planned.label: Result 2
planned.title: Enhanced United Nations system-wide coordination and stakeholder engagement to address antisemitism
planned.narrative:
It is important to strengthen coordination across the United Nations system and deepen engagement with Member States and non-State actors to address antisemitism, including Holocaust denial and distortion. The Alliance has been supporting stakeholder engagement in the implementation of the United Nations Action Plan to Enhance Monitoring and Response to Antisemitism, which provides recommendations to strengthen monitoring, education, public advocacy and coordinated responses to antisemitism across the United Nations system. Through enhanced collaboration among United Nations entities, Member States, Jewish organizations, faith actors, civil society organizations, educators, youth networks and digital platforms, the Action Plan seeks to support safer and more inclusive societies, improve awareness and understanding of antisemitism and strengthen efforts to counter antisemitic hate speech, attacks on Jewish communities and online manifestations of antisemitism.
Lessons learned and planned change
The lesson for the Alliance was that effective efforts to combat antisemitism require sustained engagement with both State and non-State actors, as well as coordinated approaches that address the root causes of religious intolerance and hate speech. The Action Plan highlighted the importance of engaging Jewish organizations, educators, faith actors, civil society organizations, youth networks and digital platforms in strengthening monitoring, awareness-raising, Holocaust education and public advocacy efforts. In applying the lesson, the Alliance will continue to facilitate consultations, partnerships and joint initiatives aimed at promoting mutual respect, protecting vulnerable communities and strengthening social cohesion and inclusion.

entities.name: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development
priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
12.2 The global economy continues to face subdued economic growth, with persistent inequalities within and among countries. Economies, particularly the most vulnerable, are affected by compounding challenges, including uncertainty related to trade, limited fiscal space, weak investment levels, high and unsustainable debt burdens, digital divides and fragile productive capacities. Therefore, fostering more inclusive and sustainable development and enhancing resilience to these challenges will continue to guide the work of UNCTAD, in accordance with the particular needs and challenges of the member States and the priority areas set out in the Geneva Consensus. In line with its mandate, UNCTAD will continue to rely on its three interrelated pillars of work: (a) conducting high-quality and evidence-based research and policy analysis that contribute to national, regional and international policies with the aim of generating inclusive and sustainable development under the principle of leaving no one behind; (b) providing technical cooperation to developing countries on the basis of such analysis; and (c) bringing member States together through its intergovernmental machinery to build consensus on policies that allow developing countries to maximize the opportunities of globalization and economic integration, as well as to address cross-cutting economic, social and environmental challenges.
12.3 UNCTAD will remain committed to addressing interrelated issues essential to all countries in attaining sustainable and equitable growth and development, while being particularly mindful of the needs and priorities of developing countries. UNCTAD will also support developing countries with work on South-South and triangular cooperation, as a complement to and not a substitute for North-South cooperation, and regional integration.
12.4 In accordance with its mandate in the interrelated areas of trade and development, and as the custodian of nine Sustainable Development Goal indicators at the global level, UNCTAD will support the implementation, monitoring and review of the 2030 Agenda and the relevant targets of the Goals, including by continuing to develop international standards and recommending methodologies for monitoring Goal indicators. It will also support the implementation of the Pact for the Future, notably the reform of the international financial architecture, the work on beyond gross domestic product (GDP), interoperable data governance and making the digital economy more inclusive. UNCTAD will also support borrower countries in addressing their debt challenges, exchanging experiences and fostering cooperation to improve their debt management practices, in line with the Sevilla Commitment.
12.5 Alongside global agendas, UNCTAD will ensure the implementation of mandates reconfirmed and reinforced at its sixteenth quadrennial session, as outlined in the Geneva Consensus. In particular, UNCTAD will further strengthen its support for the least developed countries through dedicated graduation support; for landlocked and transit developing countries, by supporting the implementation of the Awaza Programme of Action for Landlocked Developing Countries for the Decade 2024–2034; and for small island developing States, by supporting the implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Small Island Developing States: A Renewed Declaration for Resilient Prosperity, as well as by building on the UNCTAD Strategy to support Small Island Developing States. Moreover, UNCTAD will enhance the capacity of developing countries to participate in e-commerce.
12.6 To address the adverse effects of climate change and environmental degradation, which can hinder economic growth, UNCTAD will continue to contribute to new global trade, financial and policy frameworks that more fully integrate inclusiveness, climate change and the environment. This work includes supporting the scaling up of climate finance, using the potential of trade for climate action, reducing greenhouse gas emissions of the logistics of trade and global value chains, boosting sustainable investments and supporting a transition to a low-emission sustainable economy, including through critical minerals needed for renewable energy. UNCTAD will advance the issue of the integrated treatment of development economics in international forums, such as the annual sessions of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change or the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.
12.7 To support its member States in promoting structural transformation, UNCTAD will continue to support developing countries in making more accurate diagnostics, inform policy choices by measuring productive capacities and examine the growing significance of services as a new frontier for structural transformation. UNCTAD will also remain at the forefront of understanding the impact of technological advancements on structural transformation and continue its work to make digitalization a force of inclusivity, including those advancements created by emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence. Given the potential of regional economic integration for structural transformation, UNCTAD will continue to support regional and interregional integration processes, such as the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area or the Global System of Trade Preferences.
12.8 UNCTAD will continue to provide timely and high-quality statistical information and indicators in the interrelated areas of trade and development through its Statistics, Data and Digital Service. It will continue to report on developments relating to the Sustainable Development Goals by providing an update on the evolution of a selection of official indicators and on progress in the development of new concepts and methodologies, including analytical and statistical support in collaboration with other relevant international organizations on redefining development metrics of progress beyond GDP. UNCTAD will strengthen synergies between statistics and information technology to enhance its capacity in data science, artificial intelligence and digital transformation. It will foster a culture of innovation and leverage the advances in digital and emerging technologies to enhance its knowledge products and provide data-driven tools to address development challenges. Furthermore, UNCTAD will support developing countries in building their capacity to collect and compile data and measure progress in sustainable, inclusive and equitable trade, growth and development. It will use data collected and reported by countries of the South within their own frameworks to measure South-South cooperation and inform global debates on development support.
12.9 UNCTAD will continue to support countries, through technical cooperation, in building their resilience to economic shocks. It will support countries in building productive capacities related to financing for development, investment, international trade, science and technology and logistics.
12.10 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, UNCTAD will continue to combine its expertise with the reach and in-country presence of partners. Regionally, UNCTAD will work closely with partner organizations, such as the secretariat of the African Continental Free Trade Area through the UNCTAD Regional Office for Africa, as well as regional economic and business communities and strategic development partners, to foster regional economic integration and growth. UNCTAD will continue to foster cooperation with international financial institutions, multilateral development banks and other relevant intergovernmental and multilateral forums to contribute to international policy debates on trade, investment and finance.
12.11 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, UNCTAD will continue to collaborate with resident coordinator offices, including through common country assessments and United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. It will collaborate with the regional commissions through joint projects and initiatives in areas of trade facilitation, sustainable development and the integration of value chains. UNCTAD will continue to work with the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the International Trade Centre (ITC) in a complementary manner to support developing countries in integrating into and benefiting from the multilateral trading system. UNCTAD will continue to contribute to the Inter-Agency Task Force on Financing for Development and collaborate with relevant United Nations entities in the system to implement the Sevilla Commitment, including co-chairing the working group with the Bretton Woods institutions on the Principles on Promoting Responsible Sovereign Borrowing and Lending, and proposals for their implementation. UNCTAD will support the Inter-Agency and Expert Group on Sustainable Development Goal Indicators and lead the United Nations Inter-Agency Cluster on Trade and Productive Capacity in “delivering as one” operational activities at the country level. UNCTAD will support the implementation of outcomes related to science, technology and innovation of the 2030 Agenda and the Pact for the Future, including the multi-stakeholder working group on data governance. To implement the Pact for the Future, UNCTAD will collaborate with the Department of Economic and Social Affairs and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) on Beyond GDP, in support of the Secretary-General’s High-level Expert Group on Beyond GDP, and the reform of the international financial architecture, with the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the Department of Economic and Social Affairs on illicit financial flows, and with the Statistical Commission of the United Nations on South-South cooperation. In coordination with the United Nations Environment Programme, UNDP and the Climate Action Team, UNCTAD will continue to lead the United Nations Task Force on Critical Energy Transition Minerals.
12.12 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Up-to-date and accurate economic and financial information and data at the country and regional levels continue to be available and cooperation continues with relevant entities on the production of statistics;
(b) Extrabudgetary funding continues to be available for technical cooperation programmes, and conditions and capacities exist in member States to adopt and implement policies and strategies;
(c) There is political will to achieve consensus in intergovernmental meetings on matters related to UNCTAD;
(d) Member States will provide the necessary support for the implementation of mandated activities at the global, regional and national levels.
12.13 UNCTAD will continue to mainstream the cross-cutting issue of gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls in its operational activities, deliverables and results. UNCTAD will strengthen the capacity of member States to design and implement policies and establish institutions, frameworks and/or mechanisms that support women’s economic empowerment, economic security and rights and enhance their economic and digital skills and opportunities. UNCTAD will continue to work on the links between gender equality, women’s and girls’ empowerment and trade and development through its women-focused programmes, and advocate for gender-sensitive policy responses. UNCTAD will continue to analyse the barriers that prevent women from fully participating in and benefiting from trade, including as entrepreneurs.
12.14 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy and the Geneva Consensus, UNCTAD will continue its efforts to support disability inclusion in trade or technical cooperation projects. UNCTAD will further advance the work of the Inter-Agency Technical Working Group on Trade and Disability Inclusion established in conjunction with the International Labour Organization, ITC and WTO to integrate and enhance disability inclusion in trade and development agendas. UNCTAD will strive to ensure that all venues and conference facilities are accessible to persons with disabilities.
12.15 UNCTAD will also contribute to member States’ efforts to support the role of youth in sustainable development. UNCTAD will continue to engage with young people through a dedicated network and flagship events designed to integrate the youth perspective into global trade and development policies.

planned.title: borrower countries manage debt in a more efficient and sustainable way
planned.narrative:
12.32 Today, approximately 3.4 billion people live in countries that spend more on servicing their public debt than on either health or education. The Debt Management and Financial Analysis System, aimed at helping Member States to sustainably manage their debt, is currently used in over 60 countries. To further increase debt management capacity, UNCTAD has been convening meetings to support borrowing countries since 2023.
Lessons learned and planned change
12.33 The lesson for the subprogramme was that there was an increased need to support countries using the Debt Management and Financial Analysis System, particularly through new functionalities, in order to respond to the evolving nature of debt markets and the rising significance of private creditors relative to official creditors, which has added new transparency and data-quality requirements for borrower countries. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will help countries to adopt a new version of the Debt Management and Financial Analysis System, tailored to meet the additional requirements, and will focus on providing a permanent platform for coordination and knowledge-sharing. Furthermore, the subprogramme will support the establishment of the borrowers’ platform mandated by the Sevilla Commitment to help to increase cooperation, share experiences, build capacities and coordinate approaches to managing debt.

12.46 The lesson for the subprogramme was the importance of strengthening UNCTAD support for effective de-risking strategies to help channel investment and finance towards the Goals, particularly in developing countries where perceived and real risks can often constrain capital flows. performance.title: Enhanced consumer product safety
performance.narrative:
12.52 UNCTAD data indicate that approximately 40 per cent of member States have reported having product safety legislation, highlighting the potential for strengthening regulatory frameworks and fostering global alignment through increased coherence, comparability and mutual recognition of product safety regimes. As the focal point for consumer protection within the United Nations system, the subprogramme promotes the implementation of the United Nations guidelines for consumer protection by undertaking analysis, supporting countries in designing and implementing effective consumer policies and providing a forum for intergovernmental deliberations. To improve consumer product safety globally, and driven by the subprogramme’s long-standing work and consensus-building under its Intergovernmental Group of Experts on Consumer Protection Law and Policy, member States adopted the United Nations principles for consumer product safety at the Ninth United Nations Conference to Review All Aspects of the Set of Multilaterally Agreed Equitable Principles and Rules for the Control of Restrictive Business Practices, held in July 2025. These principles provide the first globally agreed blueprint for modern product safety frameworks.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: timely non-tariff measures data for better regulatory practices and economic development
planned.narrative:
12.58 Non-tariff measures can affect international trade by increasing compliance costs, making it more expensive for businesses, and can create significant obstacles to trade. Non-tariff measures are inherently complex and encompass a wide range of regulatory measures, including product requirements, health and safety regulations and import quotas, whose trade effects are not easily measurable. Due to this complexity and diversity, the timely availability of data on such measures can help to avoid high compliance costs for member States. The subprogramme has been leading the effort for global transparency in non-tariff measures by collecting and disseminating related data systematically, enabling a better understanding by policymakers and traders, especially from developing countries.
Lessons learned and planned change
12.59 The lesson for the subprogramme was the importance of improving the accessibility and timeliness of data related to non-tariff measures to facilitate analysis by policymakers, especially from developing countries. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will leverage and use artificial intelligence to collect and support more frequent updates of the non-tariff measures data in the Trade Analysis and Information System (TRAINS) database, and will enhance the capacity and knowledge of member States to use these data to support their decision-making and regulatory processes through tailored capacity-building.
