objectives: 27.II.3 The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to substantially reduce disaster risk and losses in lives, livelihoods and health and in the economic, physical, social, cultural and environmental assets of persons, businesses, communities and countries.

performance.title: Member States and stakeholders review progress on the implementation of the Sendai Framework and identify recommendations to enhance disaster risk reduction
performance.narrative:
27.II.16 United Nations General Assembly resolution 72/218 and the recurrent Assembly resolutions on disaster risk reduction recognize the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction as the global multi-stakeholder forum for review of progress on the implementation of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction. The Office organized and convened the eighth session of the Global Platform, which was held in Geneva from 2 to 6 June 2025. The Global Platform convened policymakers, practitioners and stakeholders to share successes and lessons, address common challenges and adopt innovations to accelerate the implementation of the Sendai Framework in its final five years. In line with its overarching theme, “Every day counts, act for resilience today,” the Global Platform showcased the role of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and enhanced risk information tools, in supporting faster, risk-informed action, as well as the wider use of data on climate change and early warning systems to strengthen anticipatory action.

entities.name: United Nations Environment Programme
priorities: Promotion of sustained economic growth and sustainable development

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
14.2 Delivery of the 2027 programme plan is part of the effort to implement the UNEP medium-term strategy for the period 2026–2029. By leveraging science, strengthening environmental governance and encouraging global cooperation, UNEP aims to tackle environmental challenges and support coordinated and impactful action. Its three thematic subprogrammes (climate action, nature action and chemicals and pollution action) will drive the medium-term strategy vision, while the two foundational subprogrammes (subprogramme 4, Environmental law and governance, and subprogramme 7, Science-policy) and two enabling subprogrammes (subprogramme 2, Digital transformations in supporting environmental action, and subprogramme 6, Finance and economic transformations) will, respectively, deliver the vision – through science, environmental governance, finance and economic instruments and digital tools and platforms – to enhance international cooperation, strengthen capacity-building and share good practices.
14.3 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, subregional, national and local levels, UNEP will continue to raise ambitions and promote leadership through advocacy and a normative and standard-setting approach. It will support Member States through transformative strategic partnerships that deliver sustainable solutions, integrating health, education, poverty reduction, and economic and social well-being. Its partnerships with the secretariats of multilateral environmental agreements will remain pivotal to securing stronger synergies and enhancing the impact of the work of the relevant parties. UNEP will encourage non-governmental stakeholders, including the private sector and the finance community, to increase investment in new and renewable sources of energy and improve environmental sustainability. Within the context of those partnerships, action will be aimed at making a broader impact in support of sustainable development, while strengthening the ability of countries to rapidly respond to the environmental impacts of disasters and armed conflicts.
14.4 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, UNEP, as Chair of the United Nations Environment Management Group, will continue to support and enhance coordination, cooperation and collaboration across the United Nations through system-wide strategies and common approaches on the environment, such as the common approach to biodiversity and the common approach towards a pollution-free planet. In addition, UNEP will help integrate the priorities of multilateral environmental agreements into United Nations country programming, ensuring a more coordinated and effective response to specific country needs. It will also enhance its guiding role, raise ambitions and accelerate and scale up progress to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. It will continue to focus on ensuring that its work is reflected and embedded in the new generation of United Nations country teams and the reinvigorated resident coordinator system through engagement with the Development Coordination Office and to leverage its work and expertise at the regional, subregional and country levels. UNEP will also integrate the priorities of the multilateral environmental agreements into global follow-up and review processes, in particular the 2030 Agenda.
14.5 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Member States and partners remain committed to the development and implementation of science-based environmental policies;
(b) The continued availability of extrabudgetary funding for the implementation of UNEP planned activities.
14.6 UNEP integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. UNEP will continue to support Member States in mainstreaming gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls, utilizing disaggregated data and calling for women’s meaningful participation at all levels of environmental decision-making.
14.7 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, UNEP will continue to integrate disability inclusion and related guidance into its strategic, policy, programmatic and operational interventions. Engagement with organizations of persons with disabilities will be institutionalized to ensure a participatory approach to the implementation of the UNEP programme of work. Following lessons learned from the seventh session of the United Nations Environment Assembly, UNEP will establish structured mechanisms to assess accessibility needs in advance of major meetings and will conduct accessibility audits of digital platforms in line with the standards set out in the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines.

objectives: 14.15 The objective, to which this subprogramme contributes, is to advance the transition of countries to low-emission economic development and increase their adaptation and resilience to climate change.

performance.title: Cities commit to sustainable cooling targets
performance.narrative:
14.19 In its Global Cooling Watch report for 2025, entitled The Free Degrees: How Sustainable, Passive-First Cooling Can Save Lives, Money and Food, UNEP warns that cooling demand could more than triple by 2050, reaching 10 per cent of global emissions. In the report, UNEP outlines a sustainable cooling pathway, combining passive cooling, higher energy efficiency standards and accelerated phase-down of hydrofluorocarbons, which could reduce cooling-related emissions by up to 97 per cent. In response, the subprogramme has supported the advancement of a global agenda, including convening 72 Member States under the Global Cooling Pledge, backed by the newly launched Enabling Pledge Implementation for Cooling Facility to provide technical assistance and funding for heat action plans and pilots, and initiating an Intergovernmental Committee on Cooling, launched at the 2025 United Nations Climate Change Conference. The Intergovernmental Committee on Cooling monitors and accelerates the 14 targets of the Global Cooling Pledge. Since 2025, the subprogramme has been providing national and subnational signatories of the Global Cooling Pledge access to financial support for pilot deployment, technical guidance, policy support, capacity-building and feasibility assessments through the Enabling Pledge Implementation for Cooling Facility.

14.25 In its Adaptation Gap Report 2025, entitled Running on Empty: The World Is Gearing Up for Climate Resilience – Without the Money to Get There, UNEP updated the estimated adaptation finance needs to be $310 billion annually by 2035; meanwhile, at its thirtieth session, held in Brazil, the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change emphasized robust adaptation plans and measurement, including the launch of the Belém-Addis vision on adaptation, a two-year policy alignment process by Parties, aimed at developing guidance for operationalizing the Belém Adaptation Indicators under the Belém-Addis vision on adaptation. The subprogramme provides support through a range of activities that help Member States in adopting adaptation policies and strategies. UNEP implements the Global Ecosystem-based Adaptation Fund, hosts the secretariat of the Global Adaptation Network, co-leads the World Adaptation Science Programme and effectively executes a wide portfolio of projects financed by the Global Environmental Facility, the Green Climate Fund and the Adaptation Fund.
Lessons learned and planned change
14.26 The lesson for the subprogramme was that its support for adaptation interventions was effective when the interventions were locally owned and supported by inclusive, multi-stakeholder partnerships and when there was financing available for implementation. In applying these lessons, the subprogramme will strengthen institutional capacities to lead adaptation efforts nationally and locally, replicate proven infrastructure models, increase private co-financing and enhance the availability of climate adaptation data to better support governments at different levels in developing and adopting climate adaptation strategies and policies that reflect their individual circumstances.

14.33 In 2025, the subprogramme launched EnvironmentGPT, an artificial intelligence-powered digital assistant designed to improve access to trusted, policy-relevant environmental knowledge. Developed as part of UNEP digital transformation efforts, it builds on prior investments in interoperable data governance approaches, with a focus on environmental data, knowledge management and responsible artificial intelligence. The tool enables users to query UNEP-curated environmental content through natural language, returning structured, cited responses drawn from authoritative UNEP publications and data sources. The public beta launch at the seventh session of the United Nations Environment Assembly marked a milestone in operationalizing artificial intelligence to strengthen the science-policy interface and demonstrated a shift from static knowledge repositories towards a more interactive and user-centred access model for environmental information.

14.61 Illegal trafficking of waste remains a growing transboundary challenge in the Asia-Pacific region, with evolving waste trade flows and increasing volumes of plastic and hazardous waste placing pressure on enforcement and regulatory systems. UNEP, in partnership with the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), contributed to Member State representatives of environmental authorities, customs administrations and trade and industry ministries across the region enhancing their technical and operational capacities to detect, prevent and respond to illegal waste trafficking through strengthened regional cooperation, policy dialogue and knowledge exchange mechanisms. The subprogramme, which has the responsibility for advancing legal frameworks and national strategies to address illegal waste trafficking, supported a UNODC-UNEP regional technical seminar on waste trafficking and the circular economy approaches held in Kuala Lumpur. The subprogramme also held regional meetings in Bangkok and Jakarta to facilitate policy dialogue between the European Union and Association of Southeast Asian Nations member States, including Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Viet Nam, on waste trafficking trends and related regulatory frameworks.
14.62 As a result, Member State representatives improved their understanding of waste trafficking trends and enforcement challenges, advanced the development of legal frameworks and strategies to address illegal waste trafficking, including linkages to organized crime and trade systems, and strengthened alignment with regional circular economy approaches and national action planning processes.

14.103 UNEP has continuously supported national and regional capacities to generate, harmonize and use environment-related statistics in decision-making. One of the areas where the subprogramme has provided dedicated support to Member States is in the implementation of the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting. As at December 2025, UNEP has successfully co-conducted six targeted capacity-building events, including regional workshops, seminars and national technical training sessions on the System. The events covered 12 countries from the Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean and Africa regions. UNEP also contributed to the global e-learning course on measuring material flows in the Sustainable Development Goals, organized by the Statistical Institute for Asia and the Pacific of the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific. These efforts were built on previous work and ultimately contributed to 98 countries successfully putting in place functional systems for environmental-economic accounting, of which 71 are being implemented at the tier 3 level, meaning that they have institutionalized their compilation methodologies and are now compiling data on their environmental statistical accounts on a regular basis.

14.109 The subprogramme organizes regional ministerial forums, including the Forum of Ministers and Environment Authorities of Asia-Pacific, the African Ministerial Conference on the Environment and the Forum of Ministers of Environment of Latin America and Caribbean. The goal of these forums is to seek commitments to science-policy integration for tackling climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution. The subprogramme combines these in-person convenings with online modalities leveraging UNEP resources, to ensure the full integration of technical understanding following the in-person engagement. A key component of this practice has been virtual learning, which has broadened access and ensured that practical application, targeted follow-up and in-country technical assistance was maintained following in-person engagements.
Lessons learned and planned change
14.110 The lesson for the subprogramme was that progress in translating the commitments of the in-person convenings to policymaking and action towards sustainability often hinged on institutional capacity, the continuity of trained personnel and robust interoperable data governance approaches across national agencies. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will prioritize strengthening capacity-building using UNEP knowledge, data, statistics and assessments. The subprogramme plans to intensify post-training coaching and the formal designation of data custodianship in national institutions to enhance reporting continuity, data quality and the seamless integration of scientific evidence into policy and planning. This modality will inform 12 or more capacity-building initiatives in 2026 and 2027, equipping over 500 policymakers with skills for evidence-based decisions, including the outcomes of the seventh session of the United Nations Environment Assembly.

performance.title: Global Refugee Forum pledges advance responsibility-sharing and support for refugees and host communities
performance.narrative:
25.16 As a framework for predictable and equitable responsibility-sharing, the Global Compact on Refugees is intended to transform how the world responds to refugee situations, benefiting both refugees and host communities. In December 2025, the progress review of the Global Refugee Forum assessed progress made towards achieving the Global Compacts’ objectives, reviewed the implementation and achievement of pledges and identified areas for renewed attention and support. UNHCR plays a catalytical role to ensure that the pledges benefit directly refugees, hosting States and countries of origin, and the cities and communities that support them. More than 60 new policy and financial pledges were announced, with significant commitments from States and the private sector. Together, these commitments have delivered measurable impact for refugees and communities that host them, with inclusive policies strengthening both individual self-reliance and national economies. These approaches have expanded access to decent work, increased incomes and public revenue and improved access to essential services such as health and education. For example, by 2025, legal access to the labour market enabled approximately 33 million refugees in 96 countries to pursue livelihoods and contribute to their host communities. At the community level, fulfilled pledges also fostered social inclusion and well-being, with 336,000 refugees and host community members reached through sports and other community activities that promote connection, resilience and shared opportunity.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: increased adherence to international conventions on statelessness
planned.narrative:
25.22 Statelessness remains a critical global issue, given that the absence of nationality and legal identity continues to expose individuals to long-term exclusion and vulnerability. UNHCR estimates that some 4.4 million people worldwide are stateless or of undetermined nationality, with millions more unrecorded in official data. In line with the UNHCR mandate and guided by the 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons and the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, UNHCR supports Governments in identifying and protecting stateless persons and preventing and resolving statelessness.
Lessons learned and planned change
25.23 The lesson for UNHCR was that progress in addressing statelessness was most significant when legal and policy reforms were accompanied by firm government support and sustained national engagement. While legislative reforms have advanced in several contexts, continued technical support is required for effective implementation. In applying the lesson, UNHCR will prioritize advocacy for solutions and accession to the conventions and will strengthen national capacities and share best practices to support the implementation of international legal standards. Sustained engagement at the national level will be reinforced through multi-stakeholder collaboration under the Global Alliance to End Statelessness.

overview.name: United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan
objectives: 5.III.2 The objective, to which UNMOGIP contributes, is to ensure that developments pertaining to ceasefire violations along the line of control are monitored in accordance with the mandate of UNMOGIP as contained in Security Council resolution 307 (1971).
strategy:
5.III.3 To contribute to the objective, UNMOGIP will:
(a) Continue to focus on the core mandated tasks of prevention, early warning, observation reporting and confidence-building;
(b) Provide timely and detailed reports on relevant developments in its area of operations, in accordance with the implementation of its mandate;
(c) Continue to deploy military observers on both sides of the line of control for the conduct of patrols, inspections and investigations of alleged violations of the ceasefire and the performance of other tasks in the vicinity of the line of control to the extent permitted by the host countries.
5.III.4 The above-mentioned work is expected to result in adherence to the ceasefire through the presence of United Nations military observers.
5.III.5 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Host countries cooperate with UNMOGIP in observing the ceasefire and refraining from hostilities and any action that may aggravate the situation or endanger international peace as embodied in Security Council resolution 307 (1971);
(b) India and Pakistan remain willing to support UNMOGIP in the conduct of its activities for the delivery of its mandate.
5.III.6 The mission integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. This includes ensuring that the United Nations military observers engage in a comprehensive manner with local communities, among both men and women, to ensure that the mission has a gender-sensitive understanding of community perspectives of the situation on the ground and to facilitate the conduct and planning of mission operations.
5.III.7 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, UNMOGIP will continue to collaborate with United Nations country teams in India and Pakistan for contextual insights on humanitarian and development matters, where relevant. This coordination is expected to enhance operational efficiency, including through streamlined reporting via shared platforms and reduced duplication in host country liaison.
5.III.8 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, UNMOGIP will continue to consider accessibility needs, to the extent feasible within operational constraints, in its community engagement and reporting activities, to promote broader inclusion of affected populations.

performance.title: Limited number of complaints concerning alleged ceasefire violations
performance.narrative:
5.III.12 To implement its mandate, UNMOGIP made every effort to monitor the ceasefire between India and Pakistan along the line of control. During 2025, the mission maintained supervision of the ceasefire through the continuous presence of United Nations military observers at its 10 field stations on both sides of the line of control. UNMOGIP continued to carry out its core field tasks, including patrols, inspections and investigations. The mission received eight complaints concerning alleged ceasefire violations during the year. In addition, UNMOGIP received 17 petitions from recognized political groups expressing concern over developments affecting the situation at and in the vicinity of the line of control in Jammu and Kashmir, on both the Indian and Pakistani sides.

5.III.18 Persistent tensions and periodic ceasefire violations along the line of control continue to underscore the critical importance of reliable, neutral and timely information-sharing to help reduce the risk of miscalculation and contribute to stability for affected populations. Building on its established operational framework, UNMOGIP has consistently maintained liaison and engagement with host country military authorities, delivered briefings and updates to ambassadors and military attachés of troop-contributing countries as required, ensured public transparency through the maintenance of the mission’s website and delivered the full range of mandated substantive outputs.

In applying the lesson, UNMOGIP will further systematize its established practices by prioritizing regular liaison engagements with host country military authorities and structured briefings to ambassadors and military attachés of troop-contributing countries as required. Concurrently, UNMOGIP will reduce reliance on unstructured outreach and place greater emphasis on consistent, standardized documentation and information-sharing to foster long-term mutual understanding, trust and awareness among relevant stakeholders.

performance.title: Somalia security transition took place and African Union peace support capacities strengthened
performance.narrative:
3.IV.13 The Office has been continuously involved in supporting the transition from the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM). In 2024, the Office, together with the African Union, prepared a joint report that included benchmarks with clear indicators and milestones to measure the progress made on the ground in the transition from ATMIS to AUSSOM. In addition, as part of the transition, the Office strengthened the force generation effort for AUSSOM by participating in the predeployment assessment of military contingents, formed police units and individual police officers. Pursuant to Security Council resolution 2767 (2024), the Office participated in a joint African Union-United Nations and Federal Government of Somalia benchmarking exercise in September 2025 to undertake assessments aimed at determining the conditions for authorizing subsequent phases of AUSSOM, including an updated exit strategy, and articulating a plan for further reductions in the size of the deployed force, with consideration for progress against benchmarks set in the joint report. Based on these assessments, a joint United Nations, African Union and Federal Government of Somalia report outlining progress was submitted to the Security Council in October 2025. The Office also supported continued strengthening of the African Standby Force through policy reviews, training development and technical support to readiness initiatives.

performance.title: Strengthened national capacities in reducing electoral and institutional tensions in Chad and Gabon
performance.narrative:
In 2025, through the good offices of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, UNOCA intensified diplomatic engagement across Central Africa to accompany political transitions and support electoral processes. In Chad, the Office engaged national authorities on post-transition priorities, including decentralization, disarmament, demobilization and reintegration, stabilization and inclusive development, following the country’s completion of its political transition and the holding of legislative, provincial, municipal and senatorial elections between December 2024 and March 2025, which marked the full restoration of constitutional order.
In Gabon, UNOCA maintained regular dialogue with transitional authorities and political actors, underscoring the importance of institutional reforms and supporting preparations for legislative, senatorial and local elections, which represented key steps in consolidating progress made after the presidential election of April 2025 toward restoring constitutional governance. Across the subregion, UNOCA also advanced initiatives aimed at expanding the participation of women and young people, including technical support to a mentoring programme for women’s political leadership in Gabon and regional youth engagement on peace and security priorities.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see table 33).

planned.title: Strengthened regional capacities for conflict prevention and mediation in Central Africa
planned.narrative:
In 2025, UNOCA strengthened regional capacities for conflict prevention and mediation by supporting ECCAS-led early warning and preventive diplomacy mechanisms and convening regional stakeholders through the United Nations Standing Advisory Committee on Security Questions in Central Africa. Targeted capacity-building for civil society organizations, women and youth actors, and journalists enhanced coordination, inclusive engagement and collective responses to emerging political and security risks across the subregion.
In 2027, building on close cooperation with ECCAS, UNOCA will continue supporting subregional mechanisms that reinforce early warning, dialogue and coordinated responses to political and security challenges. Additionally, UNOCA will deepen cooperation with regional and international stakeholders on thematic priorities such as climate-related security risks, transhumance-related conflicts and cross-border stabilization, informed by field assessments, engagement, local action, and joint workshops conducted in the subregion.
A lesson for the mission was the importance of structured and sustained engagement with regional and subregional organizations, particularly during periods of institutional transition on the side of ECCAS, to preserve continuity and enhance the effectiveness of preventive diplomacy. The change in ECCAS leadership in 2025 underscored the need for proactive engagement to align priorities, leverage complementarities and strengthen joint ownership of peace and security initiatives. In applying this lesson, UNOCA will deepen its strategic partnership with the renewed ECCAS leadership and its member States, while reinforcing coordination with United Nations presences, country teams and relevant international, national and civil society stakeholders.

The adoption of the Convention marks a historic milestone in international efforts to counter crimes committed via or enabled through information and communications technologies, reflecting a global consensus on the need to address cybercrime and enable the sharing of evidence in electronic form for serious crimes through a legally-binding framework. planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: strengthened normative, policy and institutional responses against organized crime globally
planned.narrative:
16.26 Transnational organized crime threatens lives, jeopardizes peace and security, endangers livelihoods and undermines the economy. The effective implementation of the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime through normative, policy and institutional measures is critical in ensuring a comprehensive global response to organized crime. The subprogramme supports Member States and regional organizations in becoming Parties to the Convention, developing strategies and laws, and strengthening institutions that prevent and combat organized crime.
Lessons learned and planned change
16.27 The lesson for the subprogramme was that the direct impact of policies and strategies against organized crime can be constrained by operational and institutional conditions, making targeted support for effective implementation paramount. In applying this lesson, the subprogramme will prioritize the establishment and strengthening of implementation-oriented institutional structures, such as central and competent authorities, victim support units or strategic analysis units, and normative frameworks. This shift is expected to ensure that adopted policies and strategies are systematically translated into practice, thereby improving responses against organized crime at the national level.

performance.title: Enhanced ability of Member States to disrupt criminal networks engaged in drug trafficking through strengthened case-based international cooperation
performance.narrative:
16.34 Law enforcement and criminal justice responses to drug trafficking often stop at seizures and arrests of low-level couriers, which have limited deterrent or disruptive impact on the broader criminal networks. The subprogramme prioritized promoting multilateral operations and building the capacity of national counterparts through strategic and operational support to Member States to address this gap. These efforts included supporting the establishment, under article 19 of the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, of case-specific joint investigation teams with law enforcement and/or judicial authorities and facilitating investigative case forums that bring together countries affected by the same drug trafficking case for coordination and potential joint action. These efforts have enabled the arrest of high-level targets and the disruption and dismantling of criminal networks operating across Latin America and the Caribbean, Africa and Europe.

performance.title: Strengthened criminal justice responses to counter terrorist financing in Côte d’Ivoire
performance.narrative:
16.60 Terrorist organizations often rely on illicit financial flows to sustain their operations, particularly in contexts where informal and cash-based economies are present. Furthermore, illicit flows in the informal economy allow terrorist organizations to move resources undetected, most notably in border areas and in the cattle industry. Addressing these challenges is essential to safeguard national and regional security. The subprogramme assisted Côte d’Ivoire on countering terrorist financing with a specific focus on analysing financial data and identifying suspicious transactions indicative of terrorist involvement. This included promoting the embedding of financial intelligence processes into judicial procedures, leading to improved inter-agency cooperation and ensuring that viable evidence contributed to prosecutions. Following these efforts, Côte d’Ivoire secured its first-ever convictions in eight terrorist financing cases (some have been appealed), thus strengthening its criminal justice response to terrorist financing.

performance.title: Improved compliance of national prison systems with international standards to promote rehabilitation
performance.narrative:
16.73 Adherence to the Nelson Mandela Rules, the Bangkok Rules and other international standards is vital in safeguarding the human rights, dignity and prospects of rehabilitation of individuals deprived of their liberty. To that end, the subprogramme has partnered with national authorities to conduct compliance assessments, deliver targeted technical assistance for infrastructure upgrades and health services, provide staff training on detention practices and develop comprehensive guidance on prison reform and social reintegration. These efforts have driven measurable progress in multiple prison systems, such as reinforced emergency responses that prioritize legality, proportionality and care for detainees; the piloting of the “Together for Rehabilitation” classification tool for risk and needs assessments; and the enhancement of information technology capacity by implementing standardized digital intake procedures that improve transparency and efficiency. Technical assistance supported the implementation of proportionate security levels, audit mechanisms and risk management protocols, all of which reinforced humane operations. Through these multifaceted efforts, the subprogramme continues to transform detention environments, upholding international human rights standards and promoting sustainable rehabilitation.

performance.title: Victims of trafficking receive comprehensive, victim-centred support through the United Nations voluntary trust fund for victims of trafficking in persons, especially women and children
performance.narrative:
16.99 Trafficking in persons has severe and lasting consequences for victims, who require both urgent protection and sustained support to rebuild their lives. Survivors face diverse needs, including emergency and medical care, psychosocial counselling, legal aid, education and reintegration into their communities. Addressing these needs in a coordinated, victim-centred manner is essential to prevent re-victimization and enable long-term recovery. The subprogramme has supported 220 projects led by local non-governmental organizations in 70 countries, directly assisting more than 100,000 victims of trafficking since the establishment of the United Nations voluntary trust fund for victims of trafficking in persons, especially women and children, in 2010. In 2025, greater emphasis was placed on supporting projects that provide comprehensive and tailored assistance to respond to both urgent and longer-term needs, resulting in 6,694 victims of trafficking receiving support, including emergency assistance, medical support, psychosocial counselling, legal aid, vocational training, formal education and repatriation and reintegration support.

priorities: Effective functioning of the organization

overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
29E.2 In compliance with General Assembly resolution 2 (I), the Office will offer administrative and support services in English and French, including direction, management and coordination in the areas of human resources, financial and budgetary resources, information and communications technology (ICT), central support services, and library and archives services. The Office, as property manager for the United Nations premises, which accommodate nearly 70 tenants, will continue to play a central role in supporting United Nations meetings and events through audiovisual and ICT services, as well as the maintenance of conference rooms and equipment. The Office will also implement policy and other functions, as determined by the Under-Secretaries-General referred to in paragraph 29E.1 above.
29E.3 The Office will provide financial, budgetary and accounting services, as well as guidance and advice, in accordance with the Financial Regulations and Rules of the United Nations and relevant standards. In addition, the Office will provide human resources services, including staff development and learning, career support and coaching, and medico-administrative occupational safety and health, and carry out staff mental health and well-being activities, as well as provide guidance and advice in accordance with the Organization’s human resources policies, rules and regulations. The Office will provide procurement, commercial activities, transportation, travel and other central support services for the Secretariat and the specialized agencies. It will also provide regional administrative services, as well as library, records, archives and knowledge services, in support of the implementation of mandated programmes and activities of the Secretariat, including to resident coordinator offices. The Office will further ensure the business continuity of administrative support and guidance for other entities in Geneva in emergency cases.
29E.4 Renovation works at the historic buildings of the Palais des Nations under the strategic heritage plan will continue throughout 2027, with substantial completion expected during the year and residual works continuing into 2028. The Office will strengthen systems supporting building operations, maintenance and energy management to reduce energy consumption, optimize asset performance and lower life-cycle costs while improving reliability and sustainability.
29E.5 Operational efficiency, cost control and client support will remain priorities in 2027. Quarterly client board meetings will continue to promote transparent service delivery, supported by regular reporting on performance indicators covering more than 20 services. Client engagement will be further strengthened through dedicated functional client forums, introduced in 2026, which provide structured opportunities for in-depth dialogue between the Office’s functional leads and subject matter experts of client entities on operational issues, performance trends and service improvements. The Office will continue to provide operational support through its Client Support Centre, delivering tier 2-level support and handling approximately 20,000 client visits and 12,000 client calls annually. In response to growing demand and increasing technical complexity related to delivering side events, cultural events and activities, client support will also be provided through the Event Support Centre, launched in January 2026. Dedicated support will also continue for client entities relocating to or from the Palais des Nations. Operational efficiency will be further strengthened through faster, more reliable network services for clients. All efforts will be supported by a targeted communications strategy informed by annual client entity and end-user surveys.
29E.6 With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will continue to collaborate with other Geneva-based United Nations system organizations and international governmental organizations, coordinating the Common Procurement Activities Group. The Office will continue to own and administer global and regional United Nations contracts, conduct annual daily subsistence allowance surveys, coordinate cost-of-living surveys, conduct place-to-place surveys and monitor the consumer price index at Geneva. The Office will also work closely with facilities managers of international organizations in Geneva to strengthen coordination on policies and procedures. In addition, the Office will collaborate with other United Nations libraries to digitize official United Nations documents and further streamline library activities by managing the common library management system and catalogue for United Nations Headquarters, the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, the Economic Commission for Africa and the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific.
29E.7 With regard to external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the planning assumption that client offices will have sufficient extrabudgetary resources to pay for services provided by the Office, when applicable.
29E.8 The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. In 2027, it will contribute to improving gender equality in supported offices, in line with the Secretary-General’s system-wide strategy on gender parity, through consultations and briefings to hiring managers and human resources focal points on the impact of selection decisions, including advice on targeted outreach and the promotion of United Nations career opportunities.
29E.9 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will continue to implement its disability inclusion action plan and support the strategic heritage plan in its efforts to incorporate accessibility features in renovation works.

planned.title: clients gain clearer insight into service performance through quarterly reporting
planned.narrative:
29E.25 The subprogramme is responsible for providing clients with a service-level agreement containing performance indicators. In its 2025 audit of the arrangements for provision of administrative services by the United Nations Office at Geneva, the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS) found that the performance indicators included in the Office’s 2025 service-level agreements were primarily service standards and did not meet the criteria of measurable performance indicators. In response to the audit recommendation, the subprogramme worked with service lines to identify 24 client-focused performance indicators, which were incorporated into the 2026 service-level agreements and shared with clients.
Lessons learned and planned change
29E.26 The lesson for the subprogramme was that client satisfaction and service delivery can be strengthened through regular reporting on performance results and structured discussion of those results with clients. In applying this lesson, the subprogramme will establish a central reporting capacity for performance indicators across all subprogrammes and produce service-line reports for discussion at quarterly client board meetings. Performance results will also be examined in greater detail through service-level client forums for each subprogramme, providing structured opportunities for dialogue on service delivery and operational issues. Based on client feedback, the performance indicators and reporting approach will be further refined to enhance their relevance and to support continuous improvement in service delivery, including as part of the implementation of a common administrative platform in Geneva.

performance.title: Assembly Hall audiovisual systems help deliver large-scale intergovernmental meetings and events
performance.narrative:
29E.46 The Assembly Hall, the largest conference room in the Palais des Nations, is used for major conferences, commemorations, concerts and award ceremonies. It underwent extensive renovation under the strategic heritage plan from June 2021 to April 2025, limiting the ability to hold large-scale events.
29E.47 The subprogramme played a central role in modernizing the Hall, upgrading audiovisual facilities while preserving the building’s heritage and ensuring the continuity of high-quality conference services. This was achieved through the dismantling, overhauling, upgrading, reinstallation and reprogramming of the entire conference system, including 681 seats with microphones, 1,032 seats with listening devices, 14 interpretation booths and 7 cameras. In addition, two large screens and an image capture system were installed, an operator control room developed and the sound system fully replaced. The renovation significantly enhanced service reliability and meeting delivery, facilitating live broadcasting and improved accessibility for delegates and participants. Close cooperation between the strategic heritage plan and the subprogramme enabled the Office to host 10 large-scale events.

planned.narrative:
29E.66 Reliable network services underpin the Office’s operations, including meetings, conferences and digital collaboration. During 2025, the subprogramme assessed options for modernizing the network infrastructure, including by replacing legacy core network switches, upgrading wireless access points, transitioning users from wired to high-performance wireless connectivity and decommissioning redundant switches to improve reliability, capacity and cost efficiency.
Lessons learned and planned change
29E.67 The lesson for the subprogramme was that improvements to network resilience and reliability can be achieved by concentrating resources on fewer, standardized network solutions, reducing dependency on legacy configurations and concentrating resources on scalable, high-impact solutions. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will replace wireless access points, optimize wireless coverage, transition users from wired to wireless connectivity and decommission redundant switches. performance.title: Irreplaceable and historic library collections protected for future generations during renovations
performance.narrative:
29E.73 The Library collections are housed in one of the main buildings of the Palais des Nations, which was constructed in the 1930s and no longer meets current fire and life safety, and building, standards. The building also experienced water intrusions, resulting in damage to and loss of materials. While strategic heritage plan renovations will address these deficiencies, the renovation period itself posed significant risks to print publications, including irreplaceable collections dating back to the sixteenth century. The collection comprises approximately 45,000 shelves and includes United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization Memory of the World Programme documents, historic library holdings and legacy United Nations documents. To mitigate these risks, the subprogramme relocated the entire collection in close coordination with the strategic heritage plan team. The collections were tracked and preservation packed as required, and a temporary reading space was established to provide access to a core collection.

planned.narrative:
29E.79 The subprogramme is custodian of approximately 15,000 linear metres of United Nations physical records and archives documenting the work of the League of Nations and Secretariat entities in Geneva. Member States and other stakeholders use these archives to analyse and support multilateral cooperation and inform future action. Following the digitization of approximately 14.5 million pages of League of Nations archives, the subprogramme identified that existing storage conditions for physical and digital archives at the Palais pose risks to their long-term preservation, while demand for archival services from other United Nations offices in Europe is increasing. In order to support proper archival storage, the subprogramme in 2023 secured donated funding for a new archive building. In 2024, due diligence and compliance checks, as well as a preliminary feasibility study, were completed.

In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will construct a purpose-built archives storage facility for the Office and other relevant United Nations offices. overview.name: Overall orientation
strategy:
29D.2 In recent years, multiple entities have relocated some of their functions and regional offices to the United Nations premises in Nairobi, including the United Nations Office for Project Services, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, the International Trade Centre, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the United Nations Population Fund and the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women. In addition, the Office is expecting an increase in personnel from the International Civil Aviation Organization and UNICEF in 2026.
29D.3 In 2027, the Office will support its clients, including through the common back-office framework and the phase 1 of the common administrative platform in Nairobi, in support of the principles of the Pact for the Future and the efficiency agenda. The Office will increase the level of utilization of its services and continue to support the United Nations common premises, through partnerships with other United Nations entities, to maximize shared infrastructure and services and achieve efficiencies.
29D.4 For 2027, the Office will maintain optimal service delivery and continue to monitor key performance indicators through the use of analytical tools. The Office will further strengthen its financial management, internal control systems, risk framework and communication strategy, including through regular key performance indicator reporting, qualitative surveys and a client relations management platform.
29D.5 The major infrastructure project on the conference facilities remains high on the programme agenda, with the project main works continuing in 2027. Business continuity will remain a major focus in order to proceed with mandated calendar meetings, including the eighth session of the United Nations Environment Assembly and the fourth open-ended meeting of the Committee of Permanent Representatives, scheduled to take place in 2027. The project will continue to focus on engineering initiatives that provide the best value for money for Member States while delivering the project within the approved scope, budget and schedule.
29D.6 With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, as the main interlocutor with the Government of Kenya, the Office will deepen its engagement with the host country Government in support of its mandate and the clients that it serves, representing all United Nations entities operating in or from Kenya.
29D.7 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a) Nairobi-based organizations of the United Nations common system maintain a commitment to collaborate with the United Nations Secretariat on ongoing activities;
(b) Extrabudgetary funding situation of client offices continues to allow for planning and implementation of the Office’s activities with adequate staffing levels, in particular for the expanded United Nations complex facilities, infrastructure and conference facility requirements.
29D.8 The Office integrates a gender perspective in its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. It supports the Secretary-General’s system-wide strategy on gender parity, provides guidance to clients on how to integrate gender parity throughout the recruitment process and keeps client entities informed of the impact of selection decisions. The Office also works to promote geographical representation and diversity, including by providing client entities with information on Member States that are unrepresented or underrepresented.
29D.9 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will ensure that all major repairs and replacements at the United Nations complex in Nairobi consider and address accessibility concerns. The Office will strengthen an inclusive organizational culture that is supportive of staff members with disabilities and staff who have dependants with disabilities, offering regular training opportunities on disability inclusion, organizing awareness-raising events and communicating available benefits and entitlements. These activities will be pursued with the active involvement of persons with disabilities and their representative organizations.

29D.18 The subprogramme enhanced the internal control integrated within the client relationship management system workflow, to reduce the processing time of the requests from clients for accounting journals. The workflow was enhanced to streamline the routing process of the requests through the appropriate levels of authorizations based on the segregation of duties, and to ensure complete documentation to fulfil audit requirements. These measures collectively ensured compliance with United Nations principles, IPSAS standards and delegation-of-authority requirements, providing robust assurance over the integrity of accounting adjustments. All enhancements were implemented in accordance with accounting guidelines and monitored against established key performance indicators. As a result, the subprogramme almost doubled the rate at which it processed accounting journals from 2023 to 2025, providing expedited services to its clients, while maintaining compliance with the internal control standards.

The subprogramme has been supporting clients in producing financial reports to donors. The subprogramme has also reduced reliance on the legacy system used prior to Umoja and produces the majority of its financial reports using Umoja. This is expected to significantly reduce the time for reconciliation and data completion, which in turn will facilitate the timeliness of the production of these reports.

In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will proactively monitor the due dates and potential issues that can delay issuance of financial reports to donors, provide its staff with up-to-date training to produce the reports, enhance the reporting functionalities of Umoja Analytics and engage closely with the clients to quickly resolve pending financial transactions.

In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will operate and manage the completed components of the conference facilities that will start to come online from 2027, as part of the Office’s complex facilities under the responsibilities of its central facilities management services. This will ensure seamless integration of conference service facilities with the entire United Nations complex facilities and infrastructure. This integration of services and facilities will meet the needs of the United Nations official calendar of meetings and the meetings of Member States and will provide adequate, safe and accessible conference and meeting spaces for delegates, participants, staff members and visitors, including the United Nations Environment Assembly and the UN-Habitat Assembly. strategy:
29F.2 The Office will continue to provide administrative services, including the provision of an enabling policy framework and enhanced decision-making through continuous monitoring, data analysis and reporting. The strategy for 2027 will continue to include: (a) coordinating with Headquarters and providing timely advice to the entities serviced on policy and administrative matters; (b) strengthening internal financial controls and streamlining financial procedures and guidelines to ensure effective financial management; (c) targeting the enhancement of leadership, learning and career support activities guided by a performance management system supporting increased accountability, staff engagement, workplace flexibility and empowerment while ensuring a diverse and inclusive workplace; (d) maintaining efficient and cost-effective travel and transportation services through best practices; (e) promoting environmental sustainability in coordination with all departments and offices; (f) strengthening the capacity of procurement staff through online training and guidance notes to procurement practitioners; (g) monitoring significant pronouncements of the International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board and improving financial data integrity; (h) integrating new technologies into the organizational business toolkit; and (i) increasing compliance with technology standards, guidelines and methodologies, information and communications technology (ICT) policies and enterprise architecture.
29F.3 With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the planning assumption that the extrabudgetary funding available to client offices and the support requirements for services provided by the Office remain stable.
29F.4 The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, including through the implementation of the Strategy for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (2022–2026) of the Office and UNODC. It will also support clients in attaining gender parity targets and will track and report on progress in promoting gender equality and the empowerment of women, in line with the Secretary-General’s system-wide strategy on gender parity.
29F.5 In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office, in coordination with other Vienna-based organizations, will continue to work towards creating a more inclusive and supportive culture for staff members who have disabilities. The Office will engage with and involve persons with disabilities and their representative organizations, offer training on disability inclusion and raise awareness on disability inclusion.

objectives: 29F.13 The objective, to which this subprogramme contributes, is to ensure sound, effective and efficient financial management by client offices.

performance.title: Maintaining programme delivery amid unexpected funding disruption
performance.narrative:
29F.16 In 2025, one of the Office’s client entities, UNODC, faced a decrease in financial resources both from the regular budget due to the liquidity situation and from extrabudgetary resources due to reductions in voluntary contributions from several donors. This decrease in resources posed a significant challenge to the continuity of UNODC operations and its ability to achieve its mandates, including its ability to provide technical cooperation to Member States.
29F.17 The subprogramme assisted UNODC by providing more frequent financial updates to senior management for decision-making and keeping Member States and donors engaged through the standing open-ended intergovernmental working group on improving the governance and financial situation of UNODC. The subprogramme held regular meetings with UNODC management and programme managers on contingency scenarios and the reallocation of available resources to areas of greater need. Consequently, planned activities continued with minimal interruption, notwithstanding significant funding uncertainty.

29F.23 Effective financial management requires timely, reliable and accessible information to support decision-making and accountability. In the light of the financial challenges experienced in recent years, the subprogramme has faced increasing demands for transparency and oversight through frequent ad hoc requests for key consolidated financial information and reports.
Lessons learned and planned change
29F.24 The lesson for the subprogramme was that fragmented and manual reporting limited the timeliness, consistency and usability of financial information for decision-makers. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme is developing standardized financial management dashboards using analytical application tools, including dedicated views for executive management and for operational managers and staff. These dashboards will be designed to consolidate key financial information and support the monitoring of financial performance across clients’ offices. The subprogramme will publish and progressively refine the dashboards on the basis of user feedback and will increase the automation of data preparation through Umoja Analytics, thereby enhancing efficiency, reliability and user relevance.

performance.title: Improved contractual modality for field-based project personnel
performance.narrative:
29F.30 Ensuring the full alignment of benefits and entitlements for field-based project personnel across the Office’s clients located in 116 duty stations is essential to promoting fairness, transparency and staff motivation and supporting the effective implementation of projects funded through Member States’ voluntary contributions. In 2025, the Office worked closely with UNODC to ensure the transition of the service provider of field service contracts from the United Nations Development Programme to the United Nations Office for Project Service (UNOPS) and, in collaboration with UNOPS, developed a dedicated formal agreement, a contractual framework and related policies and procedures tailored to operational needs. Consequently, in December 2025, 1,247 service contract holders previously administered by the United Nations Development Programme underwent a successful transition to the UNOPS local individual contractor agreement modality, ensuring continuity of operations and mandate delivery while providing improved and more harmonized employment conditions for project personnel.

planned.label: Result 3
planned.title: increased awareness of the Code of Conduct to Prevent Harassment, Including Sexual Harassment, at United Nations System Events
planned.narrative:
29F.36 The subprogramme supports efforts to ensure that all staff and personnel are treated with dignity and respect and are aware of their roles and responsibilities in maintaining a workplace free of any form of discrimination, harassment, including sexual harassment, and abuse of authority. In addition, the subprogramme seeks to ensure that events organized by client departments provide an inclusive, respectful and safe environment for all participants. United Nations staff and personnel are directed by the Secretary General’s bulletin on addressing discrimination, harassment, including sexual harassment and abuse of authority (ST/SGB/2019/8), while the Code of Conduct to Prevent Harassment, Including Sexual Harassment, at United Nations System Events applies to external visitors at events organized by the United Nations. Procedures are in place to report any prohibited conduct. Organizers of events are expected to take appropriate action in accordance with applicable policies.
Lessons learned and planned change
29F.37 The lesson for the subprogramme was that a more systematic approach was required to ensure that all participants in events organized by its client departments were aware of the Code of Conduct to Prevent Harassment, Including Sexual Harassment, at United Nations System Events, including on how to report any perceived prohibited conduct. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will work closely with event organizers to expand the awareness of the Code of Conduct through the revamped and increased distribution of information materials and announcements at the onset of the events. The subprogramme will also strengthen review mechanisms to enable an immediate review of any reports of prohibited conduct.

29F.43 The effective management of property is critical to safeguarding United Nations assets, strengthening accountability and transparency and ensuring value for money by optimizing asset use and reducing loss, misuse and replacement costs. To strengthen local accountability and improve the speed of recording, the Office decentralized property management to its clients’ field offices. Through regional training in Bangkok, Bogotá, Nairobi and Tashkent, more than 500 staff gained hands-on Umoja skills to manage assets end to end. Consequently, field assets are managed locally and more independently. As of 2025, 89 countries operated under this decentralized model.

planned.title: improved utilization of office space
planned.narrative:
29F.49 The Vienna International Centre was inaugurated in 1979 to host United Nations organizations based in Vienna, including the Office and its client organizations. Since then, while personnel numbers have increased steadily, the allocated spatial footprint within the Centre has not expanded. The limitations of the existing office layout are further compounded by changes arising from the UN80 Initiative, with personnel relocating to Vienna from higher-cost duty stations, as well as the need to accommodate a newly established entity.
Lessons learned and planned change
29F.50 The lesson for the subprogramme was the need to assess space utilization in accordance with the office space standards of the Office/UNODC to increase workspace capacity. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme conducted a baseline assessment of office space utilization in 2025 and will launch a project to increase workspace capacity. This will be achieved by implementing a more flexible use of space, while taking into account accessibility requirements for persons with disabilities, as well as safety and fire regulations, with a view to ensuring optimal space efficiency and an inclusive working environment.

performance.title: Strengthened reliability of information and communications technology operations through the consolidation of virtual infrastructure and a reduced reliance on subscription-based licences
performance.narrative:
29F.56 The Office relies on data centre operations to support Member States, intergovernmental bodies and the safe and secure operation of the Vienna International Centre. Ensuring the reliability, resilience and sustainability of these operations is therefore essential to guaranteeing uninterrupted services for the Office’s clients and minimizing the risk of system instability resulting from rapidly evolving technologies and shifting licensing models. Between 2023 and 2025, the subprogramme modernized data centre operations by consolidating fragmented and ageing infrastructure into a more resilient and centrally managed environment. This consolidation reduced the number of systems to be maintained and lowered exposure to hardware failures, thereby improving the Organization’s ability to cope with demand fluctuations, while limiting the risk of sudden increases in maintenance and energy. Consequently, the Office/UNODC strengthened the reliability of ICT operations and established a more robust foundation for future technology decisions.

29F.62 The increasing reliance on digital tools in field operations, combined with rapidly evolving threats, have significantly heightened the exposure of client departments to ICT security risks. Laptops and other computing assets used in decentralized and high-risk environments represent a key area of exposure, with implications for business continuity, data protection and operational resilience. The subprogramme has been implementing a standardized roll-out of ICT security packages to all laptops and computer assets, aligned with Secretariat-wide ICT security policies and delivered through a phased, risk-based approach.
Lessons learned and planned change
29F.63 The lesson for the subprogramme was that early engagement with field locations of client departments and the use of standardized, centrally managed security configurations were essential to ensuring consistency, scalability and sustained adoption. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will further strengthen coordination between Vienna and field locations and prioritize automation and standardization in future roll-out phases of ICT security configurations across all locations. This initiative will strengthen operational resilience, standardize security controls and support secure and reliable ICT operations in field locations to enable programme delivery.

performance.title: Sustained dialogue and continuous regional engagements in West Africa and the Sahel
performance.narrative:
In 2025, in the aftermath of the withdrawal of Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger from ECOWAS, UNOWAS conducted sustained bilateral dialogue with the three countries and with ECOWAS. The mission’s efforts contributed to sustained engagement between the Alliance of the Sahel States (AES) countries and ECOWAS. One example of such engagement was the freezing of the restrictions on free movement of people, goods and services. Moreover, in support of the ECOWAS conflict prevention and peacebuilding mandate, and in line with the UNOWAS-ECOWAS Memorandum of Understanding, UNOWAS participated in ECOWAS-led missions and high-level consultations that contributed to supporting efforts to restore constitutional order in Guinea-Bissau following the coup d’état in November 2025 and easing institutional tensions in Liberia. UNOWAS also pursued engagement with the revitalized African Union Mission for Mali and the Sahel (MISAHEL) towards fostering regional dialogue.

planned.title: conducive environment for peaceful and inclusive electoral processes in West Africa and the Sahel
planned.narrative:
In 2025, the Special Representative sustained engagement with all key political stakeholders to advocate for peaceful and inclusive elections in Cote d'Ivoire. He undertook two missions during which he encouraged dialogue and confidence-building among political actors to strengthen trust in the electoral process and mitigate the risk of violence, which contributed to reinforcing collaboration channels between stakeholders.
In 2027, UNOWAS will conduct technical and high-level missions in countries where elections will take place, including in Nigeria and The Gambia, as well as in countries where key elections are scheduled to take place in 2028, including in Ghana and Sierra Leone.
Lessons learned and planned change
The lesson for the mission was that rebuilding trust among regional stakeholders requires sustained and multilayered engagement. In applying this lesson, the mission will continue to adopt a multilayered approach and work closely with ECOWAS, the AES, and their Member States to encourage continuous dialogue and broadening of communication channels.

In 2025, the Treaty on State Border between the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan and agreements between the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan on “eternal friendship” and the joint border junction, marked major milestones in strengthening regional peace and cooperation. The mission continued its political engagement to support efforts aimed at ensuring the long-term sustainability of the border agreements, should the concerned countries request further assistance. The mission also contributed to strengthened relations between the five countries of the region through convening annual meetings of the Deputy Foreign Ministers of the Central Asian states where information exchange and discussions on regional challenges took place. The mission also provided a platform on issues of shared concerns, including on the impact of the situation in Afghanistan on the region as well as transboundary waters, impact of climate, and women’s and youth engagement.

In 2025, the network placed significant emphasis on smart online search, online monitoring, data management, cybersecurity for early warning systems, and other related areas, all of which contributed to stakeholders’ capacities to address current and emerging risks and threats.

entities.name: Office of the United Nations Representative to the Geneva International Discussions
priorities: Maintenance of international peace and security

overview.name: Office of the United Nations Representative to the Geneva International Discussions
objectives: The objective, to which this mission contributes, is to advance the main agenda items of the Geneva International Discussions, including the non-use of force/international security arrangements and addressing the issue of internally displaced persons and refugees, in the context of the Discussions and the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism.
strategy:
To contribute to the objective, the mission, in close partnership with the other Co-Chairs, will continue efforts to facilitate progress on key agenda items of the Discussions, and ensure that the regular meetings of the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism serve as results-oriented platforms for dialogue and conflict prevention.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
Contributing to the objective of transitioning the Discussions from a conflict management to a conflict transformation and resolution process;
Addressing and making progress on central issues, including the non-use of force/international security arrangements and internally displaced persons and refugees.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
All stakeholders will continue to support the Discussions and the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism and the engagement of the United Nations;
All stakeholders will support efforts to enhance the effectiveness of the Discussions;
The Co-Chairs will continue to collaborate closely to fulfil the mandate of the Discussions.
With regard to cooperation with other entities, the mission coordinates with the European Union and OSCE Co-Chairs. It maintains contact with the European Union Monitoring Mission in Georgia and OSCE, which jointly facilitate the work of the Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism in Ergneti and other relevant actors.
With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the mission cooperates closely with entities within the United Nations system so as to coordinate and strengthen the role and contribution of the United Nations within the framework of the Discussions and the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism, especially in addressing humanitarian issues.
The mission integrates a gender perspective into its activities, including engaging in advocacy for gender equality and promoting the role of women in conflict resolution and peacebuilding, including within the framework of the Co-Chairs’ joint strategy and action plan on women and peace and security.
The mission will closely cooperate with the United Nations Office at Geneva in the implementation of the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy.

performance.title: Continuation of efforts to achieve concrete results on key issues on the agenda of the Geneva International Discussions
performance.narrative:
Three rounds of the Discussions took place in 2025, on 4 and 5 March, 25 and 26 June and 11 and 12 November, respectively. The Co-Chairs organized three visits to Tbilisi, Moscow, Sukhumi and Tskhinvali, as well as Washington D.C., and New York. The Co-Chairs also briefed the OSCE Permanent Council in Vienna on 25 September 2025. In addition to traditional bilateral meetings with participants of the Geneva International Discussions rounds, the Co-Chairs, during the 64th round, conducted an information session on the issues of mobility and freedom of movement, inviting external experts, which was acknowledged by the participants. The mission undertook visits to Tbilisi, Zugdidi, Gali and Sukhumi to engage with relevant actors. Despite the mission’s efforts, no meetings of the Gali Incident Prevention and Response Mechanism took place due to persisting differences among key participants on the modalities. The mission will continue its efforts aimed at resumption of the Mechanism.

performance.title: Optimized damage claims review process for faster servicing of claimants

3.III.11 During 2025, the Office sought ways to increase the efficiency of the claims review process, with the goal of decreasing the number of unprocessed claims more rapidly. In an effort to increase the number of damage claims submitted for the decision of the Board of the Register of Damage each year, the Office, in cooperation with and with the approval of the Board, began enhancement of the eligibility matrix in the in-house database. The new matrix, rolled out in late 2025 for category A (agriculture) claims, facilitated the processing of such claims while upholding the integrity and reliability of the review process. In parallel, and up to the development of the new eligibility matrix, the Office improved the legal assessment process through the use of unified and simplified comment text, which resulted in time savings of approximately 15 minutes per claim.

performance.title: Increased access to rehabilitation support for Palestine refugees with disabilities
performance.narrative:
26.21 Palestine refugees with disabilities face persistent barriers to accessing essential services. Across several UNRWA fields of operation, conflict, displacement and protracted humanitarian crises have led to the widespread loss of equipment and infrastructure critical to daily functioning, with the most severe impacts in Gaza. It is estimated that 83 per cent of persons with disabilities in Gaza lost their assistive devices during displacement. The subprogramme delivers direct rehabilitation services to children and adults with disabilities across UNRWA fields of operation, including the provision of physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, specialized basic and vocational education and shelter modifications. Together, these interventions protect dignity and support the meaningful participation and inclusion of Palestine refugees with disabilities.

In response, the subprogramme has made student retention a core priority and has implemented a range of measures to support learners in completing basic education, including targeted student support, counselling services, subsidized school transportation and regular engagement with parents. Together, these interventions have helped to keep cumulative dropout rates at the elementary level in UNRWA schools relatively low, despite severe operational constraints.

planned.narrative:
26.53 Since 2023, over 430,000 of the 540,000 students previously enrolled in UNRWA schools have had their education disrupted due to conflict, resulting in significant learning loss and an increased risk of dropout. To support the continuity of quality education, particularly in areas most prone to emergencies, the subprogramme in 2023 conducted a needs assessment and developed a plan to enhance learning approaches. Subsequently, the subprogramme introduced blended learning, combining online and in-person pedagogy. In Gaza, where the widespread destruction of school infrastructure has severely limited in-person instruction, an adapted education in emergencies programme has been implemented to ensure that the provision of education, to the maximum extent possible under the circumstances, remains in place. In other fields of operation, blended learning has been enabled through the gradual digitalization of classrooms and the integration of digital tools into teaching and learning processes.
Lessons learned and planned change
26.54 The lesson for the subprogramme was that effective blended learning depends not only on digital infrastructure, but also on teacher capacity, appropriate learning resources and consistent classroom integration. In applying the lesson, the subprogramme will strengthen monitoring of blended learning implementation to assess effectiveness and inform future digital learning initiatives.
